And he and his daughters committed sin upon the earth, such as had not been on the earth since the days of Adam till his time; for the man lay with his daughters.

And, behold, it was commanded and engraven concerning all his seed, on the heavenly tables, to remove them and root them out, and to execute judgment upon them like the judgment of Sodom, and to leave no seed of the man on earth on the day of condemnation. And in this month Abraham moved from Hebron, and departed and dwelt between Kadesh and Shur in the mountains of Gerar.
And in the middle of the fifth month he moved from thence, and dwelt at the Well of the Oath.

And in the middle of the sixth month Yahuah (God) visited Sarah and did to her as He had spoken, and she conceived. And she bare a son in the third month, and in the middle of the month, at the time of which Yahuah (God) had spoken to Abraham, on the festival of the first-fruits of the harvest, Isaac was born.
And Abraham circumcised his son on the eighth day: he was the first that was circumcised according to the covenant which is ordained for ever.
And in the sixth year of the fourth week we came to Abraham, to the Well of the Oath, and we appeared to him as we had told Sarah that we should return to her, and she would have conceived a son.

And we returned in the seventh month, and found Sarah with child before us and we blessed him, and we announced to him all the things which had been decreed concerning him, that he should not die till he should beget six sons more, and should see (them) before he died; but (that) in Isaac should his name and seed be called:

And (that) all the seed of his sons should be nations, and be reckoned with the nations; but from the sons of Isaac one should become a holy seed, and should not be reckoned among the nations. For he should become the portion of the El Elyon (Most High), and all his seed had fallen into the possession of Elohim (God), that it should be to Yahuah (God) a people for (His) possession above all nations and that it should become a kingdom and priests and a holy nation.
And we went our way, and we announced to Sarah all that we had told him, and they both rejoiced with exceeding great joy.

And he built there an altar to Yahuah (God) who had delivered him, and who was making him rejoice in the land of his sojourning, and he celebrated a festival of joy in this month seven days, near the altar which he had built at the Well of the Oath.
And he built booths for himself and for his servants on this festival, and he was the first to celebrate the feast of tabernacles on the earth.

And during these seven days he brought each day to the altar a burnt-offering to Yahuah (God), two oxen, two rams, seven sheep, one he-goat, for a sin-offering, that he might atone thereby for himself and for his seed. And, as a thank-offering, seven rams, seven kids, seven sheep, and seven he-goats, and their fruit-offerings and their drink-offerings; and he burnt all the fat thereof on the altar, a chosen offering to Yahuah (God) for a sweet smelling savour.

And morning and evening he burnt fragrant substances, frankincense and galbanum, and stacte, and nard, and myrrh, and spice, and costum; all these seven he offered, crushed, mixed together in equal parts (and) pure.

And he celebrated this feast during seven days, rejoicing with all his heart and with all his soul, he and all those who were in his house; and there was no stranger with him, nor any that was uncircumcised.

And he blessed his Creator who had created him in his generation, for He had created him according to His good pleasure; for He knew and perceived that from him would arise the plant of righteousness for the eternal generations, and from him a holy seed, so that it should become like Him who had made all things.

And he blessed and rejoiced, and he called the name of this festival the festival of Yahuah (God), a joy acceptable to the El Elyon (Most High) Elohim (God). And we blessed him for ever, and all his seed after him throughout all the generations of the earth, because he celebrated this festival in its season, according to the testimony of the heavenly tables.

For this reason it is ordained on the heavenly tables concerning Yashar’el (Israel), that they shall celebrate the feast of tabernacles seven days with joy, in the seventh month, acceptable before Yahuah (God)–a statute for ever throughout their generations every year.

And to this there is no limit of days; for it is ordained for ever regarding Yashar’el (Israel) that they should celebrate it and dwell in booths, and set wreaths upon their heads, and take leafy boughs, and willows from the brook.

And Abraham took branches of palm trees, and the fruit of goodly trees, and every day going round the altar with the branches seven times a day in the morning, he praised and gave thanks to his Elohim (God) for all things in joy.

chapters.commentary: The chapter handles the Genesis 18–19 material — the angelic visitation at the oak of Mamre, Sarah’s laughter, the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah, the rescue of Lot, and the daughters’ incest in the cave — but the chapter’s center of gravity is what comes next: the birth of Isaac, his circumcision on the eighth day, and Abraham’s institution of the Feast of Tabernacles. A note on the angelic we. Verse 1: we appeared to Abraham, at the oak of Mamre, and we talked with him, and we announced to him that a son would be given to him by Sarah his wife. Jubilees describes the visit from inside the angelic delegation. The reader who has been catechized to read every Old Testament theophany as a Christophany — every appearance of the angel of Yahuah (God) read as a pre-incarnate Yahusha (Jesus) — needs to slow down here and let the text say what it says. Sometimes it is angels. Sometimes it is the Formed one — the Word who became flesh in Yahusha (Jesus) — appearing to the patriarchs in covenant form. Jubilees lets both happen, in different chapters, and does not collapse one into the other. The framework that the formless Father has never appeared and that all Old Testament interactions were the Formed Son in his pre-incarnate office — this framework holds, and it holds in distinction from the angelic delegations that also appeared. Both are real. Both have their offices. The chapter treats them as distinct, and so should we. The Sodom material is brief because Genesis 18–19 is fuller. Jubilees adds verse 8: And he and his daughters committed sin upon the earth, such as had not been on the earth since the days of Adam till his time; for the man lay with his daughters. The chapter does not let Lot off. The Moabites and the Ammonites — descendants of those unions — are named here as a category whose origin is judged from the heavenly tables. Genesis carries this lightly; Jubilees underlines. The chapter’s heart is verses 13–31, the birth of Isaac and the festival that follows. Isaac is born in the third month, in the middle of the month — on the festival of the first-fruits of the harvest, the same Shavuot Abraham keeps in chapter 14, the same Shavuot that goes back to Noah and to creation. The birth of the seed of promise lands on the feast that ratifies the covenant. The text will not let the calendar be a coincidence. The festivals are load-bearing in the architecture of the redemptive history. Then, in the seventh month, Abraham celebrates the feast of tabernacles (verses 20–31). He was the first to celebrate the feast of tabernacles on the earth. The feast is older than Moses, older than the wilderness wanderings the feast will later commemorate. Abraham’s keeping of it is the festival’s first earthly observance, and it is kept for seven days at the Well of the Oath, near the altar he built when Yahuah (God) appeared to him about Isaac. The feast that Christianity has labeled an obsolete Yahudi (Jewish) observance is the feast Abraham kept four hundred years before there was a Yahudi (Jew). The label is wrong. The feast is older than the labels. Verse 17 deserves a slow read: all the seed of his sons should be nations, and be reckoned with the nations; but from the sons of Isaac one should become a holy seed, and should not be reckoned among the nations. The narrowing again. Of Abraham’s sons, only Isaac carries the holy seed. Of Isaac’s sons, only one (the chapter is anticipating Jacob) will continue the line. The other branches of Abraham’s descendants are real, are blessed in their own measure (verse 17: they will be nations), and remain nations — that is, they remain in the third category, not absorbed into the second. The covenant distinction is held with care. Three categories all the way down. Verse 18 names the calling that the holy seed will bear: he should become the portion of the El Elyon (Most High), and all his seed had fallen into the possession of Elohim (God), that it should be to Yahuah (God) a people for (His) possession above all nations and that it should become a kingdom and priests and a holy nation. This is the verse Exodus 19:6 will quote, the verse 1 Peter 2:9 will re-apply to the scattered seed coming home. A kingdom of priests is not a metaphor for the church. It is the specific covenant calling of Yashar’el (Israel) — the firstborn son of Yahuah (God) — to serve as priests to the nations in the millennial reign and forever. Adam was a priest in chapter 3; the line that descends from him narrows through Seth and Enoch and Noah and Abraham and Isaac, and at Sinai the whole nation will be called what Adam was called. The priesthood the church has tried to inherit was always Yashar’el’s (Israel’s), and the recovery of it is what the gathering will produce.

chapters.title: The Departure of Hagar and Ishmael

verses.text: And in the first year of the fifth week Isaac was weaned in this jubilee, and Abraham made a great banquet in the third month, on the day his son Isaac was weaned.
And Ishmael, the son of Hagar, the Egyptian, was before the face of Abraham, his father, in his place, and Abraham rejoiced and blessed Elohim (God) because he had seen his sons

and had not died childless. . And he remembered the words which He had spoken to him on the day on which Lot had parted from him, and he rejoiced because Yahuah (God) had given him seed upon the earth to inherit the earth, and he blessed with all his mouth the Creator of all things.

And Sarah saw Ishmael playing and dancing and Abraham rejoicing with great joy, and she became jealous of Ishmael and said to Abraham, “Cast out this bondwoman and her son; for the son of this bondwoman will not be heir with my son, Isaac.”
And the thing was grievous in Abraham’s sight, because of his maidservant and because of his son, that he should drive them from him.

And Elohim (God) said to Abraham “Let it not be grievous in your sight, because of the child and because of the bondwoman; in all that Sarah has said to you, hearken to her words and do (them); for in Isaac shall your name and seed be called.

But as for the son of this bondwoman I will make him a great nation, because he is of your seed.” And Abraham rose up early in the morning and took bread and a bottle of water, and placed them on the shoulders of Hagar and the child, and sent her away.
And she departed and wandered in the wilderness of Beersheba, and the water in the bottle was spent, and the child thirsted, and was not able to go on, and fell down.

And his mother took him and cast him under an olive tree, and went and sat her down over against him, at the distance of a bow-shot; for she said, “Let me not see the death of my child,” and as she sat she wept.

And an angel of Elohim (God), one of the holy ones, said to her, “Why weep you, Hagar? Arise, take the child, and hold him in your hand; for Elohim (God) has heard your voice, and has seen the child.”

And she opened her eyes, and she saw a well of water, and she went and filled her bottle with water, and she gave her child to drink, and she arose and went towards the wilderness of Paran. And the child grew and became an archer, and Elohim (God) was with him; and his mother took him a wife from among the daughters of Egypt.

And she bare him a son, and he called his name Nebaioth; for she said, “The Yahuah (God) was nigh to me when I called upon him.” And it came to pass in the seventh week, in the first year thereof, in the first month in this jubilee, on the twelfth of this month, there were voices in heaven regarding Abraham, that he was faithful in all that He told him, and that he loved Yahuah (God), and that in every affliction he was faithful.

And the prince Mastêmâ 1 came and said before Elohim (God), “Behold, Abraham loves Isaac his son, and he delights in him above all things else; bid him offer him as a burnt-offering on the altar, and You will see if he will do this command, and You will know if he is faithful in everything wherein You do try him.”

And Yahuah (God) knew that Abraham was faithful in all his afflictions; for He had tried him through his country and with famine, and had tried him with the wealth of kings, and had tried him again through his wife, when she was torn (from him), and with circumcision, and had tried him through Ishmael and Hagar, his maid-servant, when he sent them away. 2 18. And in everything wherein He had tried him, he was found faithful, and his soul was not impatient, and he was not slow to act; for he was faithful and a lover of Yahuah (God).

chapters.commentary: Isaac is weaned. Abraham makes a great banquet. Ishmael — son of the Egyptian maidservant — is playing and dancing before Abraham, and Sarah sees, and her instinct closes around the threat. Cast out this bondwoman and her son; for the son of this bondwoman will not be heir with my son, Isaac. Abraham does not want to do it. The chapter says so: the thing was grievous in Abraham’s sight, because of his maidservant and because of his son. He loves Ishmael. He has watched him grow. He blessed Yahuah (God) when Ishmael was born (verse 2). The chapter is at pains to show the ache Abraham carries when Yahuah (God) instructs him to listen to Sarah. The expulsion is not casual. It costs him. But Yahuah (God) confirms the narrowing: in Isaac shall your name and seed be called. And Yahuah (God) confirms his care for the nation that will descend from Ishmael: as for the son of this bondwoman I will make him a great nation, because he is of your seed. Both are true, and Jubilees (like Genesis) refuses to let either truth cancel the other. The covenant narrows; the Father’s care does not. This is the chapter Galatians 4 will later reach back to in Paul’s allegory of Hagar and Sarah, and the allegory has been weaponized against Torah-keeping for fifteen hundred years. Read the allegory the way Paul wrote it, not the way the antinomian tradition has read it: Hagar represents flesh-based earning — the Judaizer inversion that made circumcision the gate of justification — and Sarah represents promise-based sonship, the order Jubilees 14 established. Cast out the bondwoman means cast out the spirit of flesh-credential earning, not cast out the Torah. Hagar herself is not the Torah; the Torah is Sinai’s gift to a free people, not a flesh-performance system. Paul’s allegory works against the Judaizer inversion of Jubilees 14–15. It does not work against the Torah Jubilees teaches. The angel of Elohim (God) finds Hagar and Ishmael in the wilderness of Beersheba, opens her eyes to the well, and the boy survives. Yahuah (God) is with him. Verse 13: the child grew and became an archer, and Elohim (God) was with him. The Father does not abandon the son outside the covenant. The Father gives him a different inheritance. The chapter closes with Mastema’s proposal. Verse 15: there were voices in heaven regarding Abraham, that he was faithful in all that He told him, and that he loved Yahuah (God), and that in every affliction he was faithful. And the prince Mastema came and said: Behold, Abraham loves Isaac his son, and he delights in him above all things else; bid him offer him as a burnt-offering on the altar, and You will see if he will do this command, and You will know if he is faithful in everything wherein You do try him. The provocation comes from Mastema. The same architecture as Job 1. The Adversary stands before the throne and accuses the righteous; the Father permits the test; the test is real, and the suffering of the tested man is real, but the leash is the Father’s. Verse 17 is the chapter’s quiet correction of every reader who has accused the Old Testament Yahuah (God) of being capricious or cruel: Yahuah (God) knew that Abraham was faithful in all his afflictions; for He had tried him through his country and with famine, and had tried him with the wealth of kings, and had tried him again through his wife, when she was torn (from him), and with circumcision, and had tried him through Ishmael and Hagar, his maid-servant, when he sent them away. Yahuah (God) already knew. The test was not a discovery. The test was a witness — Mastema needed to be put to shame, the heavens needed to see, the man’s faithfulness needed to be made visible. The same logic governs Job. The same logic governs the trials the awakening remnant is presently being walked through. The Father is not learning anything in the test. The Father is making a witness. The chapter is one of the chapters Islam requires the modern reader not to read carefully. Islam's central claim is that the Abrahamic covenant transferred to Ishmael, that the seed of promise runs through the firstborn rather than through the son of Sarah, and that the Yahudim (Jewish) and Christian readings of Isaac as the chosen son are textual corruptions of an originally Ishmaelite covenant tradition. Jubilees 17 forecloses every move in that claim. The chapter is unambiguous about Ishmael's parentage (son of the Egyptian maidservant), about the covenantal status of the maidservant's son (great nation, but not the seed of promise), and about the line through which the covenant continues (in Isaac shall your seed be called). The chapter is also unambiguous about Yahuah (God)'s care for Ishmael. The angel of Elohim (God) finds Hagar in the wilderness, opens her eyes to the well, sustains the child, and keeps him to a great nation in his own land. The Father does not abandon the son outside the covenant. The Father gives him a different inheritance. The Islamic claim that the Yahudi (Jewish) and Christian readings have suppressed Ishmael's covenant standing is contradicted by the chapter's own loving treatment of Ishmael's preservation. The covenant standing is not transferred. The care for the boy is also not withheld. Both registers are held at once, as they always are in the chapters of Jubilees that handle the elect line's narrowing. The chapter's pivot at verses 15–18 is the pivot every reader should attend to with care, because it is the point at which the Mastema architecture enters the patriarchal narrative for the long arc that will dominate the rest of the book. There were voices in heaven regarding Abraham, says verse 15. The voices were vouching for Abraham — declaring his faithfulness in every affliction, his love for Yahuah (God), his standing in every trial. And then, into the courtroom of heaven where these voices have been heard, the prince Mastêmâ came and said the words that would set the binding in motion. The architecture is the architecture of Job 1. The architecture is the architecture of the wilderness temptations of Yahusha (Jesus) in Matthew 4. The accuser stands before the throne where the Father is being praised for his servant, and the accuser proposes a test. The Father permits the test. The test is real. The suffering of the tested servant is real. But the leash is the Father's, the outcome is foreknown, and the witness the test produces is the entire point. This architecture is the corrective the modern reader needs to read the rest of the patriarchal narratives, the wilderness narratives, the prophetic narratives, and the present trials of the awakening remnant correctly. The Father is not the source of the accusation. The Father is not the source of the test. The accuser proposes; the Father permits; the test runs; the witness is produced; the accuser is put to shame. The shape of the architecture is constant from chapter 17 of Jubilees onward, through every trial the chosen body would face. The reader who has been catechized to attribute every trial to the Father's punitive will is reading the wrong attribution. The Father permits. The Father is not the proposer. The accuser proposes, and the Father permits because he knows what the proposal will produce — a witness in the heavens that the accuser cannot recover from. Verse 16: Yahuah (God) knew that Abraham was faithful in all his afflictions; for He had tried him through his country and with famine, and had tried him with the wealth of kings, and had tried him again through his wife, when she was torn (from him), and with circumcision, and had tried him through Ishmael and Hagar, his maid-servant, when he sent them away. The Father had been keeping the running score the entire time. The binding test was not the Father's discovery. The binding test was the Father's answer to the accuser's proposal — the test the accuser had asked for, the test the Father granted, the test the Father knew would silence the accuser permanently in this case.

chapters.title: The Binding of Isaac

verses.text: And Elohim (God) said to him, “Abraham, Abraham”; and he said, “Behold, (here) am I.” . And He said, “Take your beloved son whom you love, (even) Isaac, and go to the high country, and offer him on one of the mountains which I will point out to you.”

And he rose early in the morning and saddled his ass, and took his two young men with him, and Isaac his son, and clave the wood of the burnt-offering, and he went to the place on the third day, and he saw the place afar off.
And he came to a well of water, and he said to his young men, “Abide you here with the ass, and I and the lad shall go (yonder), and when we have worshipped we shall come again to you.”
And he took the wood of the burnt-offering and laid it on Isaac his son, and he took in his hand the fire and the knife, and they went both of them together to that place.
And Isaac said to his father, “Father”; and he said, “Here am I, my son.” And he said to him, “Behold the fire, and the knife, and the wood; but where is the sheep for the burnt-offering, father?”

And he said, “Elohim (God) will provide for himself a sheep for a burnt-offering, my son.” And he drew near to the place of the mount of Elohim (God). And he built an altar, and he placed the wood on the altar, and bound Isaac his son, and placed him on the wood which was upon the altar, and stretched forth his hand to take the knife to slay Isaac his son.
And I stood before him, and before the prince of the Mastêmâ, and Yahuah (God) said, “Bid him not to lay his hand on the lad, nor to do anything to him, for I have shown that he fears Yahuah (God).”
And I called to him from heaven, and said to him: “Abraham, Abraham”; and he was terrified and said: “Behold, (here) am I.”
And I said to him: “Lay not your hand upon the lad, neither do you anything to him; for now I have shown that you fear Yahuah (God), and have not withheld your son, your first-born son, from me.”

And the prince of the Mastêmâ was put to shame; and Abraham lifted up his eyes and looked, and, behold, a single ram caught … by his horns, and Abraham went and took the ram and offered it for a burnt-offering in the stead of his son. And Abraham called that place “The Yahuah (God) has seen,” so that it is said “(in the mount) Yahuah (God) has seen”: that is Mount Sion.

And Yahuah (God) called Abraham by his name a second time from heaven, as he caused us to appear to speak to him in the name of Yahuah (God). And He said: "By Myself have I sworn, says Yahuah (God), Because you have done this thing, And have not withheld your son, your beloved son, from Me, That in blessing I shall bless you And in multiplying I shall multiply your seed As the stars of heaven, And as the sand which is on the seashore. And your seed will inherit the cities of its enemies,

And in your seed will all nations of the earth be blessed; Because you have obeyed My voice, And I have shown to all that you are faithful to Me in all that I have said to you: Go in peace." And Abraham went to his young men, and they arose and went together to Beersheba, and Abraham dwelt by the Well of the Oath.
And he celebrated this festival every year, seven days with joy, and he called it the festival of Yahuah (God) according to the seven days during which he went and returned in peace.
And accordingly has it been ordained and written on the heavenly tables regarding Yashar’el (Israel) and its seed that they should observe this festival seven days with the joy of festival.

chapters.commentary: The chapter is short and almost unbearably weighted. Yahuah (God) calls Abraham — Abraham, Abraham — and Abraham answers. Take your beloved son whom you love, (even) Isaac, and go to the high country, and offer him on one of the mountains which I will point out to you. Abraham rises early in the morning. He saddles the ass. He takes the wood, the fire, the knife. He goes. Three days. The chapter holds the three days the way the text does, without elaboration. The reader who has children does not need help. The reader who has not yet had to hold the unbearable for three days will be helped by the way the text refuses to fill the silence with explanation. He went to the place on the third day, and he saw the place afar off. Isaac asks the question. Behold the fire, and the knife, and the wood; but where is the sheep for the burnt-offering, father? Abraham answers what he believes. Elohim (God) will provide for himself a sheep for a burnt-offering, my son. He does not lie. He states what he is trusting Yahuah (God) to be. The trust is the substance of the test. The altar is built. Isaac is bound. The hand reaches for the knife. And then verse 9: I stood before him, and before the prince of the Mastêmâ, and Yahuah (God) said, “Bid him not to lay his hand on the lad, nor to do anything to him, for I have shown that he fears Yahuah (God).” The angel of the presence is standing on the mountain in the moment of the knife-stroke, and the prince of the Mastema is standing there too — the accuser is at the test he demanded, watching, waiting to see Abraham fail. And the prince of the Mastêmâ was put to shame. This is what the binding accomplishes. The accuser is silenced. The witness is made. The ram caught in the thicket is the substitute Abraham’s faith already trusted Yahuah (God) to provide. Verse 13: Abraham called that place “The Yahuah (God) has seen,” so that it is said “(in the mount) Yahuah (God) has seen”: that is Mount Sion. The tradition Jubilees preserves identifies Moriah with Zion. The mountain of Abraham’s binding is the mountain of Solomon’s temple, the mountain of the prophets, the mountain of the appointed reign. The knife that did not fall on Isaac fell, in the appointed time, on a different beloved son who carried his own wood to a different point of the same mountain range. The foreshadow Jubilees keeps from the Christian commentary tradition is also there in the text — and Jubilees lets it be there without forcing it. The reader who has eyes will see it. The chapter closes with Abraham celebrating this festival every year, seven days with joy, and he called it the festival of Yahuah (God) according to the seven days during which he went and returned in peace. A festival for the binding. Seven days. Joy after the near-loss. The reader who has been told that the festivals are an arbitrary list of Yahudi (Jewish) holidays is meeting them again here as what they are: appointed times Yahuah (God) has anchored to specific acts of his covenant history, kept by the patriarchs before Sinai, kept by the body Yahuah (God) gathered at Sinai, kept by the gathered body at the appointed reign. The festivals are not optional. They are not abolished. They are the rhythm by which the covenant body remembers what the covenant body’s Father has done. The typology the chapter holds without forcing is unmistakable when it is read with the Father's whole architecture in view. The beloved son. The wood the son carries up the mountain. The three days of separation between the calling and the place. The father who knows what is being asked. The willing son who asks the question only once and then submits to being bound. The altar built. The hand raised. The substitute provided at the last moment. The mountain identified as the same mountain on which the substitute will, in the appointed time, be the firstborn Son himself. Every element of the Genesis 22 architecture lines up with every element of the Calvary architecture, point for point, and Jubilees 18 holds the typology even more openly than Genesis does because Jubilees identifies the mountain explicitly as Mount Zion. The Christian commentary tradition has read this chapter for fifteen centuries as the Old Testament foreshadow of the Calvary work. The commentary tradition has been right about the foreshadow. Where the commentary tradition has been wrong is in concluding that the foreshadow obliterates the original. The binding of Isaac is the foreshadow. The binding of Isaac also remains a real event in the patriarchal life, with its own theological work to do that is not collapsed into the work of the antitype. Both stand. The pattern of foreshadow and fulfillment is not a pattern of erasure. The shadow does not vanish when the substance arrives. The shadow continues to be read, kept, remembered, and the festival the patriarch instituted at the end of the chapter continues to be kept by the body that has received both the shadow and its substance. The festival at the chapter's close — seven days with joy, and he called it the festival of Yahuah (God) according to the seven days during which he went and returned in peace — is the pattern Yahuah (God) had been engraving in the patriarchal life from the beginning. Every covenant act gets a festival. Every great act of deliverance gets a memorial calendar appointment. The reader who has been told that the festivals are an arbitrary list of Yahudi (Jewish) holidays disconnected from any theological architecture is meeting the festivals here as what they actually are: the calendar of remembrance Yahuah (God) has built into the year so the body of the seed never forgets what the Father has done. Adam kept his festivals (chapter 3). Noah kept the Feast of Weeks at the rainbow covenant (chapter 6). Abraham kept this seven-day festival at the binding (chapter 18). Isaac will keep his (chapter 22). Jacob will institute the eighth day of Tabernacles at Bethel (chapter 32). The patriarchs are not Sinai-novel observers. The patriarchs are the engravers of the calendar Sinai will later codify, and the codification at Sinai is a re-disclosure to a body that had been in Egypt for four hundred years and had forgotten what their fathers had been keeping. The forgetting is the recurring theme. The recovery is the recurring pattern. The binding ends with the silence of the prince of the Mastema. And the prince of the Mastêmâ was put to shame. The accuser had proposed the test at chapter 17. The accuser had stood at the test, watching, waiting for Abraham to fail. The accuser had to leave the mountain in silence because the man had not failed. The witness was made. The heavens saw. The accuser's tongue was stopped on this case for the rest of the patriarchal narrative — the next time the architecture surfaces, at Job, the same accuser will propose a different test on a different righteous man, and the architecture will run again, with the same outcome. The accuser is permitted his proposals. The accuser is permitted to watch the testing. The accuser is not permitted to write the verdict. The verdict is the Father's. The verdict at chapter 18 was that Abraham feared Yahuah (God) and the line of the seed was secure. The verdict at the cross was that the Son had finished the work and the body of the seed was redeemed. The accuser was put to shame at chapter 18. The accuser was put to shame at Calvary. The accuser will be put to shame finally at the appointed reign and at the seal of Revelation 11. Every test the body of the seed is presently being walked through is one more iteration of the same architecture, with the same outcome, on the way to the same final shaming. The mountain identified at verse 13 — that is Mount Sion — is the chapter's quiet thesis, and the thesis sets up the rest of the redemptive history the book will later trace. The mountain of the binding is the mountain of the temple is the mountain of the Messiah's (Christ's) crucifixion is the mountain of the appointed reign. The geography is one geography. The covenant history is one covenant history. The scattered seed coming home in the present generation is being gathered to a mountain that has held this much for this long, and the recovery of the body to that mountain is what the prophets named.

chapters.title: The Death of Sarah and the Rise of Jacob

verses.text: And in the first year of the first week in the forty-second jubilee, Abraham returned and dwelt opposite Hebron, that is Kirjath Arba, two weeks of years.
And in the first year of the third week of this jubilee the days of the life of Sarah were accomplished, and she died in Hebron.

And Abraham went to mourn over her and bury her, and we tried him to see if his spirit were patient and he were not indignant in the words of his mouth; and he was found patient in this, and was not disturbed.
For in patience of spirit he conversed with the children of Heth, to the intent that they should give him a place in which to bury his dead.

And Yahuah (God) gave him grace before all who saw him, and he besought in gentleness the sons of Heth, and they gave him the land of the double cave over against Mamre, that is Hebron, for four hundred pieces of silver.

And they besought him, saying, “We shall give it to you for nothing”; but he would not take it from their hands for nothing, for he gave the price of the place, the money in full, and he bowed down before them twice; and after this he buried his dead in the double cave. And all the days of the life of Sarah were one hundred and twenty-seven years, that is, two jubilees and four weeks and one year: these are the days of the years of the life of Sarah.
This is the tenth trial wherewith Abraham was tried, and he was found faithful, patient in spirit.

And he said not a single word regarding the rumour in the land how that Elohim (God) had said that He would give it to him and to his seed after him, and he begged a place there to bury his dead; for he was found faithful, and was recorded on the heavenly tables as the friend of Elohim (God). 1 10. And in the fourth year thereof he took a wife for his son Isaac and her name was Rebecca the daughter of Bethuel, the son of Nahor, the brother of Abraham the sister of Laban and daughter of Bethuel; and Bethuel was the son of Mêlcâ, who was the wife of Nahor, the brother of Abraham.

And Abraham took to himself a third wife, and her name was Keturah, from among the daughters of his household servants, for Hagar had died before Sarah. And she bare him six sons, Zimram, and Jokshan, and Medan, and Midian, and Ishbak, and Shuah, in the two weeks of years.

And in the sixth week, in the second year thereof, Rebecca bare to Isaac two sons, Jacob and Esau, and Jacob was a smooth and upright man, and Esau was fierce, a man of the field, and hairy, and Jacob dwelt in tents.

And the youths grew, and Jacob learned to write; but Esau did not learn, for he was a man of the field and a hunter, and he learnt war, and all his deeds were fierce. And Abraham loved Jacob, but Isaac loved Esau.

And Abraham saw the deeds of Esau, and he knew that in Jacob should his name and seed be called; and he called Rebecca and gave commandment regarding Jacob, for he knew that she (too) loved Jacob much more than Esau.

And he said to her: "My daughter, watch over my son Jacob, For he shall be in my stead on the earth, And for a blessing in the midst of the children of men, And for the glory of the whole seed of Shem. For I know that Yahuah (God) will choose him to be a people for possession to Himself, above all peoples that are upon the face of the earth.

And behold, Isaac my son loves Esau more than Jacob, but I see that you truly love Jacob. Add still further to your kindness to him, And let your eyes be upon him in love; For he will be a blessing to us on the earth from henceforth to all generations of the earth. Let your hands be strong And let your heart rejoice in your son Jacob; For I have loved him far beyond all my sons. He will be blessed for ever, And his seed will fill the whole earth. If a man can number the sand of the earth, His seed also will be numbered. And all the blessings wherewith Yahuah (God) has blessed me and my seed shall belong to Jacob and his seed alway.
And in his seed shall my name be blessed, and the name of my fathers, Shem, and Noah, and Enoch, and Mahalalel, and Enos, and Seth, and Adam.

And these shall serve To lay the foundations of the heaven, And to strengthen the earth, And to renew all the luminaries which are in the firmament." And he called Jacob before the eyes of Rebecca his mother, and kissed him, and blessed him, and said:

“Jacob, my beloved son, whom my soul loves, may Elohim (God) bless you from above the firmament, and may He give you all the blessings wherewith He blessed Adam, and Enoch, and Noah, and Shem; and all the things of which He told me, and all the things which He promised to give me, may He cause to cleave to you and to your seed for ever, according to the days of heaven above the earth.
And the spirits of Mastêmâ shall not rule over you or over your seed to turn you from Yahuah (God), who is your Elohim (God) from henceforth for ever.
And may Yahuah Elohim (the LORD God) be a father to you and you the first-born son, and to the people alway. Go in peace, my son.”
And they both went forth together from Abraham. And Rebecca loved Jacob, with all her heart and with all her soul, very much more than Esau; but Isaac loved Esau much more than Jacob.

chapters.commentary: Sarah dies in Hebron and Abraham mourns her, and Jubilees calls the burial his tenth trial. We tried him to see if his spirit were patient and he were not indignant in the words of his mouth; and he was found patient in this, and was not disturbed. The reader who has been catechized to look only for the binding of Isaac as Abraham’s great test is being shown by Jubilees that the trials were many — country, famine, kings, wife, circumcision, Ishmael and Hagar, Isaac, and now the burial of his wife in a land Yahuah (God) had promised but had not yet given. The trials were not climactic. They were distributed across the whole life. The patience required to bury his dead in a foreign field while believing the field would one day belong to his seed is the same patience required of the awakening remnant now, asked to believe the gathering before they see it. Abraham bows twice before the sons of Heth and pays four hundred pieces of silver for a cave. He does not take the land for free, even from men who would give it to him. He buys it. The covenant body’s first foothold in the land of promise is bought and paid for. Then the chapter pivots to Rebecca and the births. Esau and Jacob are born in the sixth week, in the second year, and Jubilees gives the description the rest of the book is going to need. Jacob was a smooth and upright man, and Esau was fierce, a man of the field, and hairy, and Jacob dwelt in tents. Jacob learned to write; but Esau did not learn, for he was a man of the field and a hunter, and he learnt war, and all his deeds were fierce. The chapter is not loading the dice. The chapter is reporting the divergence the heavenly tables already had on them. One son receives the inheritance of Adam, of Enoch, of Noah — the writing, the studying of the fathers’ books, the dwelling in tents like a stranger and a sojourner. The other son receives the field, the bow, the sword. Both are real men. Both will found nations. But the line of the altar continues to narrow inside Isaac’s house the same way it narrowed inside Abraham’s — Isaac not Ishmael, Jacob not Esau — and Jubilees is willing to call the narrowing what it is. Verses 15–31 hand the reader the chapter’s load. Abraham loved Jacob, but Isaac loved Esau. And Abraham — old, near the end, watching his son favor the wrong heir — calls Rebecca and gives her a commission. My daughter, watch over my son Jacob, for he shall be in my stead on the earth, and for a blessing in the midst of the children of men, and for the glory of the whole seed of Shem. The grandfather sees what the father does not see. Yahuah (God) will choose him to be a people for possession to Himself, above all peoples that are upon the face of the earth. The chosen-seed line is asserting itself two generations ahead of the family meeting where it will be ratified. The blessings of Adam, of Enoch, of Noah, of Shem — the line stretching back through the chapter 4 genealogy — are being routed forward through Jacob, and Isaac’s preference for Esau will not stop the routing. Verse 28: the spirits of Mastêmâ shall not rule over you or over your seed to turn you from Yahuah (God), who is your Elohim (God) from henceforth for ever. The architecture from chapter 10 is still in force. Mastema has a leash. Jacob is being placed inside a covenant boundary the Adversary cannot cross. Verse 29 is the chapter’s quiet gravitational pull: may Yahuah Elohim (the LORD God) be a father to you and you the first-born son, and to the people alway. The firstborn-son language Jubilees first used of the seed of Jacob in chapter 2:20 is being applied here to Jacob the man, and through him to the people alway. Jacob is the firstborn. The twelve tribes that descend from him are the firstborn. Yahuah (God) will speak the same word to Pharaoh in Exodus 4:22 — Yashar’el (Israel) is my son, my firstborn — and the prophets will speak it again of the gathered house. The line begun in chapter 4, narrowed through chapter 11, called out of Ur in chapter 12, sealed by covenant in chapter 14, and signed in flesh in chapter 15, here lands on the man whose twelve sons will become the body the rest of the prophets will address. The body the four houses of the foundational lie all deny exists. The body Jubilees will not let be erased.

chapters.title: Abraham’s Last Words

verses.text: And in the forty-second jubilee, in the first year of the seventh week, Abraham called Ishmael, and his twelve sons, and Isaac and his two sons, and the six sons of Keturah, and their sons.

And he commanded them that they should observe the way of Yahuah (God); that they should work righteousness, and love each his neighbour, and act on this manner amongst all men; that they should each so walk with regard to them as to do judgment and righteousness on the earth.

That they should circumcise their sons, according to the covenant which He had made with them, and not deviate to the right hand or the left of all the paths which Yahuah (God) had commanded us; and that we should keep ourselves from all fornication and uncleanness, and renounce from amongst us all fornication and uncleanness.

And if any woman or maid commit fornication amongst you, burn her with fire, and let them not commit fornication with her after their eyes and their heart; and let them not take to themselves wives from the daughters of Canaan; for the seed of Canaan will be rooted out of the land.

And he told them of the judgment of the giants, and the judgment of the Sodomites, how they had been judged on account of their wickedness, and had died on account of their fornication, and uncleanness, and mutual corruption through fornication. “And guard yourselves from all fornication and uncleanness, And from all pollution of sin, Lest you make our name a curse, And your whole life a hissing, And all your sons be destroyed by the sword, And you become accursed like Sodom, And all your remnant as the sons of Gomorrah.
I implore you, my sons, love the Elohim (God) of heaven, And cleave you to all His commandments. And walk not after their idols, and after their uncleannesses,

And make not for yourselves molten or graven gods; For they are vanity, And there is no spirit in them; For they are work of (men’s) hands, And all who trust in them, trust in nothing. Serve them not, nor worship them,

But serve you the El Elyon (Most High) Elohim (God), and worship Him continually: And hope for His countenance always, And work uprightness and righteousness before Him, That He may have pleasure in you and grant you His mercy, And send rain upon you morning and evening, And bless all your works which you have wrought upon the earth, And bless your bread and your water, And bless the fruit of your womb and the fruit of your land, And the herds of your cattle, and the flocks of your sheep.

And you will be for a blessing on the earth, And all nations of the earth will desire you, And bless your sons in my name, That they may be blessed as I am.” And he gave to Ishmael and to his sons, and to the sons of Keturah, gifts, and sent them away from Isaac his son, and he gave everything to Isaac his son. And Ishmael and his sons, and the sons of Keturah and their sons, went together and dwelt from Paran to the entering in of Babylon in all the land which is towards the East facing the desert.
And these mingled with each other, and their name was called Arabs, and Ishmaelites.

chapters.commentary: Abraham assembles them all. Ishmael, and his twelve sons, and Isaac and his two sons, and the six sons of Keturah, and their sons. This is the only chapter in the patriarchal block where the whole family of Abraham is in one place, and Jubilees stages it on purpose. The elect line will narrow at the end of the chapter — gifts to the others, everything to Isaac — but before the narrowing, Abraham speaks one charge to all of them. The chapter is the patriarchal head naming the common inheritance of every line that came from his loins, before naming the specific inheritance of the chosen. The charge is plain. Observe the way of Yahuah (God); work righteousness, love each his neighbour. Circumcise their sons. Refuse fornication and uncleanness. Avoid the daughters of Canaan, because the seed of Canaan will be rooted out of the land. Verse 5 recalls the judgment of the giants and the judgment of the Sodomites — the corruption of the Watchers’ descent and the perversion of Sodom’s destruction — and presses both as warnings to Ishmael’s sons and Keturah’s sons no less than to Isaac’s. The chapter is not softening the standard for the non-elect. The same Torah ethic runs through every branch of Abraham’s line, even the branches that will not carry the priestly office or the holy seed. Verses 7–10 are the chapter’s plain heart. Love the Elohim (God) of heaven, and cleave you to all His commandments. And walk not after their idols, and after their uncleannesses… But serve you the El Elyon (Most High) Elohim (God), and worship Him continually. This is not new instruction. This is the Adamic, Noahide, Abrahamic inheritance Jubilees has been describing since chapter 3. The Torah that will be re-disclosed at Sinai is being given here, in the patriarchal mouth, to a multi-branched family some of whom carry the elect line and some of whom do not. The Adamic standard is not proprietary to Yashar’el (Israel). The Adamic standard is the standard for the sons of Adam, and the sons of Adam are the line this book has been tracking from chapter 4. The third category — the nations — sit under their own intermediate authorities and have not received this charge directly. Abraham’s family is the line of Adam, all of it, and to all of it the charge is the same. Then verse 11: he gave to Ishmael and to his sons, and to the sons of Keturah, gifts, and sent them away from Isaac his son, and he gave everything to Isaac his son. The Father’s care for the nations is real; the elect line’s distinct calling is also real. Both hold. The chapter is neither replacement (the others are erased) nor universalism (the others are equal heirs). The narrowing is in service of a calling — the seed through Isaac is going to become the priestly people who serve Yahuah (God) for the sake of the rest. The nations’ inheritance is real but distinct. Three categories all the way down. Verses 12–13 close with the geography. Ishmael’s sons and Keturah’s sons go east, from Paran to the entering in of Babylon… towards the East facing the desert, and intermingle and become the Arabs and the Ishmaelites. Jubilees is naming the historical body the reader knows by sight. The chapter does not vilify them. They are Abraham’s seed, blessed in their measure, separated to their portion, genuinely loved. They are not the line of the firstborn. Both can be true at once.

chapters.title: Abraham’s Last Words

verses.text: And in the sixth year of the seventh week of this jubilee Abraham called Isaac his son, and commanded him, saying: "I am become old, and. know not the day of my death, and am full of my days.

And behold, I am one hundred and seventy-five years old, and throughout all the days of my life I have remembered Yahuah (God), and sought with all my heart to do His will, and to walk uprightly in all His ways.
My soul has hated idols, (and I have despised those that served them, and I have given my heart and spirit) that I might observe to do the will of Him who created me.

For He is the living Elohim (God), and He is holy and faithful, and He is righteous beyond all, and there is with Him no accepting of (men’s) persons and no accepting of gifts; for Elohim (God) is righteous, and executes judgment on all those who transgress His commandments and despise His covenant.
And do you, my son, observe His commandments and His ordinances and His judgments, and walk not after the abominations and after the graven images and after the molten images.

And eat no blood at all of animals or cattle, or of any bird which flies in the heaven. And if you do slay a victim as an acceptable peace-offering, slay you it, and pour out its blood upon the altar, and all the fat of the offering offer on the altar with fine flour (and the meat-offering) mingled with oil, with its drink-offering–offer them all together on the altar of burnt-offering; it is a sweet savour before Yahuah (God).

And you will offer the fat of the sacrifice of thank-offerings on the fire which is upon the altar, and the fat which is on the belly, and all the fat on the inwards and the two kidneys, and all the fat that is upon them, and upon the loins and liver you shall remove together with the kidneys.
And offer all these for a sweet savour acceptable before Yahuah (God), with its meat-offering and with its drink-offering, for a sweet savour, the bread of the offering to Yahuah (God),

And eat its meat on that day and on the second day, and let not the sun on the second day go down upon it till it is eaten, and let nothing be left over for the third day; for it is not acceptable for it is not approved and let it no longer be eaten, and all who eat thereof will bring sin upon themselves; for thus I have found it written in the books of my forefathers, and in the words of Enoch, and in the words of Noah.

And on all your oblations you shall strew salt, and let not the salt of the covenant be lacking in all your oblations before Yahuah (God). And as regards the wood of the sacrifices, beware lest you bring (other) wood for the altar in addition to these: cypress, dêfrân, sagâd, pine, fir, cedar, savin, palm, olive, myrrh, laurel, and citron, juniper, and balsam.

And of these kinds of wood lay upon the altar under the sacrifice, such as have been tested as to their appearance, and do not lay (thereon) any split or dark wood, (but) hard and clean, without fault, a sound and new growth; and do not lay (thereon) old wood, for its fragrance is gone for there is no longer fragrance in it as before.
Besides these kinds of wood there is none other that you shall place (on the altar), for the fragrance is dispersed, and the smell of its fragrance goes not up to heaven.
Observe this commandment and do it, my son, that you may be upright in all your deeds.

And at all times be clean in your body, and wash yourself with water before you approach to offer on the altar, and wash your hands and your feet before you draw near to the altar; and when you are done sacrificing, wash again your hands and your feet. And let no blood appear upon you nor upon your clothes; be on your guard, my son, against blood, be on your guard exceedingly; cover it with dust.
And do not eat any blood, for it is the soul; eat no blood whatever.

And take no gifts for the blood of man, lest it be shed with impunity, without judgment; for it is the blood that is shed that causes the earth to sin, and the earth cannot be cleansed from the blood of man save by the blood of him who shed it.

And take no present or gift for the blood of man: blood for blood, that you may be accepted before Yahuah (God), the El Elyon (Most High) Elohim (God); for He is the defence of the good: and that you may be preserved from all evil, and that He may save you from every kind of death.. I see, my son, That all the works of the children of men are sin and wickedness, And all their deeds are uncleanness and an abomination and a pollution, And there is no righteousness with them.

Beware, lest you should walk in their ways And tread in their paths, And sin a sin to death before the El Elyon (Most High) Elohim (God). Else He will hide His face from you, And give you back into the hands of your transgression, And root you out of the land, and your seed likewise from under heaven, And your name and your seed will perish from the whole earth.
Turn away from all their deeds and all their uncleanness, And observe the ordinance of the El Elyon (Most High) Elohim (God), And do His will and be upright in all things.

And He will bless you in all your deeds, And will raise up from you the plant of righteousness through all the earth, throughout all generations of the earth, And my name and your name will not be forgotten under heaven for ever.

Go, my son, in peace. May the El Elyon (Most High) Elohim (God), my Elohim (God) and your Elohim (God), strengthen you to do His will, And may He bless all your seed and the residue of your seed for the generations for ever, with all righteous blessings, That you may be a blessing on all the earth." And he went out from him rejoicing.

chapters.commentary: Abraham calls Isaac alone now and pours into him what he could not pour into the assembly of all the sons. The chapter is one long final instruction on sacrifice and the blood, and the modern reader who has been catechized to find Old Testament sacrificial detail tedious or obsolete is the reader the chapter is for. Read it slowly. The handling of an animal life and the handling of human blood are the chapter’s subject because the handling of life and blood is the center of the priestly office Isaac is about to inherit and pass on. Verses 1–4 are Abraham’s confession before he gives the instruction. Throughout all the days of my life I have remembered Yahuah (God), and sought with all my heart to do His will, and to walk uprightly in all His ways. My soul has hated idols… that I might observe to do the will of Him who created me. For He is the living Elohim (God), and He is holy and faithful, and He is righteous beyond all, and there is with Him no accepting of (men’s) persons and no accepting of gifts. The Reformation Christian who reads Old Testament patriarchs as figures who lived under works-righteousness while waiting for the gospel of grace to be preached is reading exactly upside down. Abraham is not bragging. Abraham is testifying. The man whose faith was counted to him for righteousness in chapter 14 is here at the end of his life saying — quietly, factually — that he did the will of his Elohim (God) all his days. Justification by faith and a covenant life of obedient love are not enemies. They are sequence. Abraham preached the sequence in his living, and he is teaching it to his son in his dying. The man counted righteous by faith hated idols, kept the festivals, walked uprightly, and at the end could say so without shame. The instruction proper begins in verse 5. Observe His commandments and His ordinances and His judgments, and walk not after the abominations. Then the specifics. Eat no blood of any creature. Pour the blood of the peace-offering on the altar. Salt every oblation — let not the salt of the covenant be lacking. Use only twelve named woods on the altar (cypress, defrân, sagad, pine, fir, cedar, savin, palm, olive, myrrh, laurel, citron, juniper, balsam — fifteen by Charles’ list, but the principle is what matters). Wash hands and feet before approaching, wash again after sacrificing. Be on your guard, my son, against blood, be on your guard exceedingly; cover it with dust. And then, in verses 19–20, the human blood. Take no gifts for the blood of man, lest it be shed with impunity, without judgment; for it is the blood that is shed that causes the earth to sin, and the earth cannot be cleansed from the blood of man save by the blood of him who shed it. The chapter is naming the moral physics of Genesis 9 — whoso sheds man’s blood, by man shall his blood be shed — and pressing it on Isaac as the foundation of the priestly office. Blood guilt does not fade. It cannot be paid off. It can only be answered by the blood of the shedder, and the cleansing of the land is the body’s responsibility to enforce. Verse 24 is the chapter’s prophetic seam. He will bless you in all your deeds, and will raise up from you the plant of righteousness through all the earth, throughout all generations of the earth, and my name and your name will not be forgotten under heaven for ever. The plant of righteousness is the prophetic phrase that runs through Enoch and Jubilees, naming the elect body Yahuah (God) is growing out of the patriarchs. Isaiah 60:21, Isaiah 61:3, will pick up the same image — the branch of my planting, the work of my hands, that I may be glorified. The plant is a body. The body is the twelve tribes. The chapter is naming what the prophets will later name. Abraham knew. The plant is the people Yahuah (God) gathers out of the families of Adam, through Seth and Enoch and Noah and his own loins, into the firstborn-son body chapter 19 described. The chapter ends with Isaac going out from his father rejoicing. The father has put the priestly office, the sacrificial discipline, the blood ethic, the covenant inheritance into his son’s hand, and the son has received it without reluctance. The transmission Noah made to his sons in chapter 7 is happening again, fathered to son, in the line of the altar that has not stopped narrowing.

chapters.title: Abraham’s Last Words

verses.text: And it came to pass in the first week in the forty-fourth jubilee, in the second year, that is, the year in which Abraham died, that Isaac and Ishmael came from the Well of the Oath to celebrate the feast of weeks–that is, the feast of the first-fruits of the harvest–to Abraham, their father, and Abraham rejoiced because his two sons had come.
For Isaac had many possessions in Beersheba, and Isaac was wont to go and see his possessions and to return to his father.

And in those days Ishmael came to see his father, and they both came together, and Isaac offered a sacrifice for a burnt-offering, and presented it on the altar of his father which he had made in Hebron.

And he offered a thank-offering and made a feast of joy before Ishmael, his brother: and Rebecca made new cakes from the new grain, and gave them to Jacob, her son, to take them to Abraham, his father, from the first-fruits of the land, that he might eat and bless the Creator of all things before he died.
And Isaac, too, sent by the hand of Jacob to Abraham a best thank-offering, that he might eat and drink.

And he ate and drank, and blessed the El Elyon (Most High) Elohim (God), Who has created heaven and earth, Who has made all the fat things of the earth, And given them to the children of men That they might eat and drink and bless their Creator. “And now I give thanks to You, my Elohim (God), because You have caused me to see this day: behold, I am one hundred three score and fifteen years, an old man and full of days, and all my days have been to me peace.
The sword of the adversary has not overcome me in all that You have given me and my children all the days of my life until this day.

My Elohim (God), may Your mercy and Your peace be upon Your servant, and upon the seed of his sons, that they may be to You a chosen nation and an inheritance from amongst all the nations of the earth from henceforth to all the days of the generations of the earth, to all the ages.” And he called Jacob and said My son Jacob, may the Elohim (God) of all bless you and strengthen you to do righteousness, and His will before Him, and may He choose you and your seed that you may become a people for His inheritance according to His will alway. And do you, my son, Jacob, draw near and kiss me."

And he drew near and kissed him, and he said: "Blessed be my son Jacob And all the sons of Elohim (God) El Elyon (Most High), to all the ages: May Elohim (God) give to you a seed of righteousness; And some of your sons may He sanctify in the midst of the whole earth; May nations serve you, And all the nations bow themselves before your seed.
Be strong in the presence of men, And exercise authority over all the seed of Seth. Then your ways and the ways of your sons will be justified, So that they shall become a holy nation.

May the El Elyon (Most High) Elohim (God) give you all the blessings Wherewith he has blessed me And wherewith He blessed Noah and Adam; May they rest on the sacred head of your seed from generation to generation for ever.

And may He cleanse you from all unrighteousness and impurity, That you may be forgiven all (your) transgressions; (and) your sins of ignorance. And may He strengthen you, And bless you. And may you inherit the whole earth,

And may He renew His covenant with you, That you may be to Him a nation for His inheritance for all the ages, And that He may be to you and to your seed a Elohim (God) in truth and righteousness throughout all the days of the earth.

And do you, my son Jacob, remember my words, And observe the commandments of Abraham, your father: Separate yourself from the nations, And eat not with them: And do not according to their works, And become not their associate; For their works are unclean, And all their ways are a pollution and an abomination and uncleanness. They offer their sacrifices to the dead And they worship evil spirits, And they eat over the graves, And all their works are vanity and nothingness.

They have no heart to understand And their eyes do not see what their works are, And how they err in saying to a piece of wood: ‘You are my Elohim (God),’ And to a stone: ‘You are my Yahuah (God) and you are my deliverer.’ And they have no heart.
And as for you, my son Jacob, May the El Elyon (Most High) Elohim (God) help you And the Elohim (God) of heaven bless you And remove you from their uncleanness and from all their error.

Be you ware, my son Jacob, of taking a wife from any seed of the daughters of Canaan; For all his seed is to be rooted out of the earth. 21, For, owing to the transgression of Ham, Canaan erred, And all his seed will be destroyed from off the earth and all the residue thereof, And none springing from him will be saved on the day of judgment.

And as for all the worshippers of idols and the profane (b) There will be no hope for them in the land of the living; (e) And there will be no remembrance of them on the earth; (c) For they will descend into Sheol, (d) And into the place of condemnation will they go, As the children of Sodom were taken away from the earth So will all those who worship idols be taken away. Fear not, my son Jacob, And be not dismayed, O son of Abraham: May the El Elyon (Most High) Elohim (God) preserve you from destruction, And from all the paths of error may He deliver you. This house have I built for myself that I might put my name upon it in the earth: it is given to you and to your seed for ever, and it will be named the house of Abraham; it is given to you and to your seed for ever; for you will build my house and establish my name before Elohim (God) for ever: your seed and your name will stand throughout all generations of the earth." And he ceased commanding him and blessing him. 26: And the two lay together on one bed, and Jacob slept in the bosom of Abraham, his father’s father and he kissed him seven times, and his affection and his heart rejoiced over him.

And he blessed him with all his heart and said: “The El Elyon (Most High) Elohim (God), the Elohim (God) of all, and Creator of all, who brought me forth from Ur of the Chaldees, that He might give me this land to inherit it for ever, and that I might establish a holy seed–blessed be the El Elyon (Most High) for ever.”
And he blessed Jacob and said: “My son, over whom with all my heart and my affection I rejoice, may Your grace and Your mercy be lift up upon him and upon his seed alway.

And do not forsake him, nor set him at nought from henceforth to the days of eternity, and may Your eyes be opened upon him and upon his seed, that You may preserve him, and bless him, and may sanctify him as a nation for Your inheritance;

And bless him with all Your blessings from henceforth to all the days of eternity, and renew Your covenant and Your grace with him and with his seed according to all Your good pleasure to all the generations of the earth.”

chapters.commentary: The Feast of Weeks at Beersheba in Abraham’s last year. Isaac and Ishmael come from the Well of the Oath. Isaac sacrifices at the altar Abraham built in Hebron. Rebecca makes new cakes from the new grain. Jacob brings them to his grandfather as the first-fruits of the land. Abraham eats and drinks and blesses. The chapter is keeping the calendar in its closing scene the same way the calendar has been kept in every closing scene of every patriarch’s life so far. The Feast of Weeks Noah received and lost, Abraham recovered; the Feast of Weeks Abraham now keeps with his sons one last time before he dies. The festival is the rhythm of the covenant body. The festival is what the body comes home to. The festival is what the awakening remnant is recovering now, in this generation, in the second recovery the prophets named. Abraham’s prayer (verses 7–9) is the prayer of an old covenanted man at peace. I am one hundred three score and fifteen years, an old man and full of days, and all my days have been to me peace. The sword of the adversary has not overcome me in all that You have given me and my children all the days of my life until this day. The adversary is named — Mastema, the chapter 10 accuser — and Abraham testifies that the leash held. The Father is asked to extend the same protection to the seed of his sons, that they may be to You a chosen nation and an inheritance from amongst all the nations of the earth from henceforth to all the days of the generations of the earth, to all the ages. This is the Abrahamic prayer the prophets will quote in their own mouths. A chosen nation and an inheritance from amongst all the nations. The body is being prayed for here in distinction from the nations, not in absorption of them. Three categories. Verses 10–24 are the final blessing of Jacob. May the El Elyon (Most High) Elohim (God) give you all the blessings wherewith he has blessed me and wherewith He blessed Noah and Adam. The line of the altar, named back through Noah and Adam, is being closed on Jacob. May He cleanse you from all unrighteousness and impurity, that you may be forgiven all (your) transgressions; (and) your sins of ignorance. The plain prayer of cleansing — older than Levitical sacrifice, older than the priesthood that will mediate it — is here in the patriarch’s mouth at the festival. Verse 16 is the chapter’s hard word, and the chapter does not soften it. Separate yourself from the nations, and eat not with them: and do not according to their works, and become not their associate; for their works are unclean, and all their ways are a pollution and an abomination and uncleanness. Read this in the mouth of Jubilees, not in the mouth of any modern movement borrowing it. Abraham is naming what the seed of Jacob will need to do to keep the line distinct from the cultures that will otherwise absorb them. The Torah’s stranger-and-sojourner provisions remain — the nations who join themselves to the covenant household are loved, sheltered, welcomed, and named in the assembly Exodus 12:38 calls a mixed multitude. But the covenant body is not absorbed into the nations, and the covenant body does not reverse-Christianize itself by adopting the nations’ worship. Eat not with them is the language of separated worship, not of withheld hospitality. The book of Daniel will make the same distinction — Daniel eats vegetables and drinks water rather than the king’s meat and the king’s wine, but Daniel serves Nebuchadnezzar and Belshazzar with utter loyalty. Separate worship; integrated service. The chapter is teaching the patriarch’s sons how to live as a covenant body in the middle of nations that worship other gods, without dissolving into them and without becoming their enemies. The same lesson holds for the scattered seed coming home now. Verses 17–18 name what the nations’ worship is. They offer their sacrifices to the dead and they worship evil spirits, and they eat over the graves… saying to a piece of wood: ‘You are my Elohim (God),’ and to a stone: ‘You are my Yahuah (God) and you are my deliverer.’ Idolatry is not a polite cultural variant. Idolatry is communion with what Jubilees has been calling the unclean spirits since chapter 10 — the disembodied giants of the Watchers’ offspring, the demons under Mastema’s tenth. The prohibition against idolatry is not arbitrary stiffness. It is the protection of the covenant body from the spirits the rest of the world is unknowingly feeding. The reader who has been catechized to read the prohibition against idols as a primitive ethnocentrism is reading without the chapter 10 architecture in view. The prohibition is mercy. Verses 23–24 close with the seed-and-house promise. Fear not, my son Jacob, and be not dismayed, O son of Abraham… This house have I built for myself that I might put my name upon it in the earth: it is given to you and to your seed for ever, and it will be named the house of Abraham; it is given to you and to your seed for ever; for you will build my house and establish my name before Elohim (God) for ever. The chapter’s last image (verses 26–30) is Jacob asleep on Abraham’s bosom, and Abraham kissing him seven times before falling asleep beside him. The grandfather has poured the inheritance into the grandson and gone to bed.

chapters.title: The Death of Abraham and the Days to Come

verses.text: And he placed two fingers of Jacob on his eyes, and he blessed the Elohim (God) of gods, and he covered his face and stretched out his feet and slept the sleep of eternity, and was gathered to his fathers.
And notwithstanding all this Jacob was lying in his bosom, and knew not that Abraham, his father’s father, was dead.
And Jacob awoke from his sleep, and behold Abraham was cold as ice, and he said: “Father, father!”; but there was none that spake, and he knew that he was dead.

And he arose from his bosom and ran and told Rebecca, his mother; and Rebecca went to Isaac in the night and told him; and they went together, and Jacob with them, and a lamp was in his hand, and when they had gone in they found Abraham lying dead.
And Isaac fell on the face of his father, and wept and kissed him.

And the voices were heard in the house of Abraham, and Ishmael his son arose, and went to Abraham his father, and wept over Abraham his father, he and all the house of Abraham, and they wept with a great weeping. And his sons Isaac and Ishmael buried him in the double cave, near Sarah his wife, and they wept for him forty days, all the men of his house, and Isaac and Ishmael, and all their sons, and all the sons of Keturah in their places, and the days of weeping for Abraham were ended.

And he lived three jubilees and four weeks of years, one hundred and seventy-five years, and completed the days of his life, being old and full of days. For the days of the forefathers, of their life, were nineteen jubilees; and after the Flood they began to grow less than nineteen jubilees, and to decrease in jubilees, and to grow old quickly, and to be full of their days by reason of manifold tribulation and the wickedness of their ways, with the exception of Abraham.

For Abraham was perfect in all his deeds with Yahuah (God), and well-pleasing in righteousness all the days of his life; and behold, he did not complete four jubilees in his life, when he had grown old by reason of the wickedness and was full of his days.

And all the generations which will arise from this time until the day of the great judgment will grow old quickly, before they complete two jubilees, and their knowledge will forsake them by reason of their old age and all their knowledge will vanish away.

And in those days, if a man live a jubilee and a half of years, they will say regarding him: “He has lived long, and the greater part of his days are pain and sorrow and tribulation, and there is no peace:

For calamity follows on calamity, and wound on wound, and tribulation on tribulation, and evil tidings on evil tidings, and illness on illness, and all evil judgments such as these, one with another, illness and overthrow, and snow and frost and ice, and fever, and chills, and torpor, and famine, and death, and sword, and captivity, and all kinds of calamities and pains.” And all these will come on an evil generation, which transgresses on the earth: their works are uncleanness and fornication, and pollution and abominations.

Then they will say: “The days of the forefathers were many (even), to a thousand years, and were good; but, behold, the days of our life, if a man has lived many, are three score years and ten, and, if he is strong, four score years, and those evil and there is no peace in the days of this evil generation.”

And in that generation the sons will convict their fathers and their elders of sin and unrighteousness, and of the words of their mouth and the great wickednesses which they perpetrate, and concerning their forsaking the covenant which Yahuah (God) made between them and Him, that they should observe and do all His commandments and His ordinances and all His laws, without departing either to the right hand or to the left.

For all have done evil, and every mouth speaks iniquity and all their works are an uncleanness and an abomination, and all their ways are pollution, uncleanness and destruction. Behold the earth will be destroyed on account of all their works, and there will be no seed of the vine, and no oil; for their works are altogether faithless, and they will all perish together, beasts and cattle and birds, and all the fish of the sea, on account of the children of men.

And they will strive one with another, the young with the old, and the old with the young, the poor with the rich, and the lowly with the great, and the beggar with the prince, on account of the law and the covenant; for they have forgotten commandment, and covenant, and feasts, and months, and Sabbaths, and jubilees, and all judgments.
And they will stand (with bows and) swords and war to turn them back into the way; but they will not return until much blood has been shed on the earth, one by another.

And those who have escaped will not return from their wickedness to the way of righteousness, but they will all exalt themselves to deceit and wealth, that they may each take all that is his neighbour’s, and they will name the great name, but not in truth and not in righteousness, and they will defile the holy of holies with their uncleanness and the corruption of their pollution.

And a great punishment will befall the deeds of this generation from Yahuah (God), and He will give them over to the sword and to judgment and to captivity, and to be plundered and devoured. And He will wake up against them the sinners of the nations, who have neither mercy nor compassion, and who will respect the person of none, neither old nor young, nor any one, for they are more wicked and strong to do evil than all the children of men. And they will use violence against Yashar’el (Israel) and transgression against Jacob, And much blood will be shed upon the earth, And there will be none to gather and none to bury.
In those days they will cry aloud, And call and pray that they may be saved from the hand of the sinners, the nations; But none will be saved.

And the heads of the children will be white with grey hair, And a child of three weeks will appear old like a man of one hundred years, And their stature will be destroyed by tribulation and oppression. And in those days the children will begin to study the laws, And to seek the commandments, And to return to the path of righteousness.

And the days will begin to grow many and increase amongst those children of men, Till their days draw nigh to one thousand years, And to a greater number of years than (before) was the number of the days.
And there will be no old man Nor one who is not satisfied with his days, For all will be (as) children and youths.
And all their days they will complete and live in peace and in joy, And there will be no Satan nor any evil destroyer; For all their days will be days of blessing and healing,

And at that time Yahuah (God) will heal His servants, And they will rise up and see great peace, And drive out their adversaries. And the righteous will see and be thankful, And rejoice with joy for ever and ever, And will see all their judgments and all their curses on their enemies. And their bones will rest in the earth, And their spirits will have much joy, And they will know that it is Yahuah (God) who executes judgment, And shows mercy to hundreds and thousands and to all that love Him. And do you, Moses, write down these words; for thus are they written, and they record (them) on the heavenly tables for a testimony for the generations for ever.

chapters.commentary: The chapter is two halves and the seam between them is the most weighted page in Jubilees so far. The first half (verses 1–8) is Abraham’s death — the patriarch in Jacob’s bosom, the lamp coming in, Isaac falling on his father’s face, the burial in the double cave with Sarah. The second half (verses 9–32) is the prophetic arc from that death through every future failure of Yashar’el (Israel), through the messianic woes, through the renewed study of the law, into the promised reign of the righteous. Jubilees plants the eschatology of the whole book at the moment Abraham dies, because the death of the first patriarch of the covenant body is the moment from which everything that follows must be told. Verses 9–17 register the long decline.
