The days of the forefathers, of their life, were nineteen jubilees; and after the Flood they began to grow less than nineteen jubilees, and to decrease in jubilees, and to grow old quickly… For Abraham was perfect in all his deeds with Yahuah (God)… and behold, he did not complete four jubilees in his life. The decline is moral before it is biological. Their works are uncleanness and fornication, and pollution and abominations. The forgetting that ran through every chapter from chapter 1 — the body forgetting its calendar, its festivals, its sabbaths, its sign of the covenant — is now reported as the cause of the shortening of life itself. The earth wears out under the weight of what its inhabitants have abandoned. Verses 18–25 are the messianic woes. And they will strive one with another, the young with the old, and the old with the young… on account of the law and the covenant; for they have forgotten commandment, and covenant, and feasts, and months, and Sabbaths, and jubilees, and all judgments. The reader who came up in modern Christianity has been taught to look for the tribulation as a single seven-year future block — the Left Behind reading, the dispensational chart, the rapture-then-trouble schedule. Jubilees is not telling that story. Jubilees is telling the story the prophets told plainly: when the body forgets the covenant, the calamities come, the nations rise up, the holy is defiled, the blood is shed. He will wake up against them the sinners of the nations, who have neither mercy nor compassion… and they will use violence against Yashar’el (Israel) and transgression against Jacob, and much blood will be shed upon the earth. The Assyrian exile is in this picture. The Babylonian exile is in this picture. The Roman destruction is in this picture. The pogroms are in this picture. The Holocaust is in this picture. Every wave of violence against the covenant body, scattered or gathered, is what the chapter is saying will be — and was — because the covenant body forgot the covenant. The judgment was not that Yahuah (God) suddenly turned cruel. The judgment was that the body removed itself from under the protection of his covenant and the nations, who have neither mercy nor compassion, did what nations do when there is nothing covering the prey. Verse 26 is the seam. And in those days the children will begin to study the laws, and to seek the commandments, and to return to the path of righteousness. Read this verse slowly. The recovery does not start in the synagogues of the surviving Yahudim (Jews). The recovery does not start in the academies of institutional Christianity. The recovery starts in the children — the next generation, the ones the systems failed — beginning to study the laws, and to seek the commandments, and to return. This is the awakening Jubilees prophesied a hundred and fifty years before Yahusha (Jesus) was born. This is what Hosea 3:5 meant when he said afterward shall the children of Yashar’el (Israel) return, and seek Yahuah (God) their Elohim (God), and David their king; and shall fear Yahuah (God) and his goodness in the latter days. This is the recovery happening now — the scattered seed reaching back across the church’s seventeen centuries of mediation, opening the prophets without the lens, finding the calendar without the liturgical year laid over it, finding the Sabbath without the moved day, finding the festivals without the Christianizing labels, finding their identity as Yashar’el (Israel) without the Hebrew-roots replacement reading or the Christian replacement reading or the rabbinic replacement reading or the Islamic replacement reading. The children are studying the laws. Jubilees called it. Verses 27–31 close with the appointed reign. And the days will begin to grow many and increase amongst those children of men, till their days draw nigh to one thousand years… And there will be no Satan nor any evil destroyer; for all their days will be days of blessing and healing… And the righteous will see and be thankful, and rejoice with joy for ever and ever. The reign is on the earth. The reign is with the gathered righteous body. The reign is the long restoration to the order Adam was given in the garden — long days, peace, the absence of the accuser, the healing of the body. The reader holding a dispensational chart with a rapture, a tribulation, a parenthetical thousand-year reign, and a separate eternal state need not flinch at this chapter; the chapter does not endorse the chart, but it also does not prosecute it. Jubilees is reporting from the heavenly tables the same end the prophets reported from their own visions, with its own emphasis: the body returns, the law is studied, the years lengthen, the accuser is silenced, the bones rest. The reader who has put the chart down and is reading the prophets plainly will find that what Jubilees calls the days of the righteous is what Isaiah 11 calls the day Yahuah (God) sets his hand again to recover the remnant, what Ezekiel 37 calls the joining of the two sticks, what Zechariah 14 calls the day Yahuah (God) reigns over all the earth from Yerushalayim. One reign, many witnesses. Verse 32 is the chapter’s closing instruction to Moses, to write it down — for thus are they written, and they record (them) on the heavenly tables for a testimony for the generations for ever. The testimony is being deposited so the body that scattered will have it when the body comes home. The body is coming home now. The testimony is being read.

chapters.title: Isaac in Gerar and the Selling of the Birthright

verses.text: And it came to pass after the death of Abraham, that Yahuah (God) blessed Isaac his son, and he arose from Hebron and went and dwelt at the Well of the Vision in the first year of the third week of this jubilee, seven years.
And in the first year of the fourth week a famine began in the land, besides the first famine, which had been in the days of Abraham.

And Jacob sod lentil pottage, and Esau came from the field hungry. And he said to Jacob his brother: “Give me of this red pottage.” And Jacob said to him: “Sell to me your primogeniture, this birthright and I will give you bread, and also some of this lentil pottage.”
And Esau said in his heart: “I shall die; of what profit to me is this birthright?” And he said to Jacob: “I give it to you.”
And Jacob said “Swear to me, this day,” and he sware to him.

And Jacob gave his brother Esau bread and pottage, and he ate till he was satisfied, and Esau despised his birthright; for this reason was Esau’s name called Edom, on account of the red pottage which Jacob gave him for his birthright. And Jacob became the elder, and Esau was brought down from his dignity. And the famine was over the land, and Isaac departed to go down into Egypt in the second year of this week, and went to the king of the Philistines to Gerar, to Abimelech.
And Yahuah (God) appeared to him and said to him: “Go not down into Egypt; dwell in the land that I shall tell you of, and sojourn in this land, and I shall be with you and bless you.

For to you and to your seed shall I give all this land, and I shall establish My oath which I sware to Abraham your father, and I shall multiply your seed as the stars of heaven, and shall give to your seed all this land.

And in your seed will all the nations of the earth be blessed, because your father obeyed My voice, and kept My charge and My commandments, and My laws, and My ordinances, and My covenant; and now obey My voice and dwell in this land.” And he dwelt in Gerar three weeks of years.
And Abimelech charged concerning him, and concerning all that was his, saying: “Any man that shall touch him or aught that is his shall surely die.”
And Isaac waxed strong among the Philistines, and he got many possessions, oxen and sheep and camels and asses and a great household.
And he sowed in the land of the Philistines and brought in a hundred-fold, and Isaac became exceedingly great, and the Philistines envied him.

Now all the wells which the servants of Abraham had dug during the life of Abraham, the Philistines had stopped them after the death of Abraham, and filled them with earth. And Abimelech said to Isaac: “Go from us, for you are much mightier than we”; and Isaac departed thence in the first year of the seventh week, and sojourned in the valleys of Gerar.

And they digged again the wells of water which the servants of Abraham, his father, had digged, and which the Philistines had closed after the death of Abraham his father, and he called their names as Abraham his father had named them.

And the servants of Isaac dug a well in the valley, and found living water, and the shepherds of Gerar strove with the shepherds of Isaac, saying: “The water is ours”; and Isaac called the name of the well “Perversity,” because they had been perverse with us.

And they dug a second well, and they strove for that also, and he called its name “Enmity.” And he arose from thence and they digged another well, and for that they strove not, and he called the name of it “Room,” and Isaac said: “Now Yahuah (God) has made room for us, and we have increased in the land.”

And he went up from thence to the Well of the Oath in the first year of the first week in the forty-fourth jubilee. And Yahuah (God) appeared to him that night, on the new moon of the first month, and said to him: “I am the Elohim (God) of Abraham your father; fear not, for I am with you, and shall bless you and shall surely multiply your seed as the sand of the earth, for the sake of Abraham my servant.”
And he built an altar there, which Abraham his father had first built, and he called upon the name of Yahuah (God), and he offered sacrifice to the Elohim (God) of Abraham his father.
And they digged a well and they found living water.

And the servants of Isaac digged another well and did not find water, and they went and told Isaac that they had not found water, and Isaac said: “I have sworn this day to the Philistines and this thing has been announced to us.”

And he called the name of that place the “Well of the Oath”; for there he had sworn to Abimelech and Ahuzzath his friend and Phicol the prefect of his host. And Isaac knew that day that under constraint he had sworn to them to make peace with them. And Isaac on that day cursed the Philistines and said: "Cursed be the Philistines to the day of wrath and indignation from the midst of all nations; may Elohim (God) make them a derision and a curse and an object of wrath and indignation in the hands of the sinners the nations and in the hands of the Kittim.

And whoever escapes the sword of the enemy and the Kittim, may the righteous nation root out in judgment from under heaven; for they will be the enemies and foes of my children throughout their generations upon the earth. And no remnant will be left to them, Nor one that will be saved on the day of the wrath of judgment; For for destruction and rooting out and expulsion from the earth is the whole seed of the Philistines (reserved), And there will no longer be left for these Caphtorim a name or a seed on the earth.

For though he ascend to heaven, Thence will he be brought down, And though he make himself strong on earth, Thence will he be dragged forth, And though he hide himself amongst the nations, Even from thence will he be rooted out; And though he descend into Sheol, There also will his condemnation be great, And there also he will have no peace.

And if he go into captivity, By the hands of those that seek his life will they slay him on the way, And neither name nor seed will be left to him on all the earth; For into eternal malediction will he depart." And thus is it written and engraved concerning him on the heavenly tables, to do to him on the day of judgment, so that he may be rooted out of the earth.

chapters.commentary: The chapter braids two stories that look unrelated and are not. The selling of the birthright (verses 1–7) and Isaac’s sojourn in Gerar (verses 8–27) are joined by what the chapter is teaching about despising what one has been given. Esau despised the birthright. The Philistines stopped Abraham’s wells with earth after he died. Both are the same kind of contempt. The inheritance one has not earned is the inheritance one is most likely to throw away. Esau comes in from the field hungry. Jacob has lentil pottage. Sell to me your primogeniture, this birthright and I will give you bread, and also some of this lentil pottage. And Esau — I shall die; of what profit to me is this birthright? — sells the line of Adam, of Enoch, of Noah, of Shem, of Eber, of Abraham for a bowl of red soup. The chapter does not soften Esau’s sentence. Esau despised his birthright; for this reason was Esau’s name called Edom, on account of the red pottage which Jacob gave him for his birthright. The birthright was not just a property allocation. It was the priestly office, the line of the altar, the covenant inheritance, the firstborn-son standing the chapter 19 blessing has just placed on the older twin. Esau has no use for it. Hebrews 12:16 will name the moment by name — lest there be any fornicator, or profane person, as Esau, who for one morsel of meat sold his birthright — and the chapter agrees: this is profanity. Profanity is treating the holy as not worth the cost of it. The reader who lives in a generation where covenant standing is treated as a label one can pick up and put down at preference is reading Esau’s verdict. Then Gerar. The famine drives Isaac toward Egypt; Yahuah (God) appears and forbids the descent. Dwell in the land that I shall tell you of, and sojourn in this land, and I shall be with you and bless you. Isaac stays. The land is his inheritance and the inheritance must be kept by being lived in. He sows in the year of the famine and reaps a hundredfold (verse 15) — the chapter notes the hundredfold without comment, but the reader who hears the parable of the sower and the seed in Matthew 13 will recognize the line. The covenant body sows in the year of the famine and reaps abundantly because the Father is with the body. Isaac waxes strong. The Philistines envy. Verses 16–20 hand the chapter its other half. All the wells which the servants of Abraham had dug during the life of Abraham, the Philistines had stopped them after the death of Abraham, and filled them with earth. The wells are the chapter’s teaching metaphor. Abraham dug them. The Philistines covered them. Isaac re-digs them and called their names as Abraham his father had named them. The covenant inheritance is recovered the same way: not by inventing new wells, but by re-digging the wells the fathers dug and calling them by the names the fathers gave them. The awakening remnant in this generation is doing this exact work. The Sabbath was a well Adam dug, Noah kept, Abraham kept, Isaac kept, and the church covered with earth. The festivals were wells. The calendar was a well. The reading of Paul as a Torah-observant Israelite of the tribe of Benjamin was a well. The sons are coming back to the covered wells, removing the dirt, and re-naming them by their old names. Isaac’s wells are the awakening’s pattern. Then the new wells. Two are contested. He names them Perversity (Esek) and Enmity (Sitnah). The third is not contested. He names it Room (Rehoboth). Now Yahuah (God) has made room for us, and we have increased in the land. The room comes after the contention. The blessing comes after the patient digging through the contested seasons. There is no shortcut to Rehoboth. The covenant body finds it on the far side of Esek and Sitnah, not instead of them. Verses 28–33 are the chapter’s hardest material. Isaac curses the Philistines — cursed be the Philistines to the day of wrath and indignation from the midst of all nations — and Jubilees engraves the curse on the heavenly tables for execution on the day of judgment. The reader will wince. The wincing is not wrong. The chapter is reporting what was decreed, not modeling a posture for the awakening remnant to take toward their neighbors. The Philistines covered the wells of Abraham. The Philistines stole what they had not dug. The Philistines will, generations later, take the ark and put it before Dagon, and the prophets will name them as a category of accumulated adversaries of the covenant body. The judgment is on the system of the Philistines as a covenant adversary, not on particular Philistine men whom Yahuah (God) does not care about. This is the same distinction the series presses everywhere. Systems are dismantled. People are loved. The chapter is naming the adversary system. The reader gathers the principle without taking up the curse personally.

chapters.title: Rebecca’s Charge to Jacob

verses.text: And in the second year of this week in this jubilee, Rebecca called Jacob her son, and spake to him, saying: “My son, do not take you a wife of the daughters of Canaan, as Esau, your brother, who took him two wives of the daughters of Canaan, and they have embittered my soul with all their unclean deeds: for all their deeds are fornication and lust, and there is no righteousness with them, for (their deeds) are evil.
And I, my son, love you exceedingly, and my heart and my affection bless you every hour of the day and watch of the night.

And now, my son, hearken to my voice, and do the will of your mother, and do not take you a wife of the daughters of this land, but only of the house of my father, and of my father’s kindred. You will take you a wife of the house of my father, and the El Elyon (Most High) Elohim (God) will bless you, and your children will be a righteous generation and a holy seed.”

And then spake Jacob to Rebecca, his mother, and said to her: "Behold, mother, I am nine weeks of years old, and I neither know nor have I touched any woman, nor have I betrothed myself to any, nor even think of taking me a wife of the daughters of Canaan.

For I remember, mother, the words of Abraham, our father, for he commanded me not to take a wife of the daughters of Canaan, but to take me a wife from the seed of my father’s house and from my kindred.

I have heard before that daughters have been born to Laban, your brother, and I have set my heart on them to take a wife from amongst them. And for this reason I have guarded myself in my spirit against sinning or being corrupted in all my ways throughout all the days of my life; for with regard to lust and fornication, Abraham, my father, gave me many commands.

And, despite all that he has commanded me, these two and twenty years my brother has striven with me, and spoken frequently to me and said: ‘My brother, take to wife a sister of my two wives’; but I refuse to do as he has done.

I swear before you, mother, that all the days of my life I will not take me a wife from the daughters of the seed of Canaan, and I will not act wickedly as my brother has done. 19. Fear not, mother; be assured that I shall do your will and walk in uprightness, and not corrupt my ways for ever."

And thereupon she lifted up her face to heaven and extended the fingers of her hands, and opened her mouth and blessed the El Elyon (Most High) Elohim (God), who had created the heaven and the earth, and she gave Him thanks and praise. And she said: “Blessed be Yahuah Elohim (the LORD God), and may His holy name be blessed for ever and ever, who has given me Jacob as a pure son and a holy seed; for He is Your, and Your shall his seed be continually and throughout all the generations for evermore.
Bless him, O Yahuah (God), and place in my mouth the blessing of righteousness, that I may bless him.”

And at that hour, when the spirit of righteousness descended into her mouth, she placed both her hands on the head of Jacob, and said: "Blessed are you, Yahuah (God) of righteousness and Elohim (God) of the ages; And may He bless you beyond all the generations of men. May He give you, my son, the path of righteousness, And reveal righteousness to your seed.

And may He make your sons many during your life, And may they arise according to the number of the months of the year. And may their sons become many and great beyond the stars of heaven, And their numbers be more than the sand of the sea.
And may He give them this goodly land–as He said He would give it to Abraham and to his seed after him alway – And may they hold it as a possession for ever.
And may I see (born) to you, my son, blessed children during my life, And a blessed and holy seed may all your seed be.

And as you have refreshed your mother’s spirit during my life, The womb of her that bare you blesses you, My affection and my breasts bless you And my mouth and my tongue praise you greatly. Increase and spread over the earth, And may your seed be perfect in the joy of heaven and earth for ever; And may your seed rejoice, And on the great day of peace may it have peace.

And may your name and your seed endure to all the ages, And may the El Elyon (Most High) Elohim (God) be their Elohim (God), And may the Elohim (God) of righteousness dwell with them, And by them may His sanctuary be built to all the ages.
Blessed be he that blesses you, And all flesh that curses you falsely may it be cursed."
And she kissed him, and said to him “May Yahuah (God) of the world love you As the heart of your mother and her affection rejoice in you and bless you.” And she ceased from blessing.

chapters.commentary: The chapter is one long mother-and-son scene, and the chapter is in no hurry. Rebecca sees what Esau has done — taken two Canaanite wives, embittered her soul — and she will not let Jacob make the same mistake. Do not take you a wife of the daughters of this land, but only of the house of my father, and of my father’s kindred. The instruction is the same one Abraham gave Isaac in chapter 19, gave Ishmael and Keturah’s sons in chapter 20. The covenant body protects the line by marrying inside it. Not because the daughters of Canaan are beneath them as people, but because the worship of Canaan would be carried into the covenant household by the wife who came from it, and the third generation would be lost. The pattern is the protection. Jacob’s response (verses 4–10) is one of the chapter’s quiet weights. He is nine weeks of years old — sixty-three years — unmarried, untouched, and faithful to the instruction his grandfather and his father have laid on him. I have heard before that daughters have been born to Laban, your brother, and I have set my heart on them to take a wife from amongst them. He has already chosen. The chapter is not staging a moral wrestle here to be resolved. Jacob has been carrying his fathers’ instruction in his body. I swear before you, mother, that all the days of my life I will not take me a wife from the daughters of the seed of Canaan, and I will not act wickedly as my brother has done. The chapter is showing the reader what it looks like for a son of the covenant to absorb the instruction and live it without needing to be re-pressured into it. Then Rebecca’s blessing (verses 11–23). The spirit of righteousness descended into her mouth, and she places her hands on his head and blesses him. The blessing is long and escapes the chapter’s neat summary, but the load is in verses 20–22. Increase and spread over the earth, and may your seed be perfect in the joy of heaven and earth for ever; and may your seed rejoice, and on the great day of peace may it have peace. And may your name and your seed endure to all the ages, and may the El Elyon (Most High) Elohim (God) be their Elohim (God), and may the Elohim (God) of righteousness dwell with them, and by them may His sanctuary be built to all the ages. The great day of peace. This is the same day chapter 23 named as the days of the righteous. This is the day Isaiah 2:4 and Micah 4:3 will name as the day the swords are beaten into plowshares and the spears into pruning hooks. This is the day Zechariah 14 will name as the day Yahuah (God) reigns over all the earth and the nations come up year by year to keep the Feast of Tabernacles. The mother on her knees, blessing the son she has chosen, is praying the gathered-body’s promise into him at the level of his body. By them may His sanctuary be built to all the ages. The temple Solomon will build is contained in this prayer. The temple Ezekiel will see is contained in this prayer. The body the prophets call the holy mountain in the latter days is contained in this prayer. The covenant body’s worship is the sanctuary, and the sanctuary is what the body Yahuah (God) gathers into the appointed reign will keep. The chapter’s posture toward Jacob is the chapter’s posture toward the awakening remnant. The mother who blesses her son does not lecture him about the doctrines he has gotten wrong. She prays into him what Yahuah (God) is going to do through him. She trusts the Father with the unfolding. The reader who is meeting the awakening for the first time and is anxious about the friends and family who have not yet come home can lean on this chapter. Bless them. Trust the Father. The covenant prayer landed on the covenant son. The covenant prayer lands on the covenant body too.

chapters.title: The Blessing of the Firstborn

verses.text: And in the seventh year of this week Isaac called Esau, his elder son, and said to him: “I am old, my son, and behold my eyes are dim in seeing, and I know not the day of my death.

And now take your hunting weapons, your quiver and your bow, and go out to the field, and hunt and catch me (venison), my son, and make me savoury meat, such as my soul loves, and bring it to me that I may eat, and that my soul may bless you before I die.”
But Rebecca heard Isaac speaking to Esau.
And Esau went forth early to the field to hunt and catch and bring home to his father.

And Rebecca called Jacob, her son, and said to him: “Behold, I heard Isaac, your father, speak to Esau, your brother, saying: ‘Hunt for me, and make me savoury meat, and bring (it) to me that I may eat and bless you before Yahuah (God) before I die.’

And now, my son, obey my voice in that which I command you: Go to your flock and fetch me two good kids of the goats, and I will make them savoury meat for your father, such as he loves, and you shall bring (it) to your father that he may eat and bless you before Yahuah (God) before he die, and that you may be blessed.” And Jacob said to Rebecca his mother: “Mother, I shall not withhold anything which my father would eat, and which would please him: only I fear, my mother, that he will recognise my voice and wish to touch me.

And you know that I am smooth, and Esau, my brother, is hairy, and I shall appear before his eyes as an evildoer, and shall do a deed which he had not commanded me, and he will be wroth with me, and I shall bring upon myself a curse, and not a blessing.”
And Rebecca, his mother, said to him: “Upon me be your curse, my son, only obey my voice.”
And Jacob obeyed the voice of Rebecca, his mother, and went and fetched two good and fat kids of the goats, and brought them to his mother, and his mother made them (savoury meat) such as he loved.

And Rebecca took the goodly raiment of Esau, her elder son, which was with her in the house, and she clothed Jacob, her younger son, (with them), and she put the skins of the kids upon his hands and on the exposed parts of his neck. And she gave the meat and the bread which she had prepared into the hand of her son Jacob.
And Jacob went in to his father and said: “I am your son: I have done according as you bade me: arise and sit and eat of that which I have caught, father, that your soul may bless me.”
And Isaac said to his son: “How have you found so quickly, my son?”
And Jacob said: “Because Yahuah (God) your Elohim (God) caused me to find.”
And Isaac said to him: “Come near, that I may feel you, my son, if you are my son Esau or not.” And Jacob went near to Isaac, his father, and he felt him and said:

“The voice is Jacob’s voice, but the hands are the hands of Esau,” and he discerned him not, because it was a dispensation from heaven to remove his power of perception and Isaac discerned not, for his hands were hairy as (his brother) Esau’s, so that he blessed him.
And he said: “Art you my son Esau?” and he said: “I am your son and he said,”Bring near to me that I may eat of that which you have caught, my son, that my soul may bless you."
And he brought near to him, and he did eat, and he brought him wine and he drank.

And Isaac, his father, said to him: “Come near and kiss me, my son.” And he came near and kissed him. And he smelled the smell of his raiment, and he blessed him and said: "Behold, the smell of my son is as the smell of a (full) field which Yahuah (God) has blessed. And may Yahuah (God) give you of the dew of heaven And of the dew of the earth, and plenty of corn and oil: Let nations serve you, And peoples bow down to you.

Be lord over your brethren, And let your mother’s sons bow down to you; And may all the blessings wherewith Yahuah (God) has blessed me and blessed Abraham, my father, Be imparted to you and to your seed for ever Cursed be he that curses you, And blessed be he that blesses you." And it came to pass as soon as Isaac had made an end of blessing his son Jacob, and Jacob had gone forth from Isaac his father he hid himself and Esau, his brother, came in from his hunting.
And he also made savoury meat, and brought (it) to his father, and said to his father: “Let my father arise, and eat of my venison that your soul may bless me.”
And Isaac, his father, said to him: “Who are you?” And he said to him: “I am your first born, your son Esau: I have done as you have commanded me.”

And Isaac was very greatly astonished, and said: “Who is he that has hunted and caught and brought (it) to me, and I have eaten of all before you came, and have blessed him: (and) he shall be blessed, and all his seed for ever.”

And it came to pass when Esau heard the words of his father Isaac that he cried with an exceeding great and bitter cry, and said to his father: “Bless me, (even) me also, father.” And he said to him: “Your brother came with guile, and has taken away your blessing.” And he said: “Now I know why his name is named Jacob: behold, he has supplanted me these two times: he took away my birth-right, and now he has taken away my blessing.”

And he said: “Have you not reserved a blessing for me, father?” and Isaac answered and said to Esau: “Behold, I have made him your lord, And all his brethren have I given to him for servants, And with plenty of com and wine and oil have I strengthened him: And what now shall I do for you, my son?” And Esau said to Isaac, his father: “Have you but one blessing, O father? Bless me, (even) me also, father”: And Esau lifted up his voice and wept.
And Isaac answered and said to him: “Behold, far from the dew of the earth shall be your dwelling, And far from the dew of heaven from above.

And by your sword will you live, And you will serve your brother. And it shall come to pass when you become great, And do shake his yoke from off your neck, You will sin a complete sin to death, And your seed will be rooted out from under heaven.” And Esau kept threatening Jacob because of the blessing wherewith his father blessed him, and he said in his heart: “May the days of mourning for my father now come, so that I may slay my brother Jacob.”

chapters.commentary: The deception scene, told in Jubilees with the same weight Genesis gives it, but with one detail Genesis does not press. He discerned him not, because it was a dispensation from heaven to remove his power of perception. The blindness was not failure of Isaac’s senses. The blindness was a heavenly act. The blessing was being routed where it had to go, and the path of routing was through the mother’s plan and the son’s smooth neck and the hairy gloves she wrapped him in. This is the chapter the inherited Christian commentary tradition has the hardest time with. Jacob lies. Rebecca conspires. Together they steal a blessing from a blind father who is not in on the plan. The Sunday school version sometimes tries to clean this up. The cleaning is wrong. The chapter is not saying Jacob was without sin in this. The chapter is saying that the blessing was always going to land on him because the heavenly tables had it on them already, and the means by which it landed were the means available in a household where the father loved the wrong son and would not let go of him. Yahuah (God)’s sovereignty threads through human moral ambiguity, and the chapter does not hide either. Jacob will limp out of Peniel later for a reason. The means do not become righteous because the end was decreed. Jacob carries the consequence of his deception in his body and in his life — twenty years of Laban’s deceptions, the deception of Joseph’s brothers, the years of mourning a son he believes is dead — and Yahuah (God) walks him through every layer of it. The chapter is teaching the reader to hold both: the decree was firm; the manner was costly. Verses 22–24 are the blessing itself, and the chapter records that Isaac smelled Esau’s raiment on Jacob and said: Behold, the smell of my son is as the smell of a (full) field which Yahuah (God) has blessed. The covenant body is named a field which Yahuah (God) has blessed. The same metaphor will run through the prophets — the vineyard, the field, the planting, the orchard. The body is being grown by the Father, watered by his rain, increased by his sun. The blessing then names the substance: let nations serve you, and peoples bow down to you. Be lord over your brethren, and let your mother’s sons bow down to you; and may all the blessings wherewith Yahuah (God) has blessed me and blessed Abraham, my father, be imparted to you and to your seed for ever. The Abrahamic deposit, the Adamic deposit, the Noahide deposit — passed down again, sealed on Jacob. Esau’s bitter cry in verses 29–33 is the chapter’s most unbearable scene. Bless me, even me also, father. He weeps. He gets a blessing — by your sword will you live, and you will serve your brother — but the blessing he wants is gone. The chapter is unmoved. He has supplanted me these two times: he took away my birth-right, and now he has taken away my blessing. And then verse 34’s prophetic addendum: and it shall come to pass when you become great, and do shake his yoke from off your neck, you will sin a complete sin to death, and your seed will be rooted out from under heaven. The Edomite line will rise. The Edomites and the Idumeans will play their roles in the generations to come. They will reach into the second temple period under Herod, the Idumean king who slaughtered the children of Bethlehem in Matthew 2 — Esau’s seed throwing off Jacob’s yoke and reaching at the new-born Messiah (Christ) himself. The chapter saw it. The chapter named it. Edom in Jubilees is the same Edom in Obadiah, and the same Edom in Ezekiel 35, and the same Edom in Malachi 1. The pattern is consistent. The chapter ends with Esau threatening Jacob and Jacob having to flee. The blessing has landed; the cost is now beginning to be paid. The covenant body’s calling has never been free of cost.

chapters.title: Jacob’s Ladder at Bethel

verses.text: And the words of Esau, her elder son, were told to Rebecca in a dream, and Rebecca sent and called Jacob her younger son, and said to him:
“Behold Esau your brother will take vengeance on you so as to kill you.

Now, therefore, my son, obey my voice, and arise and flee you to Laban, my brother, to Haran, and tarry with him a few days until your brother’s anger turns away, and he remove his anger from you, and forget all that you have done; then I will send and fetch you from thence.”
And Jacob said: “I am not afraid; if he wishes to kill me, I will kill him.”
But she said to him: “Let me not be bereft of both my sons on one day.”

And Jacob said to Rebecca his mother: “Behold, you know that my father has become old, and does not see because his eyes are dull, and if I leave him it will be evil in his eyes, because I leave him and go away from you, and my father will be angry, and will curse me. I will not go; when he sends me, then only will I go.” And Rebecca said to Jacob: “I will go in and speak to him, and he will send you away.”

And Rebecca went in and said to Isaac: “I loathe my life because of the two daughters of Heth, whom Esau has taken him as wives; and if Jacob take a wife from among the daughters of the land such as these, for what purpose do I further live; for the daughters of Canaan are evil.”
And Isaac called Jacob and blessed him, and admonished him and said to him:

“Do not take you a wife of any of the daughters of Canaan; arise and go to Mesopotamia, to the house of Bethuel, your mother’s father, and take you a wife from thence of the daughters of Laban, your mother’s brother.

And El Shaddai (God Almighty) bless you and increase and multiply you that you may become a company of nations, and give you the blessings of my father Abraham, to you and to your seed after you, that you may inherit the land of your sojournings and all the land which Elohim (God) gave to Abraham: go, my son, in peace.” And Isaac sent Jacob away, and he went to Mesopotamia, to Laban the son of Bethuel the Syrian, the brother of Rebecca, Jacob’s mother.
And it came to pass after Jacob had arisen to go to Mesopotamia that the spirit of Rebecca was grieved after her son, and she wept.
And Isaac said to Rebecca: "My sister, weep not on account of Jacob, my son; for he goes in peace, and in peace will he return.
The El Elyon (Most High) Elohim (God) will preserve him from all evil, and will be with him; for He will not forsake him all his days;

For I know that his ways will be prospered in all things wherever he goes, until he return in peace to us, and we see him in peace. Fear not on his account my sister, for he is on the upright path and he is a perfect man: and he is faithful and will not perish. Weep not."
And Isaac comforted Rebecca on account of her son Jacob, and blessed him.

And Jacob went from the Well of the Oath to go to Haran on the first year of the second week in the forty-fourth Jubilee, and he came to Luz on the mountains, that is, Bethel, on the new moon of the first month of this week, and he came to the place at even and turned from the way to the west of the road that night: and he slept there; for the sun had set.
And he took one of the stones of that place and laid it (at his head) under the tree, and he was journeying alone, and he slept.

And he dreamt that night, and behold a ladder set up on the earth, and the top of it reached to heaven, and behold, the angels of Yahuah (God) ascended and descended on it: and behold, Yahuah (God) stood upon it. And He spake to Jacob and said: “I am Yahuah Elohim (the LORD God) of Abraham, your father, and the Elohim (God) of Isaac; the land whereon you are sleeping, to you shall I give it, and to your-seed after you.

And your seed will be as the dust of the earth, and you will increase to the west and to the east, to the north and the south, and in you and in your seed will all the families of the nations be blessed.
And behold, I shall be with you, and shall keep you whithersoever you go, and I shall bring you again into this land in peace; for I shall not leave you until I do everything that I told you of.”

And Jacob awoke from his sleep, and said, “Truly this place is the house of Yahuah (God), and I knew it not.” And he was afraid and said:" Dreadful is this place which is none other than the house of Elohim (God), and this is the gate of heaven."

And Jacob arose early in the morning, and took the stone which he had put under his head and set it up as a pillar for a sign, and he poured oil upon the top of it. And he called the name of that place Bethel; but the name of the place was Luz at the first. And Jacob vowed a vow to Yahuah (God), saying: “If Yahuah (God) will be with me, and will keep me in this way that I go, and give me bread to eat and raiment to put on, so that I come again to my father’s house in peace, then shall Yahuah (God) be my Elohim (God), and this stone which I have set up as a pillar for a sign in this place, shall be Yahuah (God)’s house, and of all that you give me, I shall give the tenth to you, my Elohim (God).”

chapters.commentary: The chapter is short and the chapter is famous. The reader has seen the picture in catechism books — angels going up and down a ladder, Jacob asleep on a stone, the heavens open. The chapter is asking the reader to slow down and read it as Jubilees has taught the reader to read so far: the heavens are not just open. The heavens are populated. The angels are not decorative attendants on a vision; they are the same angelic body that has been narrating Jubilees from chapter 1 — the angels of the presence, the angels of sanctification, the holy ones who keep the sabbath in heaven. They are coming down and going up because the ladder is the route of communication between the heavenly tables and the man Yahuah (God) has chosen to write his promise into. Jacob is being shown the architecture. And behold, Yahuah (God) stood upon it. The Formed one — the Word who walked with Adam, who closed the door of the ark, who appeared at Mamre, who wrestled at Peniel, who came in flesh in Yahusha (Jesus) — stands at the top of the ladder, and the covenant promise is renewed in the same form it was given to Abraham and to Isaac. I am Yahuah Elohim (the LORD God) of Abraham, your father, and the Elohim (God) of Isaac. The same name. The same line. The land whereon you are sleeping, to you shall I give it, and to your seed after you. And your seed will be as the dust of the earth, and you will increase to the west and to the east, to the north and the south, and in you and in your seed will all the families of the nations be blessed. That last clause — in you and in your seed will all the families of the nations be blessed — is the verse the inherited Christian reading has been mining since Constantine. The reading goes: the nations are blessed by being absorbed into the seed, and the absorption is what grafted in means in Romans 11. That reading is wrong, and Jubilees has been correcting it since chapter 9. The nations are blessed because of the seed — through the seed’s witness, through the seed’s priestly office, through the seed’s mediation of the Father’s character to the families that are not the seed. The blessing flows. It does not assimilate. The natural branches and the wild olive branches of Romans 11 are both Yashar’el (Israel) — the covenant body that retained identity and the scattered seed that grew wild in exile — being reattached to their natural root. The nations remain the nations, blessed and welcomed and loved as the stranger and the sojourner, not absorbed into the body the seed of Jacob will become. The promise to Jacob preserves both realities the way every Abrahamic and Isaacian and Jacobian promise has preserved both: the seed becomes a people, and the people are a blessing to the families of the earth without becoming the families of the earth. Jacob wakes. Truly this place is the house of Yahuah (God), and I knew it not. He pours oil on the stone. He calls the place Bethel — house of Elohim (God). He vows the tithe. If Yahuah (God) will be with me… then shall Yahuah (God) be my Elohim (God)… and of all that you give me, I shall give the tenth to you, my Elohim (God). The tithe is older than Levi. The chapter 13 priest of El Elyon (Most High) received the tithe from Abraham; here Jacob vows it again at Bethel before there is a tribe of Levi to receive it. The institution of the tithe will be ratified at Sinai through the Levites in Numbers 18; the pattern of the tithe is here, with the patriarch on the road, naming the rock that became the gate of heaven and pouring oil on it. Worship is older than the temple. Worship was always older than the temple. The figure standing on the ladder rewards the careful naming the rest of Jubilees has been preparing the reader for. Yahuah (God) is on the ladder. Yahuah (God) is also the formless source from which all things proceed, the infinite the eye cannot see, the one whom no man has seen at any time. Both registers are true, and both registers are required, and the ladder at Bethel is the chapter that holds the two together more openly than almost any other chapter in the book. The Father — the formless infinite — has never been seen, and yet Yahuah (God) stood upon it. The standing one is the formed expression of the formless, the Word who walked in the cool of the day with Adam in chapter 3, who closed the door of the ark in chapter 5, who appeared at the oak of Mamre in chapter 16, who would later wrestle with Jacob himself at Peniel and would in the appointed time come in flesh in Yahusha (Jesus). The ladder is the architecture by which the formed one descends to renew the covenant promise to the patriarch, and the angels going up and down are not decorative — they are the active body of the heavenly host moving on the appointed traffic between the Father's throne and the man on the stone. The ladder is the architecture every covenant communication has run on since the beginning. The architecture has not been retired. The architecture has been clarified in the body of the Messiah (Christ) who later said, truly I say to you, hereafter you shall see heaven open, and the angels of Elohim (God) ascending and descending upon the Son of man (John 1:51) — the Son who is, in his own person, the new Bethel, the gate of heaven, the place where the formed one stands and the angels do their appointed work. The anointing of the stone in the morning is the first oil-anointing recorded in scripture, and it sets the template for everything that follows. The patriarch takes the stone he has slept on, sets it up as a pillar, and pours oil on its top. The act is the act of consecration. The stone becomes the marker of the place where heaven was open, the place where the formed one stood, the place to which the patriarch will return at chapter 32 to keep the festival the heavenly tables had appointed. The anointing of stones, of pillars, of priests, of kings, of the head of the suffering servant in the gospel — all of it runs back to this moment. Jacob did not invent the anointing. The anointing is given to him to give to the body. The body that pours the oil is consecrating the place to the Father, naming the place as the Father's house, marking it for return. Bethel is not a one-time vision. Bethel is the place to come back to, and the patriarch will come back, and the body of Yashar'el (Israel) coming home in the present generation is, in its own way, returning to the same Bethel — the house of Elohim (God), the place where the formed one stands at the top of the ladder, the place where the angels are still moving on the same traffic. The vow Jacob makes at the chapter's close is the architecture of patriarchal covenant the body of the seed has carried forward in every generation since. If Yahuah (God) will be with me... then shall Yahuah (God) be my Elohim (God)... and of all that you give me, I shall give the tenth to you, my Elohim (God). The vow is conditional in form, but the form is the form of patriarchal covenant — a recognition that the covenant is initiated by the Father and the patriarch's appropriate response is to enter the covenant by oath, to commit to the relationship by name, and to seal the commitment by the tithe. The tithe is older than Levi. The tithe was given by Abram to the priest of the El Elyon (Most High) at chapter 13. The tithe is given again here by Jacob, before there is a tribe of Levi to receive it, before there is a tabernacle to bring it to. The tithe is the patriarch's recognition that the substance he is being given belongs first to the Father, and the proportion that returns to the Father is the proportion that confesses the patriarch's understanding of the gift. The institution of the tithe at Sinai through the Levites in Numbers 18 is the ratification of a pattern that is already running in the patriarchal household. Worship was older than the temple. The tithe was older than the priesthood. Both were given to the household head, to be kept in the household, until the body had grown large enough to need a centralized priesthood and a centralized place of altar. After the temple's destruction, both return to the household where they began.

chapters.title: Jacob in Mesopotamia

verses.text: And he went on his journey, and came to the land of the east, to Laban, the brother of Rebecca, and he was with him, and served him for Rachel his daughter one week.
And in the first year of the third week he said to him: “Give me my wife, for whom I have served you seven years;” and Laban said to Jacob. “I will give you your wife.”

And Laban made a feast, and took Leah his elder daughter, and gave (her) to Jacob as a wife, and gave her Zilpah his handmaid for an handmaid; and Jacob did not know, for he thought that she was Rachel.

And he went in to her, and behold, she was Leah; and Jacob was angry with Laban, and said to him: “Why have you dealt thus with me? Did not I serve you for Rachel and not for Leah? Why have you wronged me? Take your daughter, and I will go; for you have done evil to me.”
For Jacob loved Rachel more than Leah; for Leah’s eyes were weak, but her form was very handsome; but Rachel had beautiful eyes and a beautiful and very handsome form.

And Laban said to Jacob: “It is not so done in our country, to give the younger before the elder.” And it is not right to do this; for thus it is ordained and written in the heavenly tables, that no one should give his younger daughter before the elder–but the elder one gives first and after her the younger–and the man who does so, they set down guilt against him in heaven, and none is righteous that does this thing, for this deed is evil before Yahuah (God). And command you the children of Yashar’el (Israel) that they do not this thing; let them neither take nor give the younger before they have given the elder, for it is very wicked.

And Laban said to Jacob: “Let the seven days of the feast of this one pass by, and I shall give you Rachel, that you may serve me another seven years, that you may pasture my sheep as you did in the former week.”

And on the day when the seven days of the feast of Leah had passed, Laban gave Rachel to Jacob, that he might serve him another seven years, and he gave to Rachel Bilhah, the sister of Zilpah as a handmaid.
And he served yet other seven years for Rachel, for Leah had been given to him for nothing.

And Yahuah (God) opened the womb of Leah, and she conceived and bare Jacob a son, and he called his name Reuben, on the fourteenth day of the ninth month, in the first year of the third week. But the womb of Rachel was closed, for Yahuah (God) saw that Leah was hated and Rachel loved.
And again Jacob went in to Leah, and she conceived, and bare Jacob a second son, and he called his name Simeon, on the twenty-first of the tenth month, and in the third year of this week.

And again Jacob went in to Leah, and she conceived, and bare him a third son, and he called his name Levi, in the new moon of the first month in the sixth year of this week. And again Jacob went in to her, and she conceived, and bare him a fourth son, and he called his name Yahudah (Judah), on the fifteenth of the third month, in the first year of the fourth week.

And on account of all this Rachel envied Leah, for she did not bear, and she said to Jacob: “Give me children”; and Jacob said: “Have I withheld from you the fruits of your womb? Have I forsaken you?”

And when Rachel saw that Leah had borne four sons to Jacob, Reuben and Simeon and Levi and Yahudah (Judah), she said to him: “Go in to Bilhah my handmaid, and she will conceive, and bear a son to me.”

(And she gave (him) Bilhah her handmaid to wife.) And he went in to her, and she conceived, and bare him a son, and he called his name Dan, on the ninth of the sixth month, in the sixth year of the third week.

And Jacob went in again to Bilhah a second time, and she conceived, and bare Jacob another son, and Rachel called his name Naphtali, on the fifth of the seventh month, in the second year of the fourth week. And when Leah saw that she had become sterile and did not bear, she envied (Rachel) and she also gave her handmaid Zilpah to Jacob to wife, and she conceived, and bare a son, and Leah called his name Gad, on the twelfth of the eighth month, in the third year of the fourth week.
And he went in again to her, and she conceived, and bare him a second son, and Leah called his name Asher, on the second of the eleventh month, in the fifth year of the fourth week.
And Jacob went in to Leah, and she conceived, and bare a son, and she called his name Issachar, on the fourth of the fifth month, in the fourth year of the fourth week, and she gave him to a nurse.

And Jacob went in again to her, and she conceived, and bare two (children), a son and a daughter, and she called the name of the son Zebulon, and the name of the daughter Dinah, in the seventh of the seventh month, in the sixth year of the fourth week.

And Yahuah (God) was gracious to Rachel, and opened her womb, and she conceived, and bare a son, and she called his name Joseph, on the new moon of the fourth month, in the sixth year in this fourth week. And in the days when Joseph was born, Jacob said to Laban: “Give me my wives and sons, and let me go to my father Isaac, and let me make me an house; for I have completed the years in which I have served you for your two daughters, and I will go to the house of my father.”
And Laban said to Jacob: “Tarry with me for your wages 1, and pasture my flock for me again, and take your wages.”
And they agreed with one another that he should give him as his wages those of the lambs and kids which were born black and spotted and white, 2 (these) were to be his wages.

And all the sheep brought forth spotted and speckled and black, variously marked, 3 and they brought forth again lambs like themselves, and all that were spotted were Jacob’s and those which were not were Laban’s.

And Jacob’s possessions multiplied exceedingly, and he possessed oxen and sheep 4 and asses and camels, and menservants and maidservants. And Laban and his sons envied Jacob, and Laban took back his sheep from him, and he observed him with evil intent.

chapters.commentary: The chapter is long because it is a household. Jacob serves seven years for Rachel, is given Leah, serves another seven for Rachel, and the children begin to come. The chapter records each birth with date and month — Reuben on the fourteenth of the ninth month, Simeon on the twenty-first of the tenth, Levi at the new moon of the first month, Yahudah (Judah) on the fifteenth of the third month. The chapter’s calendar precision is doing work the reader should not skim past. The twelve sons of the covenant body are born inside the calendar Jubilees has taught from chapter 6. Their births are not generic. They are dated. They are anchored. The body is being assembled month by month, on the year-of-the-jubilee track that is engraved on the heavenly tables. Verses 6–7 hand the reader Jubilees’ commentary on Laban’s deception. It is not so done in our country, to give the younger before the elder. And it is not right to do this; for thus it is ordained and written in the heavenly tables, that no one should give his younger daughter before the elder. Laban claims the custom; the heavenly tables endorse the custom. The chapter is not taking Laban’s side against Jacob — Laban is going to be exposed as the deceiver he is in chapter 29 — but the chapter is admitting that on this one point Laban has the law on his side. Jacob, who supplanted his elder brother for the blessing, now finds himself supplanted by an elder sister he did not ask for. The chapter is reporting the moral physics: the deception you performed in your father’s tent will be performed on you in your uncle’s tent, and Yahuah (God) does not let his men move past their patterns without facing them. Jacob’s seven extra years for Rachel are the price of Esau’s stolen birthright, paid in another man’s currency. Leah is hated, and Yahuah (God) opens her womb. Rachel is loved and barren. The chapter holds the disparity without softening it. Rachel envies. Leah envies. The handmaids are pulled into the production. The four mothers of the twelve sons — Leah, Rachel, Bilhah, Zilpah — are not equally loved by Jacob, but the twelve sons are equally Yashar’el (Israel). The covenant body is not born from a pristine household. The covenant body is born from the realest possible household — favoritism, jealousy, deception, desperation, and over all of it the patient hand of Yahuah (God) opening wombs and giving children. The reader who comes from a household less than tidy is being told by this chapter that the twelve tribes did too. The patriarchal narratives do not airbrush. By the end of the chapter Jacob has six sons and a daughter from Leah, two sons from Bilhah, two from Zilpah, and Joseph from Rachel. Eleven sons; the twelfth, Benjamin, will come in chapter 32 with Rachel’s death. Jacob is rich in flocks. Laban’s eyes have darkened. The chapter ends on the coiled spring that chapter 29 will release. The calendar precision the chapter brings to the births of the twelve sons rewards an even slower read than the existing commentary has given it. Reuben on the fourteenth of the ninth month. Simeon on the twenty-first of the tenth. Levi at the new moon of the first month. Yahudah (Judah) on the fifteenth of the third month. Each birth is dated. Each birth lands on a specific day of a specific month in a specific year of a specific week of a specific jubilee. The chapter is not interested in the birthday cake. The chapter is interested in the architecture. The covenant body that will become the twelve tribes of Yashar'el (Israel) is being assembled in time, on the calendar engraved on the heavenly tables, with each member of the body anchored to a date the heavenly record knows precisely. The Father is not assembling his covenant body at random. The Father is assembling his covenant body on the appointed times. The births of the twelve are themselves a calendar, and the calendar is the calendar Jubilees 6 had taught — the same three-hundred-and-sixty-four-day reckoning, the same fixed festivals, the same engraved tables. The body that will keep the festivals at Sinai is being born inside the festivals already. The four mothers of the twelve sons are the chapter's quietest scandal and the chapter's most patient pastoral note. Leah, the unwanted elder. Rachel, the loved younger. Bilhah, the maidservant of Rachel. Zilpah, the maidservant of Leah. The body of Yashar'el (Israel) that the prophets will later trace, the body Yahuah (God) will call his firstborn son, the body the apostolic letters will speak of as the body of the seed of Jacob — that body is not born from a single pristine union. That body is born from a household full of favoritism, jealousy, sister-rivalry, handmaid-induction, and the long patience of a Father who opens wombs in his own time and gives sons to women whose husbands did not want them as they wanted other women. Leah's first four sons are born in the heat of her ache for Jacob's notice. Bilhah's two sons are born from Rachel's despair. Zilpah's two sons are born from Leah's competition. Issachar and Zebulun and Dinah come at the end of Leah's run after the mandrakes negotiation. Joseph comes only after Rachel has waited longer than she could bear. Twelve sons. Four mothers. One covenant body. The reader who has been carrying the weight of a household less than tidy is being told by this chapter that the foundational household of the covenant body was less than tidy too, and the Father's hand was on the household the entire time. The pattern is not the pattern of the catechism poster. The pattern is the pattern of the actual book. Laban's deception is the chapter's mirror to Jacob, and the mirror is held up without editorial. Jacob deceived his elder brother for the blessing in chapter 26. Laban deceives Jacob with the elder sister in chapter 28. The exchange is not random. The exchange is the moral physics Jubilees has been teaching since chapter 4 — the architecture in which the deceiver's deception comes back around in another currency, in another household, at another time, but inevitably and unavoidably, until the deceiver has met the pattern he ran on someone else. Jacob's seven extra years of service for Rachel are the price Esau's stolen birthright extracted, paid through Laban's hand. The Father lets the exchange run because the exchange is the discipline that makes the deceiver into a man fit to bear the body's name. By the time Jacob crosses Jabbok in the next chapter and wrestles for the new name, the deceiver has been worked on for fourteen years. The Yashar'el (Israel) name comes only after the deceiver has carried what he gave. The pattern still runs. The body that has been in any of the four houses will, in the appointed season, be made to face the patterns those houses installed. The Father is patient, the Father is thorough, and the new name comes at the end of the work, not at the front of it.

chapters.title: Jacob’s Return

verses.text: And it came to pass when Rachel had borne Joseph, that Laban went to shear his sheep; for they were distant from him a three days’ journey.
And Jacob saw that Laban was going to shear his sheep, and Jacob called Leah and Rachel, and spake kindly to them that they should come with him to the land of Canaan.

For he told them how he had seen everything in a dream, even all that He had spoken to him that he should return to his father’s house; and they said: “To every place whither you go we will go with you.”

And Jacob blessed the Elohim (God) of Isaac his father, and the Elohim (God) of Abraham his father’s father, and he arose and mounted his wives and his children, and took all his possessions and crossed the river, and came to the land of Gilead, and Jacob hid his intention from Laban and told him not.

And in the seventh year of the fourth week Jacob turned (his face) toward Gilead in the first month, on the twenty-first thereof. And Laban pursued after him and overtook Jacob in the mountain of Gilead in the third month, on the thirteenth thereof.

And Yahuah (God) did not suffer him to injure Jacob; for He appeared to him in a dream by night. And Laban spake to Jacob, And on the fifteenth of those days Jacob made a feast for Laban, and for all who came with him, and Jacob sware to Laban that day, and Laban also to Jacob, that neither should cross the mountain of Gilead to the other with evil purpose.
And he made there a heap for a witness; wherefore the name of that place is called: “The Heap of Witness,” after this heap.

But before they used to call the land of Gilead the land of the Rephaim; for it was the land of the Rephaim, and the Rephaim were born (there), giants whose height was ten, nine, eight down to seven cubits.
And their habitation was from the land of the children of Ammon to Mount Hermon, and the seats of their kingdom were Karnaim and Ashtaroth, and Edrei, and Mîsûr, and Beon.

And Yahuah (God) destroyed them because of the evil of their deeds; for they were very malignant, and the Amorites dwelt in their stead, wicked and sinful, and there is no people to-day which has wrought to the full all their sins, and they have no longer length of life on the earth. And Jacob sent away Laban, and he departed into Mesopotamia, the land of the East, and Jacob returned to the land of Gilead. And he passed over the Jabbok in the ninth month, on the eleventh thereof. And on that day Esau, his brother, came to him, and he was reconciled to him, and departed from him to the land of Seir, but Jacob dwelt in tents.

And in the first year of the fifth week in this jubilee he crossed the Jordan, and dwelt beyond the Jordan, and he pastured his sheep from the sea of the heap to Bethshan, and to Dothan and to the forest of Akrabbim.
And he sent to his father Isaac of all his substance, clothing, and food, and meat, and drink, and milk, and butter, and cheese, and some dates of the valley,

And to his mother Rebecca also four times a year, between the times of the months, between ploughing and reaping, and between autumn and the rain (season) and between winter and spring, to the tower of Abraham.

For Isaac had returned from the Well of the Oath and gone up to the tower of his father Abraham, and he dwelt there apart from his son Esau. For in the days when Jacob went to Mesopotamia, Esau took to himself a wife Mahalath, the daughter of Ishmael, and he gathered together all the flocks of his father and his wives, and went up and dwelt on Mount Seir, and left Isaac his father at the Well of the Oath alone.
And Isaac went up from the Well of the Oath and dwelt in the tower of Abraham his father on the mountains of Hebron,
And thither Jacob sent all that he did send to his father and his mother from time to time, all they needed, and they blessed Jacob with all their heart and with all their soul.

chapters.commentary: The flight, the heap of witness, the brief reconciliation with Esau, and the long support of Isaac and Rebecca — the chapter covers years in a few verses but plants something the rest of the book will need. Verses 9–11 hand the reader a small note that has more weight than its size. But before they used to call the land of Gilead the land of the Rephaim; for it was the land of the Rephaim, and the Rephaim were born (there), giants whose height was ten, nine, eight down to seven cubits. The Rephaim are the post-Flood remnant of the corruption Jubilees first named in chapter 5 — the Watchers’ offspring did not all die in the Flood, and the spiritual residue of their architecture (chapter 10’s demons) was not the only residue. There was a physical residue too. The giants of the land of Canaan that the spies in Numbers 13 will report, the Anakim that Joshua and Caleb will face, the Og of Bashan whose iron bedstead Deuteronomy 3 measures — these are all in this verse. Yahuah (God) destroyed them because of the evil of their deeds; for they were very malignant, and the Amorites dwelt in their stead, wicked and sinful. The Amorites inherited the land of the Rephaim and inherited their wickedness. The conquest under Joshua, when Yashar’el (Israel) takes the land, is taking it back from a population that had been warned across centuries and had not turned. Chapter 14 already told the reader: the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet full. Chapter 29 is updating: by Jacob’s day, the iniquity is much further along, and Yahuah (God) has already removed the Rephaim. The Conquest is not a colonial campaign. The Conquest is the next phase of a judgment that started before Abraham was born. Verses 13–14 record the brief reconciliation of Jacob and Esau on the day Jacob crossed Jabbok. Jubilees does not narrate the wrestling at Peniel here — that account is preserved in Genesis 32 — but Jubilees lets the reconciliation stand. He was reconciled to him, and departed from him to the land of Seir, but Jacob dwelt in tents. The reconciliation is real, in the moment. It will not hold (chapters 37 and 38 will show what Esau’s sons do later), but for that day the brothers part in peace, and Jacob crosses into Canaan to begin the long support of his parents in their last years. Verses 14–20 close the chapter with a domestic detail Genesis does not press: Jacob sent to his father Isaac of all his substance, clothing, and food, and meat, and drink, and milk, and butter, and cheese, and some dates of the valley. Four times a year Rebecca received provision — between the times of the months, between ploughing and reaping, between autumn and rains, between winter and spring. The covenant son honors his parents with consistent material support during their old age. This is not an incidental detail in a chapter heavy with theology. This is the chapter telling the reader what covenant honor looks like in a household. Honor your father and mother (the fifth commandment, given at Sinai) is not new at Sinai. Jacob was already keeping it, every quarter, with food carried up to the tower of Abraham. The Adamic standard, again, in the patriarch’s hand. The note on the Rephaim at verses 9–11 rewards the reader who has carried the architecture forward from chapter 5 and chapter 10. The Watchers' offspring did not all die in the flood. Some of the genetic corruption survived in the Rephaim, the Anakim, the Emim, the Zamzummim, the Og of Bashan whose iron bedstead Deuteronomy 3 measured at nine cubits. The Conquest under Joshua is not a colonial campaign waged by a tribal people against indigenous inhabitants. The Conquest is the next phase of the judgment Yahuah (God) had begun against the Watchers' architecture in the days of Noah and continued through the systematic removal of the corrupted lines from the land Yahuah (God) had assigned to Shem at chapter 8. By Joshua's day, the Rephaim that Jubilees mentions here at chapter 29 have already been largely removed. The Amorites who inherited the land from the Rephaim have inherited the wickedness too, and Yahuah (God) has been waiting four hundred years for the cup to fill (chapter 14:16). The body of Yashar'el (Israel) is the instrument of the long-awaited verdict. The verdict was not about Yashar'el (Israel)'s racial superiority. The verdict was about the cup of accumulated covenant-breaking that the Amorites had been filling without correction since the days of Noah's grandsons. The reader who has been catechized to find the Conquest morally embarrassing is reading the wrong category onto the chapter. The Conquest is judicial. The Conquest is the verdict of a Father who waited longer than any human judge would. The brief reconciliation between Jacob and Esau at verses 13–14 is the chapter's most poignant line and the chapter's most sober warning. He was reconciled to him, and departed from him to the land of Seir. The reconciliation was real on that day. It was also temporary. By chapters 37 and 38 the descendants of Esau will be marshaling armies against the descendants of Jacob, and the reconciliation of the patriarchs will not have held into the next generation. The pattern has consequences for the awakening reader's posture toward the four houses. A peace made today between the body of the seed and the bodies of the four houses is real on the day it is made. The peace may not hold across generations. The reader is not commanded to refuse the peace because the peace will not hold. The reader is commanded to make the peace and to do the right work in front of the Father, and to let the next generation answer for itself when its trial comes. Jacob's reconciliation with Esau on the day of Jabbok did not need to be tarnished by the awareness of what Esau's grandsons would later do. The day's peace was the day's gift. The body of the seed is to make peace with the bodies of the four houses on the days peace is offered, and to leave the future to the Father whose architecture has accounted for everything the future will hold. The closing detail about Jacob's quarterly provision to his parents — clothing, food, meat, drink, milk, butter, cheese, dates of the valley — is the chapter's quiet pastoral note for the awakening reader. The fifth commandment of the Sinai tables is not Sinai-novel. The covenant son was already keeping it before the tables were given, in the form of seasonal provision carried up the road to the tower where his aged parents lived. The Adamic standard was running. The Adamic standard runs in any household that will receive it. The reader who has aging parents — believer or unbeliever, in any of the four houses or in none — is being shown by this chapter what covenant honor of parents looks like in practical material form. The reader does not need a Sinai pulpit to know the standard. The standard is older than the pulpit. The standard is in the patriarch carrying food up the road four times a year. The Adamic priest of his own household was already keeping the law of his household, and the reader who walks into that pattern is walking into a much older inheritance than the Sunday service the four houses installed in its place.

chapters.title: Dinah and the Choice of Levi

verses.text: And in the first year of the sixth week he went up to Salem, to the east of Shechem, in peace, in the fourth month.

And there they carried off Dinah, the daughter of Jacob, into the house of Shechem, the son of Hamor, the Hivite, the prince of the land, and he lay with her and defiled her, and she was a little girl, a child of twelve years.

And he besought his father and her brothers that she might be given to him to wife. And Jacob and his sons were wroth because of the men of Shechem; for they had defiled Dinah, their sister, and they spake to them with evil intent and dealt deceitfully with them and beguiled them.

And Simeon and Levi came unexpectedly to Shechem and executed judgment on all the men of Shechem, and slew all the men whom they found in it, and left not a single one remaining in it: they slew all in torments because they had dishonoured their sister Dinah.

And thus let it not again be done from henceforth that a daughter of Yashar’el (Israel) be defiled; for judgment is ordained in heaven against them that they should destroy with the sword all the men of the Shechemites because they had wrought shame in Yashar’el (Israel).

And Yahuah (God) delivered them into the hands of the sons of Jacob that they might exterminate them with the sword and execute judgment upon them, and that it might not thus again be done in Yashar’el (Israel) that a virgin of Yashar’el (Israel) should be defiled. And if there is any man who wishes in Yashar’el (Israel) to give his daughter or his sister to any man who is of the seed of the nations he shall surely die, and they shall stone him with stones; for he has wrought shame in Yashar’el (Israel); and they shall burn the woman with fire, because she has dishonoured the name of the house of her father, and she shall be rooted out of Yashar’el (Israel).

And let not an adulteress and no uncleanness be found in Yashar’el (Israel) throughout all the days of the generations of the earth; for Yashar’el (Israel) is holy to Yahuah (God), and every man who has defiled (it) shall surely die: they shall stone him with stones.
For thus has it been ordained and written in the heavenly tables regarding all the seed of Yashar’el (Israel): he who defiles (it) shall surely die, and he shall be stoned with stones.

And to this law there is no limit of days, and no remission, nor any atonement: but the man who has defiled his daughter shall be rooted out in the midst of all Yashar’el (Israel), because he has given of his seed to Moloch, and wrought impiously so as to defile it.

And do you, Moses, command the children of Yashar’el (Israel) and exhort them not to give their daughters to the nations, and not to take for their sons any of the daughters of the nations, for this is abominable before Yahuah (God). For this reason I have written for you in the words of the Law all the deeds of the Shechemites, which they wrought against Dinah, and how the sons of Jacob spake, saying: “We shall not give our daughter to a man who is uncircumcised; for that were a reproach to us.”
And it is a reproach to Yashar’el (Israel), to those who give, and to those who take the daughters of the nations; for this is unclean and abominable to Yashar’el (Israel).
And Yashar’el (Israel) will not be free from this uncleanness if it has a wife of the daughters of the nations, or has given any of its daughters to a man who is of any of the nations.

For there will be plague upon plague, and curse upon curse, and every judgment and plague and curse will come (upon him): if he do this thing, or hide his eyes from those who commit uncleanness, or those who defile the sanctuary of Yahuah (God), or those who profane His holy name, (then) will the whole nation together be judged for all the uncleanness and profanation of this (man).

And there will be no respect of persons and no consideration of persons, and no receiving at his hands of fruits and offerings and burnt-offerings and fat, nor the fragrance of sweet savour, so as to accept it: and so fare every man or woman in Yashar’el (Israel) who defiles the sanctuary. For this reason I have commanded you, saying: "Testify this testimony to Yashar’el (Israel): see how the Shechemites fared and their sons: how they were delivered into the hands of two sons of Jacob, and they slew them under tortures, and it was (reckoned) to them for righteousness, and it is written down to them for righteousness.

And the seed of Levi was chosen for the priesthood, and to be Levites, that they might minister before Yahuah (God), as we, continually, and that Levi and his sons may be blessed for ever; for he was zealous to execute righteousness and judgment and vengeance on all those who arose against Yashar’el (Israel).
And so they inscribe as a testimony in his favour on the heavenly tables blessing and righteousness before the Elohim (God) of all:

And we remember the righteousness which the man fulfilled during his life, at all periods of the year; until a thousand generations they will record it, and it will come to him and to his descendants after him, and he has been recorded on the heavenly tables as a friend and a righteous man.

All this account I have written for you, and have commanded you to say to the children of Yashar’el (Israel), that they should not commit sin nor transgress the ordinances nor break the covenant which has been ordained for them, (but) that they should fulfil it and be recorded as friends. But if they transgress and work uncleanness in every way, they will be recorded on the heavenly tables as adversaries, and they will be destroyed out of the book of life, and they will be recorded in the book of those who will be destroyed and with those who will be rooted out of the earth.

And on the day when the sons of Jacob slew Shechem a writing was recorded in their favour in heaven that they had executed righteousness and uprightness and vengeance on the sinners, and it was written for a blessing.

And they brought Dinah, their sister, out of the house of Shechem, and they took captive everything that was in Shechem, their sheep and their oxen and their asses, and all their wealth, and all their flocks, and brought them all to Jacob their father.
And he reproached them because they had put the city to the sword; for he feared those who dwelt in the land, the Canaanites and the Perizzites.
And the dread of Yahuah (God) was upon all the cities which are around about Shechem, and they did not rise to pursue after the sons of Jacob; for terror had fallen upon them.

chapters.commentary: The chapter begins with the worst sentence in the book so far. And there they carried off Dinah, the daughter of Jacob, into the house of Shechem, the son of Hamor, the Hivite, the prince of the land, and he lay with her and defiled her, and she was a little girl, a child of twelve years. The chapter does not soften what Genesis 34 narrates and Jubilees does not cushion the reader. A girl, a child, taken and defiled. The brothers’ rage is not editorialized. The covenant body’s reaction is not weighed on some modern scale of proportionality. Simeon and Levi go in, unannounced, and execute the men of the city. They slew all in torments because they had dishonoured their sister Dinah. Then the chapter moves to the legislation that follows.
