Verses 7–17 are the heavenly tables’ verdict on the giving of Yashar’el (Israel)‘s daughters to the seed of the nations and the taking of nations’ daughters as wives for Yashar’el (Israel)’s sons. The penalty is severe. The tone is unflinching. The reader who comes from a tradition where intermarriage is a non-issue, or where Galatians 3:28 has been read as collapsing every covenant distinction, has to decide what to do with this chapter. Two clarifications matter. First, the chapter is not a racial purity ordinance. The chapter is a covenant-purity ordinance. The issue named throughout is worship — the daughter who marries into a household that worships Moloch will raise sons who pass through the fire. The son who marries into a Canaanite household will raise children who eat the dead and worship evil spirits (chapter 22). The chapter’s penalties are aimed at protecting the covenant body from the spiritual contamination the chapter is naming, not at building a racial wall. The Torah’s own provision for the stranger who joins himself to the covenant — Ruth from Moab, Rahab from Jericho, the mixed multitude from Egypt — is not contradicted here. A stranger who turns to Yahuah (God), keeps the sabbath, takes hold of the covenant (Isaiah 56:6) is not the problem the chapter names. The problem is the unconverted intermarriage that drags the covenant son into the pagan household’s worship, and the daughter into the same. The distinction matters. Second, the chapter’s invocation of the book of life and the book of those who will be destroyed (verses 20–22) is plain heavenly-tables language. The chapter is not a sermon. The chapter is reporting that the covenant body’s actions are recorded in heaven, and the recording matters. They will be recorded on the heavenly tables as adversaries, and they will be destroyed out of the book of life… and they will be recorded in the book of those who will be destroyed and with those who will be rooted out of the earth. Revelation 20:15 will quote the same image. Daniel 7:10 already showed the books being opened. The architecture is consistent. Verses 18–20 are the chapter’s pivot to Levi. The seed of Levi was chosen for the priesthood, and to be Levites, that they might minister before Yahuah (God), as we, continually, and that Levi and his sons may be blessed for ever; for he was zealous to execute righteousness and judgment and vengeance on all those who arose against Yashar’el (Israel). The priesthood is given to Levi here, on the strength of his zeal at Shechem, two generations before Aaron is born. The reader who has been taught that the Levitical priesthood begins at Sinai needs to read this chapter slowly. The choosing happens in Jacob’s lifetime, inside Jacob’s house, on the basis of one son’s willingness to spend his life on the line for the covenant body’s holiness. The pattern of priesthood is older than Sinai — Adam at the gate of Eden in chapter 3, Enoch in the garden in chapter 4, Noah at the altar in chapter 6, Melchizedek in chapter 13 — the Genesis 14 priest of the El Elyon (Most High) — Abraham building altars at every stop, Levi here at the Shechem judgment. The line of the altar is being kept by men whose calling proceeded by zeal, by covenant standing, by Yahuah (God)’s direct selection — not by genealogy alone. Levi’s office will be ratified by lineage at Sinai, but the office itself was claimed by his act here. The chapter ends with the dread of Yahuah (God) falling on the cities around Shechem. They did not rise to pursue after the sons of Jacob; for terror had fallen upon them. The covenant body’s holiness, when the body acts on it, propagates a fear of Yahuah (God) into the nations. The reader who has been catechized to find Old Testament militant holiness embarrassing is being shown by Jubilees that the militant holiness is the protection. The cities did not pursue. The household of Jacob lived. The twelve sons grew. The line continued.

chapters.title: The Blessing of Levi and Yahudah (Judah)

verses.text: And on the new moon of the month Jacob spake to all the people of his house, saying: “Purify yourselves and change your garments, and let us arise and go up to Bethel, where I vowed a vow to Him on the day when I fled from the face of Esau my brother, because He has been with me and brought me into this land in peace, and put you away the strange gods that are among you.”

And they gave up the strange gods and that which was in their ears and which was on their necks, and the idols which Rachel stole from Laban her brother she gave wholly to Jacob. And he burnt and brake them to pieces and destroyed them, and hid them under an oak which is in the land of Shechem.

And he went up on the new moon of the seventh month to Bethel. And he built an altar at the place where he had slept, and he set up a pillar there, and he sent word to his father Isaac to come to him to his sacrifice, and to his mother Rebecca. And Isaac said: “Let my son Jacob come, and let me see him before I die.”

And Jacob went to his father Isaac and to his mother Rebecca, to the house of his father Abraham, and he took two of his sons with him, Levi and Yahudah (Judah), and he came to his father Isaac and to his mother Rebecca.
And Rebecca came forth from the tower to the front of it to kiss Jacob and embrace him; for her spirit had revived when she heard: “Behold Jacob your son has come”; and she kissed him.

And she saw his two sons, and she recognised them, and said to him: “Are these your sons, my son?” and she embraced them and kissed them, and blessed them, saying: “In you shall the seed of Abraham become illustrious, and you will prove a blessing on the earth.”

And Jacob went in to Isaac his father, to the chamber where he lay, and his two sons were with him, and he took the hand of his father, and stooping down he kissed him, and Isaac clung to the neck of Jacob his son, and wept upon his neck. And the darkness left the eyes of Isaac, and he saw the two sons of Jacob, Levi and Yahudah (Judah), and he said: “Are these your sons, my son? for they are like you.”
And he said to him that they were truly his sons: “And you have truly seen that they are truly my sons.”
And they came near to him, and he turned and kissed them and embraced them both together.
And the spirit of prophecy came down into his mouth, and he took Levi by his right hand and Yahudah (Judah) by his left.

And he turned to Levi first, and began to bless him first, and said to him:, ’May the Elohim (God) of all, the very Yahuah (God) of all the ages, bless you and your children throughout all the ages. And may Yahuah (God) give to you and to your seed greatness and great glory, and cause you and your seed, from among all flesh, to approach Him to serve in His sanctuary as the angels of the presence and as the holy ones. (Even) as they, will the seed of your sons be for glory and greatness and holiness, and may He make them great to all the ages.

And they will be princes and judges, and chiefs of all the seed of the sons of Jacob; They will speak the word of Yahuah (God) in righteousness, And they will judge all His judgments in righteousness. And they will declare My ways to Jacob And My paths to Yashar’el (Israel). The blessing of Yahuah (God) will be given in their mouths To bless all the seed of the beloved.

Your mother has called your name Levi, And justly has she called your name; You will be joined to Yahuah (God) And be the companion of all the sons of Jacob; Let His table be your, And do you and your sons eat thereof; And may your table be full to all generations, And your food fail not to all the ages.
And let all who hate you fall down before you, And let all your adversaries be rooted out and perish; And blessed be he that blesses you, And cursed be every nation that curses you.

And to Yahudah (Judah) he said: May Yahuah (God) give you strength and power To tread down all that hate you; A prince shall you be, you and one of your sons, over the sons of Jacob; May your name and the name of your sons go forth and traverse every land and region. Then will the nations fear before your face, And all the nations will quake And all the peoples will quake. In you shall be the help of Jacob, And in you be found the salvation of Yashar’el (Israel).

And when you sit on the throne of the honour of your righteousness, There will be great peace for all the seed of the sons of the beloved, And blessed will he be that blesses you; And all that hate you and afflict you and curse you Shall be rooted out and destroyed from the earth and accursed." And turning he kissed him again and embraced him, and rejoiced greatly; for he had seen the sons of Jacob his son in very truth.
And he went forth from between his feet and fell down and worshipped him. And he blessed them. And (Jacob) rested there with Isaac his father that night, and they ate and drank with joy.
And he made the two sons of Jacob sleep, the one on his right hand and the other on his left and it was counted to him for righteousness.
And Jacob told his father everything during the night, how Yahuah (God) had shown him great mercy, and how He had prospered (him in) all his ways, and protected him from all evil.

And Isaac blessed the Elohim (God) of his father Abraham, who had not withdrawn His mercy and His righteousness from the sons of His servant Isaac. And in the morning Jacob told his father Isaac the vow which he had vowed to Yahuah (God), and the vision which he had seen, and that he had built an altar, and that everything was ready for the sacrifice to be made before Yahuah (God) as he had vowed, and that he had come to set him on an ass.

And Isaac said to Jacob his son: “I am not able to go with you; for I am old, and not able to bear the way: go, my son, in peace; for I am one hundred and sixty-five years this day; I am no longer able to journey, set your mother (on an ass) and let her go with you.
And I know, my son, that you have come on my account, and may this day be blessed on which you have seen me alive, and I also have seen you, my son.

May you prosper and fulfil the vow which you have vowed, and put not off your vow; for you will be called to account as touching the vow; now therefore make haste to perform it, and may He be pleased who has made all things, to whom you have vowed the vow.”

And he said to Rebecca: “Go with Jacob your son”; and Rebecca went with Jacob her son, and Deborah with her, and they came to Bethel. And Jacob remembered the prayer with which his father had blessed him and his two sons, Levi and Yahudah (Judah), and he rejoiced and blessed the Elohim (God) of his fathers, Abraham and Isaac.

And he said: “Now I know that I have an eternal hope, and my sons also, before the Elohim (God) of all;” and thus is it ordained concerning the two; and they record it as an eternal testimony to them on the heavenly tables how Isaac blessed them.

chapters.commentary: The chapter sets the household into motion. Jacob orders his people to purify yourselves and change your garments, and let us arise and go up to Bethel. The strange gods are gathered — including the household idols Rachel stole from Laban — and Jacob buries them under the oak in Shechem. The covenant body’s preparation for going up to the place of vow is the same preparation Yashar’el (Israel) will be told to make for going up to the place where Yahuah (God) puts his name. Wash, change, give up the false gods. The pattern is not new in Exodus 19 or in Joshua 24. The pattern is here, in the patriarch’s own household, in the move from Shechem to Bethel. The center of the chapter is verses 12–20, Isaac’s blessing of Levi and Yahudah (Judah). Two grandsons, two callings, both prophesied with weight. And the spirit of prophecy came down into his mouth. This is the chapter where the structure of priest-and-king that will run through all of Yashar’el (Israel)’s history is named in advance. Levi for the altar. Yahudah (Judah) for the throne. The grandfather, blind to natural sight but given prophetic mouth, lays his right hand on Levi and his left on Yahudah (Judah). To Levi: cause you and your seed, from among all flesh, to approach Him to serve in His sanctuary as the angels of the presence and as the holy ones… they will speak the word of Yahuah (God) in righteousness, and they will judge all His judgments in righteousness. And they will declare My ways to Jacob and My paths to Yashar’el (Israel). The Levitical office is being given the role of teaching as much as the role of sacrificing. Malachi 2:7 will quote it back: the priest’s lips should keep knowledge, and they should seek the law at his mouth: for he is the messenger of Yahuah of hosts. The teacher office is older than the prophets. The chapter places it on Levi through Isaac’s mouth two generations before Aaron’s vestments. To Yahudah (Judah): a prince shall you be, you and one of your sons, over the sons of Jacob; may your name and the name of your sons go forth and traverse every land and region. Then will the nations fear before your face… In you shall be the help of Jacob, and in you be found the salvation of Yashar’el (Israel). The salvation of Yashar’el (Israel) in the mouth of Isaac, two millennia before David is anointed and four millennia before any modern reader picks up the chapter. The line of kings will run through Yahudah (Judah). The Messiah (Christ) — the lion of the tribe of Yahudah (Judah) Revelation 5:5 will name — will run through Yahudah (Judah). And the salvation of Yashar’el (Israel) — all twelve tribes, the whole covenant body, the firstborn son of chapter 19 — will come through Yahudah’s (Judah’s) seed. This is the chapter the inherited Christian reading has the hardest time hearing in its native register. The Messiah (Christ) is from Yahudah (Judah). His mission is to the lost sheep of the house of Yashar’el (Israel) (Matthew 15:24, Matthew 10:6). The salvation that comes through Yahudah (Judah) is the gathering of the scattered tribes whose covenant identity exile took from them. Yahudah (Judah) is not the destination. Yahudah (Judah) is the way through which the firstborn son is gathered back. Three categories. Two houses. One Messiah (Christ). The reader who has carried the Jew and Gentile binary all their reading life can put it down here. The chapter has been operating on three categories from the beginning. Yahudah (Judah) is one tribe of twelve, and one house of two. The other ten tribes — the house of Yashar’el (Israel) the prophets call Ephraim, Yosef (Joseph), the northern kingdom — are scattered out and being gathered in. They are not Yahudim (Jews); they are the wild olive branches of Romans 11 grafted back into their own root. The nations remain the nations, blessed in their measure, not absorbed into the body. Isaac’s blessing of Yahudah (Judah) is the prophetic seed of the salvation that gathers both houses without dissolving the third category. The chapter holds it. The chapter closes (verses 26–32) with Jacob and Rebecca journeying to Bethel together. Rebecca is going to die before this chapter is many pages further. The mother who blessed Jacob in chapter 25 walks with him to Bethel one last time, and the chapter notes Jacob’s awareness: now I know that I have an eternal hope, and my sons also, before the Elohim (God) of all. The eternal hope is named at Bethel. The eternal hope is the covenant body’s inheritance. The eternal hope is what Jubilees has been describing from the heavenly tables down.

chapters.title: Levi’s Priesthood and the Birth of Benjamin

verses.text: And he abode that night at Bethel, and Levi dreamed that they had ordained and made him the priest of the El Elyon (Most High) Elohim (God), him and his sons for ever; and he awoke from his sleep and blessed Yahuah (God).

And Jacob rose early in the morning, on the fourteenth of this month, and he gave a tithe of all that came with him, both of men and cattle, both of gold and every vessel and garment, yea, he gave tithes of all.

And in those days Rachel became pregnant with her son Benjamin. And Jacob counted his sons from him upwards and Levi fell to the portion of Yahuah (God), and his father clothed him in the garments of the priesthood and filled his hands.

And on the fifteenth of this month, he brought to the altar fourteen oxen from amongst the cattle, and twenty-eight rams, and forty-nine sheep, and seven lambs, and twenty-one kids of the goats as a burnt-offering on the altar of sacrifice, well pleasing for a sweet savour before Elohim (God).
This was his offering, in consequence of the vow which he had vowed that he would give a tenth, with their fruit-offerings and their drink-offerings.

And when the fire had consumed it, he burnt incense on the fire over the fire, and for a thank-offering two oxen and four rams and four sheep, four he-goats, and two sheep of a year old, and two kids of the goats; and thus he did daily for seven days. And he and all his sons and his men were eating (this) with joy there during seven days and blessing and thanking Yahuah (God), who had delivered him out of all his tribulation and had given him his vow.
And he tithed all the clean animals, and made a burnt sacrifice, but the unclean animals he gave (not) to Levi his son, and he gave him all the souls of the men.

And Levi discharged the priestly office at Bethel before Jacob his father in preference to his ten brothers, and he was a priest there, and Jacob gave his vow: thus he tithed again the tithe to Yahuah (God) and sanctified it, and it became holy to Him.

And for this reason it is ordained on the heavenly tables as a law for the tithing again the tithe to eat before Yahuah (God) from year to year, in the place where it is chosen that His name should dwell, and to this law there is no limit of days for ever.

This ordinance is written that it may be fulfilled from year to year in eating the second tithe before Yahuah (God) in the place where it has been chosen, and nothing shall remain over from it from this year to the year following. For in its year shall the seed be eaten till the days of the gathering of the seed of the year, and the wine till the days of the wine, and the oil till the days of its season.
And all that is left thereof and becomes old, let it be regarded as polluted: let it be burnt with fire, for it is unclean.
And thus let them eat it together in the sanctuary, and let them not suffer it to become old.

And all the tithes of the oxen and sheep shall be holy to Yahuah (God), and shall belong to His priests, which they will eat before Him from year to year; for thus is it ordained and engraven regarding the tithe on the heavenly tables. And on the following night, on the twenty-second day of this month, Jacob resolved to build that place, and to surround the court with a wall, and to sanctify it and make it holy for ever, for himself and his children after him.
And Yahuah (God) appeared to him by night and blessed him and said to him: “Your name shall not be called Jacob, but Yashar’el (Israel) shall they name your name.”

And He said to him again: “I am Yahuah (God) who created the heaven and the earth, and I shall increase you and multiply you exceedingly, and kings will come forth from you, and they will judge everywhere wherever the foot of the sons of men has trodden.

Ana I shall give to your seed all the earth which is under heaven, and they will judge all the nations according to their desires, and after that they will get possession of the whole earth and inherit it for ever.”

And He finished speaking with him, and He went up from him, and Jacob looked till He had ascended into heaven. And he saw in a vision of the night, and behold an angel descended from heaven with seven tablets in his hands, and he gave them to Jacob, and he read them and knew all that was written therein which would befall him and his sons through- out all the ages.

And he showed him all that was written on the tablets, and said to him: “Do not build this place, and do not make it an eternal sanctuary, and do not dwell here; for this is not the place. Go to the house of Abraham your father and dwell with Isaac your father until the day of the death of your father.
For in Egypt you will die in peace, and in this land you will be buried with honour in the sepulchre of your fathers, with Abraham and Isaac.
Fear not, for as you have seen and read it, thus will. it all be; and do you write down everything as you have seen and read.”

And Jacob said: “Yahuah (God), how can I remember all that I have read and seen?” And he said to him: “I will bring all things to your remembrance.” And he went up from him, and he awoke from his sleep, and he remembered everything which he had read and seen, and he wrote down all the words which he had read and seen.

And he celebrated there yet another day, and he sacrificed thereon according to all that he sacrificed on the former days, and called its name “Addition,” for this day was added, and the former days he called “The Feast.”
And thus it was manifested that it should be, and it is written on the heavenly tables: wherefore it was revealed to him that he should celebrate it, and add it to the seven days of the feast.
And its name was called “Addition,” because that it was recorded amongst the days of the feast days, according to the number of the days of the year.

And in the night, on the twenty-third of this month, Deborah Rebecca’s nurse died, and they buried her beneath the city under the oak of the river, and he called the name of this place, “The river of Deborah,” and the oak, “The oak of the mourning of Deborah.” And Rebecca went and returned to her house to his father Isaac, and Jacob sent by her hand rams and sheep and he-goats that she should prepare a meal for his father such as he desired.
And he went after his mother till he came to the land of Kabrâtân, and he dwelt there.

And Rachel bare a son in the night, and called his name “Son of my sorrow”; for she suffered in giving him birth: but his father called his name Benjamin, on the eleventh of the eighth month in the first of the sixth week of this jubilee.
And Rachel died there and she was buried in the land of Ephrath, the same is Bethlehem, and Jacob built a pillar on the grave of Rachel, on the road above her grave.

chapters.commentary: The chapter delivers what chapter 30 set up. Levi dreams that he has been ordained the priest of the El Elyon (Most High) Elohim (God). Jacob counts his sons from the youngest upward, and Levi falls to the portion of Yahuah (God), and Jacob clothed him in the garments of the priesthood and filled his hands. The tithe is given. The vow at Bethel is paid. The chapter sets the priestly office on Levi at his father’s hand, and the chapter records the tithe as engraved on the heavenly tables — to this law there is no limit of days for ever (verse 10). The Adamic, patriarchal, pre-Sinai pattern is being named again as the heavenly-tables baseline. Sinai will not invent the priestly service or the tithe. Sinai will re-disclose it to a body that had been four hundred years in Egypt and had forgotten. Verses 16–29 hand the reader two more institutions in plain form. First, Jacob’s name is changed. Your name shall not be called Jacob, but Yashar’el (Israel) shall they name your name. The man becomes the body. From this moment on the seed will be called by the name of the patriarch, and the patriarch carries in his name the wrestling-with-Elohim Genesis 32 narrated. The covenant body is named after a man who held on through the night. This is the body the prophets will address. This is the body Yahuah (God) will divorce and gather. This is the firstborn son. Second, the eighth day of Tabernacles is instituted. He celebrated there yet another day, and he sacrificed thereon… and called its name “Addition,” for this day was added. The eighth day of the Feast of Tabernacles — the day John 7:37 will quote when Yahusha (Jesus) stood and cried, saying, “If any man thirst, let him come to me and drink” — is instituted in Jacob’s hand at Bethel before there is a Yashar’el (Israel) in the wilderness or a temple on Mount Zion. The festival’s seven-plus-one structure is engraved here. The reader who has been told the festivals were arbitrary Yahudi (Jewish) accretions to a more universal religion is meeting them again as what they are: the rhythms Yahuah (God) put on his covenant body in the patriarchs’ time, kept by Adam’s line, kept by Abraham, kept by Jacob — kept by Yahusha (Jesus) — and kept by the gathered body at the appointed reign (Zechariah 14:16–19). The festivals are not optional. They were never abolished. They are the calendar of the covenant. Verses 21–26 hand the reader something rarely emphasized. He saw in a vision of the night, and behold an angel descended from heaven with seven tablets in his hands, and he gave them to Jacob, and he read them and knew all that was written therein which would befall him and his sons throughout all the ages. Seven tablets. Read in one night. The future of Yashar’el (Israel) — every one of his sons, every generation, every tribulation, every gathering — given to him to read. And Jacob asks the question every reader of prophecy asks: Yahuah (God), how can I remember all that I have read and seen? The answer is the chapter’s quiet promise. I will bring all things to your remembrance. This is the line John 14:26 will echo when Yahusha (Jesus) tells his disciples that the Ruach HaKodesh (Holy Spirit) will bring all things to their remembrance. The mechanism is older than the upper room. Jacob received it at Bethel. The Father has been promising remembrance to his prophets since the beginning. The chapter closes hard. And Rachel bare a son in the night, and called his name “Son of my sorrow”; for she suffered in giving him birth: but his father called his name Benjamin… And Rachel died there. The twelfth son is born. The mother of two of the twelve dies in the birthing. The covenant body is complete in Jacob’s living, and the cost of completing it is Rachel’s life. The reader sits with the chapter’s grief without moralizing it. The body the prophets will gather is born from real flesh and real loss.

chapters.title: Reuben’s Sin and the Sons of Jacob

verses.text: And Jacob went and dwelt to the south of Magdalâdrâ’êf. And he went to his father Isaac, he and Leah his wife, on the new moon of the tenth month.
And Reuben saw Bilhah, Rachel’s maid, the concubine of his father, bathing in water in a secret place, and he loved her.
And he hid himself at night, and he entered the house of Bilhah at night, and he found her sleeping alone on a bed in her house.

And he lay with her, and she awoke and saw, and behold Reuben was lying with her in the bed, and she uncovered the border of her covering and seized him, and cried out, and discovered that it was Reuben.
And she was ashamed because of him, and released her hand from him, and he fled.

And she lamented because of this thing exceedingly, and did not tell it to any one. And when Jacob returned and sought her, she said to him: “I am not clean for you, for I have been defiled as regards you; for Reuben has defiled me, and has lain with me in the night, and I was asleep, and did not discover until he uncovered my skirt and slept with me.”
And Jacob was exceedingly wroth with Reuben because he had lain with Bilhah, because he had uncovered his father’s skirt.
And Jacob did not approach her again because Reuben had defiled her. And as for any man who uncovers his father’s skirt his deed is wicked exceedingly, for he is abominable before Yahuah (God).

For this reason it is written and ordained on the heavenly tables that a man should not lie with his father’s wife, and should not uncover his father’s skirt, for this is unclean: they shall surely die together, the man who lies with his father’s wife and the woman also, for they have wrought uncleanness on the earth.

And there shall be nothing unclean before our Elohim (God) in the nation which He has chosen for Himself as a possession. And again, it is written a second time: “Cursed he be who lies with the wife of his father, for he has uncovered his father’s shame”; and all the holy ones of Yahuah (God) said “So be it; so be it.”

And do you, Moses, command the children of Yashar’el (Israel) that they observe this word; for it (entails) a punishment of death; and it is unclean, and there is no atonement for ever to atone for the man who has committed this, but he is to be put to death and slain, and stoned with stones, and rooted out from the midst of the people of our Elohim (God).
For to no man who does so in Yashar’el (Israel) is it permitted to remain alive a single day on the earth, for he is abominable and unclean.

And let them not say: to Reuben was granted life and forgiveness after he had lain with his father’s concubine, and to her also though she had a husband, and her husband Jacob, his father, was still alive.

For until that time there had not been revealed the ordinance and judgment and law in its completeness for all, but in your days (it has been revealed) as a law of seasons and of days, and an everlasting law for the everlasting generations. And for this law there is no consummation of days, and no atonement for it, but they must both be rooted out in the midst of the nation: on the day whereon they committed it they shall slay them.

And do you, Moses, write (it) down for Yashar’el (Israel) that they may observe it, and do according to these words, and not commit a sin to death; for Yahuah our Elohim (the LORD our God) is judge, who respects not persons and accepts not gifts.

And tell them these words of the covenant, that they may hear and observe, and be on their guard with respect to them, and not be destroyed and rooted out of the land; for an uncleanness, and an abomination, and a contamination, and a pollution are all they who commit it on the earth before our Elohim (God).

And there is no greater sin than the fornication which they commit on earth; for Yashar’el (Israel) is a holy nation to Yahuah (God) its Elohim (God), and a nation of inheritance, and a priestly and royal nation and for (His own) possession; and there shall no such uncleanness appear in the midst of the holy nation. And in the third year of this sixth week Jacob and all his sons went and dwelt in the house of Abraham, near Isaac his father and Rebecca his mother.

And these were the names of the sons of Jacob: the first-born Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Yahudah (Judah), Issachar, Zebulon, the sons of Leah; and the sons of Rachel, Joseph and Benjamin; and the sons of Bilhah, Dan and Naphtali, and the sons of Zilpah, Gad and Asher; and Dinah, the daughter of Leah, the only daughter of Jacob.

And they came and bowed themselves to Isaac and Rebecca, and when they saw them they blessed Jacob and all his sons, and Isaac rejoiced exceedingly, for he saw the sons of Jacob, his younger son, and he blessed them.

chapters.commentary: Reuben sleeps with Bilhah, his father’s concubine. The chapter does not soften it. Bilhah is asleep when he comes in; she wakes to find him with her; she is ashamed; she releases him and he flees. She lives the rest of her life under the weight of an assault she did not ask for. Jacob hears later, and he is exceedingly wroth and never approaches Bilhah again. The chapter is reporting an act of violence against a woman who had no power to refuse, and the chapter calls the act abominable before Yahuah (God). Verses 9–17 are the chapter’s legal treatment. He shall surely die… they shall slay them on the day whereon they committed it. The capital penalty for incest with a father’s wife is named, engraved on the heavenly tables, and recorded as without remission. The reader who has been catechized to read these penalties as evidence of Old Testament barbarism — and who reads forward to the New Testament expecting grace to soften the penalties — is reading the wrong category onto the text. The penalties name the seriousness of the violation. They were not all carried out in every case (Reuben himself was not killed), which is the chapter’s next move. Verses 15–18 are the chapter’s quiet admission. And let them not say: to Reuben was granted life and forgiveness after he had lain with his father’s concubine, and to her also though she had a husband, and her husband Jacob, his father, was still alive. For until that time there had not been revealed the ordinance and judgment and law in its completeness for all, but in your days (it has been revealed) as a law of seasons and of days, and an everlasting law for the everlasting generations. Read this slowly. The chapter is saying that the law was disclosed in fullness at Sinai, and that Reuben’s pre-Sinai violation was treated according to a less complete disclosure. This is not law abolished and grace begun. This is partial disclosure and full disclosure. The full disclosure does not invalidate what came before; the full disclosure ratifies what was always true and forecloses the kind of leniency Reuben received from his father’s bare anger. The chapter is preparing the reader for Sinai not as the introduction of a brand-new system, but as the complete disclosure of what was already engraved on the heavenly tables and partially known to Adam, Noah, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. The chapter’s conclusion (verses 18–20) is what the reader needs to hold above everything else. Yashar’el (Israel) is a holy nation to Yahuah (God) its Elohim (God), and a nation of inheritance, and a priestly and royal nation and for (His own) possession; and there shall no such uncleanness appear in the midst of the holy nation. The body has a calling, and the calling generates the standard. The standard is not a punishment imposed from outside the body. The standard is what the body’s calling requires. A priestly and royal nation has different ground rules than a non-priestly nation. This is what Exodus 19:6 will repeat at Sinai and what 1 Peter 2:9 will repeat to the scattered seed: a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a peculiar people. The verse that the inherited Christian commentary tradition has spent fifteen hundred years re-applying to the church is being placed by Jubilees on the twelve sons of Jacob in chapter 33. Where the church found the verse, it found it in 1 Peter, where it had been re-applied by Peter to the strangers scattered throughout Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia — the diaspora the Assyrian and Babylonian exiles produced. The scattered seed of Yashar’el (Israel). 1 Peter is not a letter to Greek pagans; 1 Peter is a letter to the dispersed northern kingdom living under Roman provincial labels in Asia Minor. The verse is in its right place when it lands on them. The verse is in the wrong place when it is lifted off the body and given to a substitute. Verse 22 closes by listing the twelve sons in order — Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Yahudah (Judah), Issachar, Zebulon… Joseph and Benjamin… Dan and Naphtali… Gad and Asher; and Dinah, the daughter of Leah. The body is named, in its parts, before the chapter ends. The reader who has read the prophets is meeting the names that will run through Isaiah 11, Jeremiah 31, Ezekiel 37, Hosea 1–2. The roster is not a list of the dead. The roster is the body the Father gathers in the latter days.

chapters.title: The Amorite War and the Loss of Joseph

verses.text: And in the sixth year of this week of this forty-fourth jubilee Jacob sent his sons to pasture their sheep, and his servants with them, to the pastures of Shechem.
And the seven kings of the Amorites assembled themselves together against them, to slay them, hiding themselves under the trees, and to take their cattle as a prey.

And Jacob and Levi and Yahudah (Judah) and Joseph were in the house with Isaac their father; for his spirit was sorrowful, and they could not leave him: and Benjamin was the youngest, and for this reason remained with his father.

And there came the kings of Tâphû, and the kings of ’Arêsa, and the kings of Sêragân, and the kings of Sêlô, and the kings of Gâ’as, and the king of Bêthôrôn, and the king of Ma’anîsâkîr, and all those who dwell in these mountains (and) who dwell in the woods in the land of Canaan.
And they announced this to Jacob saying: “Behold, the kings of the Amorites have surrounded your sons, and plundered their herds.”

And he arose from his housel he and his three sons and all the servants of his father, and his own servants, and he went against them with six thousand men, who carried swords. And he slew them in the pastures of Shechem, and pursued those who fled, and he slew them with the edge of the sword, and he slew ’Arêsa and Tâphû and Sarêgân and Sêlô and ’Amânîsakîr and Gâgâ’as, and he recovered his herds.
And he prevailed over them, and imposed tribute on them that they should pay him tribute, five fruit products of their land, and he built Rôbêl and Tamnâtârês
And he returned in peace, and made peace with them, and they became his servants, until the day that he and his sons went down into Egypt.
And in the seventh year of this week he sent Joseph to learn about the welfare of his brothers from his house to the land of Shechem, and he found them in the land of Dothan.

And they dealt treacherously with him, and formed a plot against him to slay him, but changing their minds, they sold him to Ishmaelite merchants, and they brought him down into Egypt, and they sold him to Potiphar, the eunuch of Pharaoh, the chief of the cooks, priest of the city of ’Êlêw. And the sons of Jacob slaughtered a kid, and dipped the coat of Joseph in the blood, and sent (it) to Jacob their father on the tenth of the seventh month.

And he mourned all that night, for they had brought it to him in the evening, and he became feverish with mourning for his death, and he said: “An evil beast has devoured Joseph”; and all the members of his house mourned with him that day, and they were grieving and mourning with him all that day.
And his sons and his daughter rose up to comfort him, but he refused to be comforted for his son.

And on that day Bilhah heard that Joseph had perished, and she died mourning him, and she was living in Qafrâtêf and Dinah also, his daughter, died after Joseph had perished. And there came these three mournings upon Yashar’el (Israel) in one month.

And they buried Bilhah over against the tomb of Rachel, and Dinah also, his daughter, they buried there. And he mourned for Joseph one year, and did not cease, for he said “Let me go down to the grave mourning for my son.”

For this reason it is ordained for the children of Yashar’el (Israel) that they should afflict themselves on the tenth of the seventh month–on the day that the news which made him weep for Joseph came to Jacob his father–that they should make atonement for themselves thereon with a young goat on the tenth of the seventh month, once a year, for their sins; for they had grieved the affection of their father regarding Joseph his son.

And this day has been ordained that they should grieve thereon for their sins, and for all their transgressions and for all their errors, so that they might cleanse themselves on that day once a year. And after Joseph perished, the sons of Jacob took to themselves wives. The name of Reuben’s wife is ’Adâ and the name of Simeon’s wife is ’Adîbâ’a, a Canaanite; and the name of Levi’s wife is Mêlkâ, of the daughters of Aram, of the seed of the sons of Terah; and the name of Yahudah’s (Judah’s) wife, Bêtasû’êl, a Canaanite; and the name of Issachar’s wife, Hêzaqâ; and the name of Zebulon’s wife, Nî’îmân; and the name of Dan’s wife, ’Êglâ; and the name of Naphtali’s wife, Rasû’û, of Mesopotamia; and the name of Gad’s wife, Mâka; and the name of Asher’s wife, ’Îjônâ; and the name of Joseph’s wife, Asenath, the Egyptian; and the name of Benjamin’s wife, ’Îjasaka.
And Simeon repented, and took a second wife from Mesopotamia as his brothers.

chapters.commentary: The chapter has three movements that look unrelated and are not. First, the seven Amorite kings attack Jacob’s sons in the pastures of Shechem (verses 1–9). Second, Joseph is sold into Egypt (verses 10–17). Third, the Day of Atonement is instituted (verses 18–19). One chapter; one underlying theme — the covenant body’s grief is being woven into the calendar of the heavenly tables. The Amorite war is told briefly. Seven kings — of Tâphû, ’Arêsa, Sêragân, Sêlô, Gâ’as, Bêthôrôn, and Ma’anîsâkîr — assemble against Jacob’s sons. Jacob and Levi and Yahudah (Judah) and Joseph are home with Isaac because Isaac’s spirit is sorrowful and they cannot leave him. Jacob takes six thousand men with swords and goes against the kings, and they fall before him. The chapter notes that Jacob prevailed over them, and imposed tribute on them. The same Jacob who fled from Esau is now leading a body of six thousand into pitched battle and winning. The covenant body has matured into a fighting force. The promise of the seed multiplied is being lived out in real soldiers. Then the loss of Joseph. And in the seventh year of this week he sent Joseph to learn about the welfare of his brothers from his house to the land of Shechem, and he found them in the land of Dothan. And they dealt treacherously with him, and formed a plot against him to slay him, but changing their minds, they sold him to Ishmaelite merchants, and they brought him down into Egypt. The chapter is unsentimental about the brothers. The hatred of Joseph that Jubilees does not narrate at length here (Genesis 37 fills it in) is what produces the sale. The same Levi who was zealous at Shechem in chapter 30 is now part of the group that sells his brother. The covenant body’s holiness is not yet uniformly distributed. The same household that produces the Levitical priesthood produces the brothers who throw their own brother into a pit and sell him for twenty pieces of silver. The reader who has been told that the awakening remnant must be spotless before it can be the awakening remnant is being corrected by this chapter. The body the prophets gather is the body of these brothers, with all of this on the record. Then the threefold mourning. And on that day Bilhah heard that Joseph had perished, and she died mourning him, and she was living in Qafrâtêf and Dinah also, his daughter, died after Joseph had perished. And there came these three mournings upon Yashar’el (Israel) in one month. Bilhah dies. Dinah dies. The chapter does not say the deaths are caused by Joseph’s loss in a direct sense — the chapter just notes the convergence — but Jubilees reports the convergence because the convergence matters. The covenant body suffers compounded loss. One man’s violence (Reuben in chapter 33) and ten men’s treachery (Joseph sold) reverberate through the household for years. Bilhah, the woman Reuben violated, dies grieving the boy who was sold. Dinah, the girl who was violated at Shechem, dies in the same season. The chapter is naming the cost of unaddressed sin in the covenant household. The bodies of the violated do not always recover. Then verses 18–19 hand the reader the chapter’s third movement, and the most weighted line in the entire patriarchal block. For this reason it is ordained for the children of Yashar’el (Israel) that they should afflict themselves on the tenth of the seventh month — on the day that the news which made him weep for Joseph came to Jacob his father — that they should make atonement for themselves thereon with a young goat on the tenth of the seventh month, once a year, for their sins; for they had grieved the affection of their father regarding Joseph his son. And this day has been ordained that they should grieve thereon for their sins, and for all their transgressions and for all their errors, so that they might cleanse themselves on that day once a year. Yom Kippur — the Day of Atonement — is being instituted here, in Jubilees, in connection with the day Jacob received the bloody coat. The annual atonement is not a generic sacrificial system delivered to Moses without context. The annual atonement is attached to the day the patriarch was made to weep by his sons’ betrayal. They grieved the affection of their father regarding Joseph his son. The covenant body’s annual self-affliction is in remembrance of grief brought on the patriarch by the betrayal of his own children. Read this and the New Testament resonance is unavoidable. The Father is grieved by his own. The Father’s beloved son is sold by his brothers. The annual atonement points back through Joseph’s brothers selling Joseph and forward through every betrayal of the covenant body that has wounded the Father’s heart, and all of it is folded into one day on which the body is asked to afflict itself, fast, weep, and be cleansed. The chapter holds the full weight without spelling it out. The reader who is hearing it for the first time can sit in the quiet of what Jubilees is saying. The Day of Atonement is not arbitrary. The Day of Atonement is the body’s annual return to the day the brothers grieved the Father. The chapter closes (verses 20–21) with the marriages of Jacob’s sons. The names of the wives — Adâ, Adîba’a, Mêlkâ, Bêtasû’êl, Hêzaqâ, Nî’îmân, Êglâ, Rasû’û, Mâka, Îjônâ, Asenath, Îjasaka — some Aramean, some Canaanite, some Mesopotamian, some Egyptian. The chapter is reporting that the twelve tribes’ wives came from many sources. The covenant body is not ethnically pure. The covenant body never has been. The bloodline narrows on the patriarchal side; the maternal side is mixed across nations from Genesis to Exodus. Simeon repented, and took a second wife from Mesopotamia as his brothers — even the corrections are noted. The body is a real body. The lineage is a real lineage. The Father has been working with what he chose, not with an imagined purity that was never there.

chapters.title: Rebecca’s Last Words and Death

verses.text: And in the first year of the first week of the forty-fifth jubilee Rebecca called Jacob, her son, and commanded him regarding his father and regarding his brother, that he should honour them all the days of his life.
And Jacob said: “I will do everything as you have commanded me; for this thing will be honour and greatness to me, and righteousness before Yahuah (God), that I should honour them.
And you too, mother, know from the time I was born until this day, all my deeds and all that is in my heart, that I always think good concerning all.
And how should I not do this thing which you have commanded me, that I should honour my father and my brother!
Tell me, mother, what perversity have you seen in me and I shall turn away from it, and mercy will be upon me.”

And she said to him: “My son, I have not seen in you all my days any perverse but (only) upright deeds. And yet I shall tell you the truth, my son: I shall die this, year, and I shall not survive this year in my life; for I have seen in a dream the day of my death, that I should not live beyond a hundred and fifty-five years: and behold I have completed all the days of my life which I am to live.” And Jacob laughed at the words of his mother, because his mother had said to him that she should die; and she was sitting opposite to him in possession of her strength, and she was not infirm in her strength; for she went in and out and saw, and her teeth were strong, and no ailment had touched her all the days of her life.

And Jacob said to her: “Blessed am I, mother, if my days approach the days of your life, and my strength remain with me thus as your strength: and you will not die, for you are jesting idly with me regarding your death.”

And she went in to Isaac and said to him: "One petition I make to you: make Esau swear that he will not injure Jacob, nor pursue him with enmity; for you know Esau’s thoughts that they are perverse from his youth, and there is no goodness in him; for he desires after your death to kill him.

And you know all that he has done since the day Jacob his brother went to Haran until this day; how he has forsaken us with his whole heart, and has done evil to us; your flocks he has taken to himself, and carried off all your possessions from before your face.

And when we implored and besought him for what was our own, he did as a man who was taking pity on us. And he is bitter against you because you did bless Jacob your perfect and upright son; for there is no evil but only goodness in him, and since he came from Haran to this day he has not robbed us of aught, for he brings us everything in its season always, and rejoices with all his heart when we take at his hands, and he blesses us, and has not parted from us since he came from Haran until this day, and he remains with us continually at home honouring us."

And Isaac said to her: "I, too, know and see the deeds of Jacob who is with us, how that with all his heart he honours us; but I loved Esau formerly more than Jacob, because he was the first-born; but now I love Jacob more than Esau, for he has done manifold evil deeds, and there is no righteousness in him, for all his ways are unrighteousness and violence, and there is no righteousness around him.

And now my heart is troubled because of all his deeds, and neither he nor his seed is to be saved, for they are those who will be destroyed from the earth, and who will be rooted out from under heaven, for he has forsaken the Elohim (God) of Abraham and gone after his wives and after their uncleanness and after their error, he and his children.
And you do bid me make him swear that he will not slay Jacob, his brother; even if he swear he will not abide by his oath, and he will not do good but evil only.

But if he desires to slay Jacob, his brother, into Jacob’s hands will he be given, and he will not escape from his hands, for he will descend into his hands. And fear you not on account of Jacob; for the guardian of Jacob is great and powerful and honoured, and praised more than the guardian of Esau."
And Rebecca sent and called Esau, and he came to her, and she said to him: “I have a petition, my son, to make to you, and do you promise to do it, my son.”
And he said: “I will do everything that you say to me, and I will not refuse your petition.”

And she said to him: “I ask you that the day I die, you will take me in and bury me near Sarah, your father’s mother, and that you and Jacob will love each other, and that neither will desire evil against the other, but mutual love only, and (so) you will prosper, my sons, and be honoured in the midst of the land, and no enemy will rejoice over you, and you will be a blessing and a mercy in the eyes of all those that love you.”

And he said: "I will do all that you have told me, and I shall bury you on the day you die near Sarah, my father’s mother, as you have desired that her bones may be near your bones. And Jacob, my brother, also, I shall love above all flesh; for I have not a brother in all the earth but him only: and this is no great merit for me if I love him; for he is my brother, and we were sown together in your body, and together came we forth from your womb, and if I do not love my brother, whom shall I love?

And I, myself, beg you to exhort Jacob concerning me and concerning my sons, for I know that he will assuredly be king over me and my sons, for on the day my father blessed him he made him the higher and me the lower.
And I swear to you that I shall love him, and not desire evil against him all the days of my life but good only." And he sware to her regarding all this matter.
And she called Jacob before the eyes of Esau, and gave him commandment according to the words which she had spoken to Esau.

And he said: “I shall do your pleasure; believe me that no evil will proceed from me or from my sons against Esau, and I shall be first in naught save in love only.” And they ate and drank, she and her sons that night, and she died, three jubilees and one week and one year old, on that night, and her two sons, Esau and Jacob, buried her in the double cave near Sarah, their father’s mother.

chapters.commentary: The chapter is short and devastating. Rebecca calls Jacob to her, charges him to honor Isaac and Esau all the days of his life. Jacob promises. Then Rebecca goes to Isaac and asks him to make Esau swear an oath against violence toward Jacob. Isaac’s answer (verses 13–17) is the chapter’s pivot, and the chapter’s most surprising sentence. I, too, know and see the deeds of Jacob who is with us, how that with all his heart he honours us; but I loved Esau formerly more than Jacob, because he was the first-born; but now I love Jacob more than Esau, for he has done manifold evil deeds, and there is no righteousness in him. Isaac, who blessed Esau in chapter 26 and would have blessed him again if Rebecca had not intervened, says here at the end of his life: now I love Jacob more than Esau. The preference has reversed. The man who could not see it twenty years ago has come to see it. Neither he nor his seed is to be saved, for they are those who will be destroyed from the earth, and who will be rooted out from under heaven, for he has forsaken the Elohim (God) of Abraham and gone after his wives and after their uncleanness and after their error, he and his children. The verdict on Esau is not Jacob’s verdict; it is Isaac’s, and it has come slowly, watched at close range, observed across decades. The chapter is showing the reader what discernment looks like when it ripens. The covenant body’s fathers do not always see clearly in their younger years. They come to see. The reader who is grieving the slowness of older believers in their family who have not yet seen what the awakening sees can lean on this chapter. Isaac came around. He came around late, but he came around. The Father was patient. Verse 17 is the chapter’s quiet doctrine. Fear you not on account of Jacob; for the guardian of Jacob is great and powerful and honoured, and praised more than the guardian of Esau. The architecture chapter 15 named — over the nations He has placed spirits in authority to lead them astray from Him, but over Yashar’el (Israel) He did not appoint any angel or spirit, for He alone is their ruler — is sitting under this verse. Esau’s guardian is one of the spirits over the nations. Jacob’s guardian is Yahuah (God) himself, or the Formed one acting as Adonai (Lord) of the covenant body. The asymmetry is not even close. Isaac is reassuring his wife: do not be afraid; the brother on the wrong side of the line is under a power that cannot stand against the power on the right side of the line. Daniel 10 will narrate the same architecture when the prince of Persia is held back by Michael, the prince of Yashar’el (Israel). The chapter is consistent. Esau swears the oath Rebecca asks for (verses 18–24). Then Rebecca dies that night. She died, three jubilees and one week and one year old, on that night, and her two sons, Esau and Jacob, buried her in the double cave near Sarah, their father’s mother. The brothers come together to bury their mother. Esau’s oath is fresh. The chapter does not yet say whether it will hold. The next two chapters will report it does not. But for one night, after one funeral, the brothers stand together at the cave. The chapter records the moment. Yahuah (God) does not throw away the moment because of what comes after.

chapters.title: Isaac’s Last Words and Death

verses.text: And in the sixth year of this week Isaac called his two sons, Esau and Jacob, and they came to him, and he said to them: "My sons, I am going the way of my fathers, to the eternal house where my fathers are.

Wherefore bury me near Abraham my father, in the double cave in the field of Ephron the Hittite, where Abraham purchased a sepulchre to bury in; in the sepulchre which I digged for myself, there bury me.

And this I command you, my sons, that you practise righteousness and uprightness on the earth, so that Yahuah (God) may bring upon you all that Yahuah (God) said that he would do to Abraham and to his seed.

And love one another, my sons, your brothers as a man who loves his own soul, and let each seek in what he may benefit his brother, and act together on the earth; and let them love each other as their own souls.

And concerning the question of idols, I command and admonish you to reject them and hate them, and love them not; for they are full of deception for those that worship them and for those that bow down to them.

Remember you, my sons, Yahuah Elohim (the LORD God) of Abraham your father, and how I too worshipped Him and served Him in righteousness and in joy, that He might multiply you and increase your seed as the stars of heaven in multitude, and establish you on the earth as the plant of righteousness which will not be rooted out to all the generations for ever. And now I shall make you swear a great oath–for there is no oath which is greater than it by the name glorious and honoured and great and splendid and wonderful and mighty, which created the heavens and the earth and all things together–that you will fear Him and worship Him.

And that each will love his brother with affection and righteousness, and that neither will desire evil against his brother from henceforth for ever all the days of your life, so that you may prosper in all your deeds and not be destroyed.

And if either of you devises evil against his brother, know that from henceforth every one that devises evil against his brother will fall into his hand, and will be rooted out of the land of the living, and his seed will be destroyed from under heaven.

But on the day of turbulence and execration and indignation and anger, with flaming devouring fire as He burnt Sodom, so likewise will He burn his land and his city and all that is his, and he will be blotted out of the book of the discipline of the children of men, and not be recorded in the book of life, but in that which is appointed to destruction, and he will depart into eternal execration; so that their condemnation may be always renewed in hate and in execration and in wrath and in torment and in indignation and in plagues and in disease for ever.

I say and testify to you, my sons, according to the judgment which will come upon the man who wishes to injure his brother." And he divided all his possessions between the two on that day, and he gave the larger portion to him that was the first-born, and the tower and all that was about it, and all that Abraham possessed at the Well of the Oath.
And he said, “This larger portion I shall give to the first-born.”
And Esau said, “I have sold to Jacob and given my birthright to Jacob; to him let it be given, and I have not a single word to say regarding it, for it is his.”

And Isaac said, “May a blessing rest upon you, my sons, and upon your seed this day, for you have given me rest, and my heart is not pained concerning the birthright, lest you should work wickedness on account of it.

May the El Elyon (Most High) Elohim (God) bless the man that works righteousness, him and his seed for ever.” And he ended commanding them and blessing them, and they ate and drank together before him, and he rejoiced because there was one mind between them, and they went forth from him and rested that day and slept.

And Isaac slept on his bed that day rejoicing; and he slept the eternal sleep, and died one hundred and eighty years old. He completed twenty-five weeks and five years; and his two sons Esau and Jacob buried him.
And Esau went to the land of Edom, to the mountains of Seir, and dwelt there.

And Jacob dwelt in the mountains of Hebron, in the tower of the land of the sojournings of his father Abraham, and he worshipped Yahuah (God) with all his heart and according to the visible commands according as He had divided the days of his generations.

And Leah his wife died in the fourth year of the second week of the forty-fifth jubilee, and he buried her in the double cave near Rebecca his mother, to the left of the grave of Sarah, his father’s mother. And all her sons and his sons came to mourn over Leah his wife with him, and to comfort him regarding her, for he was lamenting her.

For he loved her exceedingly after Rachel her sister died; for she was perfect and upright in all her ways and honoured Jacob, and all the days that she lived with him he did not hear from her mouth a harsh word, for she was gentle and peaceable and upright and honourable.
And he remembered all her deeds which she had done during her life, and he lamented her exceedingly; for he loved her with all his heart and with all his soul.

chapters.commentary: Isaac, knowing he is dying, calls Esau and Jacob and says what his father Abraham said to him in chapters 20–22, but compressed into a single chapter and pitched between the two sons rather than to one. Practise righteousness and uprightness on the earth, so that Yahuah (God) may bring upon you all that Yahuah (God) said that he would do to Abraham and to his seed. And love one another, my sons, your brothers as a man who loves his own soul. The dying patriarch knows what his sons are about to do. The chapter knows. Esau will break his oath. Esau’s sons will war on Jacob. The patriarch’s last words are nevertheless a charge to love. The chapter is showing the reader what it looks like to leave a witness to a household that will not honor it. Isaac speaks the truth without softening; he warns about the consequence — every one that devises evil against his brother will fall into his hand, and will be rooted out of the land of the living — and he leaves the rest to the sons’ choices. Verses 7–11 are an oath, and the oath is by the name glorious and honoured and great and splendid and wonderful and mighty, which created the heavens and the earth and all things together. Isaac will not name the four-letter Name in the oath to his sons; he names by the qualities. The reverence chapter 36 shows toward the divine Name is the reverence the third commandment built into the covenant body from Sinai forward. The patriarchs honored the Name by not lightly invoking it. The covenant body recovered the Name as part of recovering the covenant. The reader who has been told that the third commandment is only about not using the Name as profanity has been told a small piece of a larger thing. The third commandment is also about not using the Name as a magical or political tool, not bearing the Name in unworthy fashion, not invoking it where it is not needed and dishonoring it where it is. The patriarchs swore by the qualities of the Name when they did not need to invoke the Name itself. The awakening remnant is recovering this care. Verses 12–17 hand Esau the moment he had been waiting twenty years to refuse. I have sold to Jacob and given my birthright to Jacob; to him let it be given, and I have not a single word to say regarding it, for it is his. Esau says it. In Isaac’s hearing. With Jacob standing there. The birthright is closed. May a blessing rest upon you, my sons… May the El Elyon (Most High) Elohim (God) bless the man that works righteousness, him and his seed for ever. And then the patriarch rests, and sleeps the eternal sleep, one hundred and eighty years old. His two sons bury him. The chapter’s last note (verses 21–24) is the death of Leah, and the note is the most affectionate the patriarchal block has made. He loved her exceedingly after Rachel her sister died; for she was perfect and upright in all her ways and honoured Jacob, and all the days that she lived with him he did not hear from her mouth a harsh word, for she was gentle and peaceable and upright and honourable. And he remembered all her deeds which she had done during her life, and he lamented her exceedingly; for he loved her with all his heart and with all his soul. The Leah who was hated in chapter 28 was loved by Jacob at the end. The Leah whose eyes were weak gave him six sons and a daughter and outlived her sister. The Leah who was slipped into the bridal chamber by her father and lived twenty-two years as the unwanted wife was, by the time she died, the wife the patriarch had come to honor with all his soul. The chapter is saying — quietly, without sentimentality — that the Father runs the long arc, and what looks like mismatch in chapter 28 ripens into beloved by chapter 36. Yahuah (God) does not waste the long obedience of the unfavored. The reader leans on this. The covenant body has many Leahs in it. Yahuah (God) honors them at the end.

chapters.title: The War with Esau

verses.text: And on the day that Isaac the father of Jacob and Esau died, the sons of Esau heard that Isaac had given the portion of the elder to his younger son Jacob and they were very angry.
And they strove with their father, saying: “Why has your father given Jacob the portion of the elder and passed over you, although you are the elder and Jacob the younger?”

And he said to them “Because I sold my birthright to Jacob for a small mess of lentils; and on the day my father sent me to hunt and catch and bring him something that he should eat and bless me, he came with guile and brought my father food and drink, and my father blessed him and put me under his hand.

And now our father has caused us to swear, me and him, that we shall not mutually devise evil, either against his brother, and that we shall continue in love and in peace each with his brother and not make our ways corrupt.”

And they said to him, “We shall not hearken to you to make peace with him; for our strength is greater than his strength, and we are more powerful than he; we shall go against him and slay him, and destroy him and his sons. And if you will not go with us, we shall do hurt to you also.

And now hearken to us: Let us send to Aram and Philistia and Moab and Ammon, and let us choose for ourselves chosen men who are ardent for battle, and let us go against him and do battle with him, and let us exterminate him from the earth before he grows strong.” And their father said to them, “Do not go and do not make war with him lest you fall before him.”
And they said to him, “This too, is exactly your mode of action from your youth until this day, and you are putting your neck under his yoke. We shall not hearken to these words.”
And they sent to Aram, and to ’Adurâm to the friend of their father, and they hired along with them one thousand fighting men, chosen men of war.

And there came to them from Moab and from the children of Ammon, those who were hired, one thousand chosen men, and from Philistia, one thousand chosen men of war, and from Edom and from the Horites one thousand chosen fighting men, and from the Kittim mighty men of war.

And they said to their father: “Go forth with them and lead them, else we shall slay you.” And he was filled with wrath and indignation on seeing that his sons were forcing him to go before (them) to lead them against Jacob his brother.

But afterward he remembered all the evil which lay hidden in his heart against Jacob his brother; and he remembered not the oath which he had sworn to his father and to his mother that he would devise no evil all his days against Jacob his brother.

And notwithstanding all this, Jacob knew not that they were coming against him to battle, and he was mourning for Leah, his wife, until they approached very near to the tower with four thousand warriors and chosen men of war.

And the men of Hebron sent to him saying, “Behold your brother has come against you, to fight you, with four thousand girt with the sword, and they carry shields and weapons”; for they loved Jacob more than Esau. So they told him; for Jacob was a more liberal and merciful man than Esau.

But Jacob would not believe until they came very near to the tower. And he closed the gates of the tower; and he stood on the battlements and spake to his brother Esau and said, “Noble is the comfort wherewith you have come to comfort me for my wife who has died. Is this the oath that you did swear to your father and again to your mother before they died? You have broken the oath, and on the moment that you did swear to your father were you condemned.”

And then Esau answered and said to him, "Neither the children of men nor the beasts of the earth have any oath of righteousness which in swearing they have sworn (an oath valid) for ever; but every day they devise evil one against another, and how each may slay his adversary and foe.
And you do hate me and my children for ever. And there is no observing the tie of brotherhood with you.

Hear these words which I declare to you, If the boar can change its skin and make its bristles as soft as wool, Or if it can cause horns to sprout forth on its head like the horns of a stag or of a sheep, Then shall I observe the tie of brotherhood with you. And if the breasts separated themselves from their mother; for you have not been a brother to me.

And if the wolves make peace with the lambs so as not to devour or do them violence, And if their hearts are towards them for good, Then there will be peace in my heart towards you. And if the lion becomes the friend of the ox and makes peace with him, And if he is bound under one yoke with him and ploughs with him, Then shall I make peace with you.

And when the raven becomes white as the râzâ, Then know that -I have loved you And shall make peace with you. You shall be rooted out, And your sons shall be rooted out, And there shall be no peace for you." And when Jacob saw that he was (so) evilly disposed towards him with his heart, and with all his soul as to slay him, and that he had come springing like the wild boar which comes upon the spear that pierces and kills it, and recoils not from it;
Then he spake to his own and to his servants that they should attack him and all his companions.

chapters.commentary: Isaac is barely buried and Esau’s sons are already at their father’s throat about a birthright that was settled forty years earlier. Why has your father given Jacob the portion of the elder and passed over you? The question has a tell. The sons do not ask Esau whether the portion was rightly transferred. They assume the wrong and demand he avenge it. Esau has a moment, here, to say what he said in Isaac’s hearing in chapter 36 — I have sold to Jacob and given my birthright to Jacob; to him let it be given — and to refuse the war. He does not. He explains the history to his sons (verse 3) and then admits the oath he swore to his parents (verse 4), and then collapses under his sons’ contempt. This too is exactly your mode of action from your youth until this day, and you are putting your neck under his yoke. The sons drag the father into a war the father knew better than to fight. The chapter is showing the reader how the Edomite line forms: not by a single act of malice but by sons learning to override the better instinct of fathers who are not strong enough to hold the line they themselves swore. The coalition Esau’s sons assemble (verses 6, 9–10) names the geography that surrounds the chosen-seed body and stands ready to crush it: Aram, Philistia, Moab, Ammon, Edom, the Horites, the Kittim. Four thousand fighting men marched against Jacob’s tower at Hebron. The numbers carry weight. The seed Yahuah (God) had narrowed across three generations to preserve the covenant body is, at this moment in the narrative, vastly outnumbered by the surrounding peoples who have been ratifying their opposition the whole time. The chapter is not embarrassed about the asymmetry. It records it. The covenant body in the world has never been the bigger demographic, and Jubilees does not pretend otherwise. Verses 17–23 are the chapter’s center. Jacob stands on the battlements of the tower and reminds Esau, in plain hearing of the host, of the oath. Is this the oath that you did swear to your father and again to your mother before they died? You have broken the oath, and on the moment that you did swear to your father were you condemned. Esau’s answer (verses 18–23) is the most candid speech the patriarch makes in the whole book. Neither the children of men nor the beasts of the earth have any oath of righteousness which in swearing they have sworn (an oath valid) for ever; but every day they devise evil one against another, and how each may slay his adversary and foe. This is the line that sets Esau’s house permanently. He is not denying the oath. He is denying that any oath holds its weight under the sun. He has decided in his heart that the world runs on rivalry, that brotherhood is a romantic concept the strong do not honor, that the only law is the law of who can slay whom. Then come the famous adynata: the boar will not change its skin, the wolves will not befriend the lambs, the lion will not yoke with the ox, the raven will not turn white. And there shall be no peace for you. Esau is not declaring his hatred for the day; he is declaring his hatred for the age. For ever is the framing he chooses. The Edom that scripture later names as standing against Yashar’el (Israel) at every crisis — Obadiah, the Psalms, the prophets — is being given its mouth here. The chapter is not interpreting Edom for the reader; it is letting Edom interpret itself. Verse 24’s image is precise. Jacob saw that Esau had come springing like the wild boar which comes upon the spear that pierces and kills it, and recoils not from it. The boar runs onto the weapon. There is no de-escalation possible because the attacker has chosen not to recoil. The covenant body in this age must reckon with that pattern. There are wars that come because the other side has decided they will run onto the spear and never turn. Edom in chapter 37 is one such war. The chapter prepares the reader for what chapter 38 will then do: not a war Jacob sought, but a war that did not allow him to refuse it. Two notes for the awakening reader. First, the line between Esau and his descendants and the systems that operate as Edom in any age is not erased by the centuries. The Edomite spirit — the spirit that swears and breaks, that resents the chosen-seed body for being chosen, that organizes coalitions of nations to destroy the covenant body — is what the prophets call out, and what the antichrist system in any house mimics when it denies the gathering. The four houses have all, in different costumes, made some version of Esau’s speech: there is no oath that holds, the covenant has been transferred, the inheritance is ours, the gathering will not come. The chapter is dismantling that speech before it gets made by anyone besides Esau. Second, the people inside the houses that preach the Edomite version of the gospel are not the boar of verse 24. The systems are. The grandmother who hangs a cross is not the Edomite spirit. The pulpit that taught her the cross replaced the Sabbath is. Every reader of this chapter is to keep the distinction.

chapters.title: The War with Esau

verses.text: And after that Yahudah (Judah) spake to Jacob, his father, and said to him: “Bend your bow, father, and send forth your arrows and cast down the adversary and slay the enemy; and may you have the power, for we shall not slay your brother, for he is such as you, and he is like you: let us give him (this) honour.”
Then Jacob bent his bow and sent forth the arrow and struck Esau, his brother, (on his right breast) and slew him.
And again he sent forth an arrow and struck ’Adôrân the Aramaean, on the left breast, and drove him backward and slew him.
And then went forth the sons of Jacob, they and their servants, dividing themselves into companies on the four sides of the tower.

And Yahudah (Judah) went forth in front, and Naphtali and Gad with him and fifty servants with him on the south side of the tower, and they slew all they found before them, and not one individual of them escaped.

And Levi and Dan and Asher went forth on the east side of the tower, and fifty (men) with them, and they slew the fighting men of Moab and Ammon. And Reuben and Issachar and Zebulon went forth on the north side of the tower, and fifty men with them, and they slew the fighting men of the Philistines.

And Simeon and Benjamin and Enoch, Reuben’s son, went forth on the west side of the tower, and fifty (men) with them, and they slew of Edom and of the Horites four hundred men, stout warriors; and six hundred fled, and four of the sons of Esau fled with them, and left their father lying slain, as he had fallen on the hill which is in ’Adûrâm.
And the sons of Jacob pursued after them to the mountains of Seir. And Jacob buried his brother on the hill which is in ’Adûrâm, and he returned to his house.
And the sons of Jacob pressed hard upon the sons of Esau in the mountains of Seir, and bowed their necks so that they became servants of the sons of Jacob.

And they sent to their father (to inquire) whether they should make peace with them or slay them. And Jacob sent word to his sons that they should make peace, and they made peace with them, and placed the yoke of servitude upon them, so that they paid tribute to Jacob and to his sons always.
And they continued to pay tribute to Jacob until the day that he went down into Egypt.

And the sons of Edom have not got quit of the yoke of servitude which the twelve sons of Jacob had imposed on them until this day. And these are the kings that reigned in Edom before there reigned any king over the children of Yashar’el (Israel) until this day in the land of Edom.
And Bâlâq, the son of Beor, reigned in Edom, and the name of his city was Danâbâ.
And Bâlâq died, and Jobab, the son of Zârâ of Bôsêr, reigned in his stead.
And Jobab died, and ’Asâm, of the land of Têmân, reigned in his stead.

And ’Asâm died, and ’Adâth, the son of Barad, who slew Midian in the field of Moab, reigned in his stead, and the name of his city was Avith. And ’Adâth died, and Salman, from ’Amâsêqâ, reigned in his stead.
And Salman died, and Saul of Râ’abôth (by the) river, reigned in his stead.
And Saul died, and Ba’êlûnân, the son of Achbor, reigned in his stead.
And Ba’êlûnân, the son of Achbor, died, and ’Adâth reigned in his stead, and the name of his wife was Maiṭabîth, the daughter of Mâṭarat, the daughter of Mêtabêdzâ’ab.
These are the kings who reigned in the land of Edom.

chapters.commentary: The chapter opens with Yahudah (Judah) at his father’s elbow. Yahudah (Judah) spake to Jacob, his father, and said to him: “Bend your bow, father, and send forth your arrows and cast down the adversary and slay the enemy; and may you have the power, for we shall not slay your brother, for he is such as you, and he is like you: let us give him (this) honour.” Two things to mark. First, Yahudah (Judah) is the one who speaks. The line of the messianic blessing — the lion who will not depart from between the feet, the one to whom the gathering of the peoples shall be — is already acting as the spokesman of the covenant body before its enemies. The book is foreshadowing. The honor of the kill belongs to the patriarch because the patriarch is the one whose oath was broken. Yahudah (Judah) gives him the line he will use; the king’s role is being modeled here. The chapter is preparing the reader for the kingship that will narrow into Yahudah’s (Judah’s) house. Second, the deference Yahudah (Judah) shows — we shall not slay your brother — is honor of a kind the surrounding nations would not extend. The covenant body fights its kin only when the kin first runs onto the spear. Even then, the dignity of the patriarch is not erased by the act. The chapter is not glorifying war. It is depicting what war looks like when a covenant body is forced to fight one and is still required to be just.
