Jacob slays Esau (verse 2) and slays ’Adôrân the Aramaean, the friend of Esau (verse 3). Then the sons of Jacob divide into four companies and deploy on the four sides of the tower (verse 4). Pause on the formation. Yahudah (Judah) went forth in front, and Naphtali and Gad with him on the south side. Levi and Dan and Asher on the east. Reuben and Issachar and Zebulon on the north. Simeon and Benjamin and Enoch, Reuben’s son, on the west. The twelve sons (with Levi included and Joseph absent in Egypt) hold a four-cornered defense around the tower of Hebron, the patriarchs’ resting place. The numerology lines up: the twelve tribes ringing the camp on the four sides, the four-cornered arrangement that Numbers 2 will later codify for the wilderness encampment, the same fourfold pattern Ezekiel will see at the throne and that Revelation will see at the new Jerusalem. The pattern is older than Sinai. Jubilees plants it here at Hebron, in a battle scene, before any of those later witnesses give it doctrinal weight. The covenant body is being shown as already four-cornered before it ever crosses the Jordan. Verses 8–14 close the engagement. Six hundred Edomites flee with four of Esau’s sons and leave Esau lying slain. Jacob’s sons pursue them to the mountains of Seir, bow their necks, and place the yoke of servitude upon them. And they continued to pay tribute to Jacob until the day that he went down into Egypt. And the sons of Edom have not got quit of the yoke of servitude which the twelve sons of Jacob had imposed on them until this day. The tribute frame matters. Jubilees is not narrating a genocide. The covenant body absorbs Edom’s surrender, accepts the tribute, and lets the defeated brother-line live in subordinated relationship. This is the pattern the Torah will later structure into the laws of war that protect the city offering peace. The covenant body’s victories do not erase the defeated; they bind them under tribute and let them live. Christianity’s seventeen-century habit of reading Old Testament war narratives as ethnic-cleansing manuals is dismantled by Jubilees’ own framing here. The chapter shows what subjugation-rather-than-extermination looks like when the covenant body wins. Verses 15–24 list the kings of Edom. Eight names. Bâlâq the son of Beor heads the list — and the reader who has just spent the chapter watching Esau run onto the spear notices that the same name will reappear in Numbers 22 as the king who hires Balaam to curse Yashar’el (Israel). The kingship of Edom is a single line stretching from chapter 38 forward to the wilderness, and it is the same spirit each time. These are the kings that reigned in Edom before there reigned any king over the children of Yashar’el (Israel) until this day. The phrase is not nostalgic. Jubilees notes the temporal ordering — Edom had kings first — without conceding priority. Edom built its political house before the chosen-seed body did. The chapter is letting the reader feel why: Esau was the elder, Esau chose the world’s pattern early, Esau’s sons organized themselves the way the surrounding nations organized themselves. The covenant body would take centuries to ask for a king, and when it did the prophet would warn it that it was asking to be like the nations (1 Samuel 8). Jubilees has already shown the reader why that ask would be a step backward. The reader who is being told, from any of the four houses, that the chosen-seed body has been replaced by a more enlightened or universal group is being told the Edomite story dressed up in covenant clothing. The Edomite line organized faster, built kings earlier, claimed priority on the strength of being the elder, and stood in nation-coalition against Jacob from the moment of the death of his father. Replacement theology in any house — Christianity’s church replacing Yashar’el (Israel), Hebrew roots’ Torah-keepers replacing the specific covenant body, Islam’s transfer to Ishmael, Judaism’s collapse of the twelve into Yahudah (Judah) alone — is the late costume the same elder-claim wears. Jubilees is showing the reader where that claim was buried, on the hill of ’Adûrâm, beside Esau.

chapters.title: Joseph in Potiphar’s House

verses.text: And Jacob dwelt in the land of his father’s sojournings in the land of Canaan.
These are the generations of Jacob. And Joseph was seventeen years old when they took him down into the land of Egypt, and Potiphar, an eunuch of Pharaoh, the chief cook bought him.
And he set Joseph over all his house, and the blessing of Yahuah (God) came upon the house of the Egyptian on account of Joseph, and Yahuah (God) prospered him in all that he did.
And the Egyptian committed everything into the hands of Joseph; for he saw that Yahuah (God) was with him, and that Yahuah (God) prospered him in all that he did.
And Joseph’s appearance was comely and very beautiful was his appearance, and his master’s wife lifted up her eyes and saw Joseph, and she loved him, and besought him to lie with her.

But he did not surrender his soul, and he remembered Yahuah (God) and the words which Jacob, his father, used to read from amongst the words of Abraham, that no man should commit fornication with a woman who has a husband; that for him the punishment of death has been ordained in the heavens before the El Elyon (Most High) Elohim (God), and the sin will be recorded against him in the eternal books continually before Yahuah (God). And Joseph remembered these words and refused to lie with her.
And she besought him for a year, but he refused and would not listen.

But she embraced him and held him fast in the house in order to force him to lie with her, and closed the doors of the house and held him fast; but he left his garment in her hands and broke through the door and fled without from her presence.

And the woman saw that he would not lie with her, and she calumniated him in the presence of his lord, saying: “Your Hebrew servant, whom you love, sought to force me so that he might lie with me; and it came to pass when I lifted up my voice that he fled and left his garment in my hands when I held him, and he brake through the door.”

And the Egyptian saw the garment of Joseph and the broken door, and heard the words of his wife, and cast Joseph into prison into the place where the prisoners were kept whom the king imprisoned. And he was there in the prison; and Yahuah (God) gave Joseph favour in the sight of the chief of the prison guards and compassion before him, for he saw that Yahuah (God) was with him, and that Yahuah (God) made all that he did to prosper.

And he committed all things into his hands, and the chief of -the prison guards knew of nothing that was with him, for Joseph did everything, and Yahuah (God) perfected it. And he remained there two years. And in those days Pharaoh, king of Egypt, was wroth against his two eunuchs, against the chief butler and against the chief baker, and he put them in ward in the house of the chief cook, in the prison where Joseph was kept.
And the chief of the prison guards appointed Joseph to serve them; and he served before them.
And they both dreamed a dream, the chief butler and the chief baker, and they told it to Joseph.
And as he interpreted to them so it befell them, and Pharaoh restored the chief butler to his office, and the (chief) baker he slew, as Joseph had interpreted to them.
But the chief butler forgot Joseph in the prison, although he had informed him what would befall him, and did not remember to inform Pharaoh how Joseph had told him for he forgot.

chapters.commentary: The chapter opens with a hinge sentence. Jacob dwelt in the land of his father’s sojournings in the land of Canaan. These are the generations of Jacob. Genesis 37 marks the same hinge with the same phrase. Jubilees preserves it. The chapter is announcing that the patriarchal narrative has shifted: the body of Jacob is now the subject, and the next several chapters will trace what happens to that body when its favored son is ripped out of it and the rest of the brothers are left at Hebron without him. Joseph is seventeen years old when he is taken down into Egypt (verse 2) — the age the earlier commentary on chapter 34 already noted as the age of the loss that gave Yom Kippur its grief. The number echoes forward. The covenant body’s deepest wounds are dated in years. Joseph’s purity in Potiphar’s house is the chapter’s first body. Joseph’s appearance was comely and very beautiful was his appearance, and his master’s wife lifted up her eyes and saw Joseph, and she loved him, and besought him to lie with her. But he did not surrender his soul, and he remembered Yahuah (God) and the words which Jacob, his father, used to read from amongst the words of Abraham, that no man should commit fornication with a woman who has a husband. Pause on what Jubilees is saying. Joseph’s resistance is not a private moral instinct. It is a remembered reading. The words which Jacob, his father, used to read from amongst the words of Abraham. The covenant body had a Torah before Sinai. Abraham left writings, the tradition was kept by Jacob, the household read them aloud, and Joseph as a boy in Hebron heard those readings often enough to recall the relevant clause in Egypt under temptation. The inherited Christian frame says the moral law was given at Sinai and was unknown before. Jubilees says the moral law was on Adam and Enoch and Abraham and Jacob, was read in households, and was the force that kept Joseph from sin in a foreign house when he was alone. The Torah is older than Sinai. The new covenant of Jeremiah 31:33 — Torah written on the heart by the Ruach HaKodesh (Holy Spirit) — is the recovery of what was already supposed to be in households since Adam. It is not the introduction of a new way. It is the restoration of the original way. That for him the punishment of death has been ordained in the heavens before the El Elyon (Most High) Elohim (God), and the sin will be recorded against him in the eternal books continually before Yahuah (God). The phrase the eternal books is one Jubilees keeps using, and it has been pressing the same architecture from chapter 4 (Enoch writing) through chapter 30 (the Shechem account engraved as a testimony) and will press it again in chapter 39 here and in chapter 49’s Passover ordinance and in chapter 50’s Sabbath close. The heavenly tables are not metaphor. The chapter is saying Joseph in his early twenties already knew that what he did in Potiphar’s bedroom would be recorded in heaven, and he refused on the strength of that knowledge. The 1234 of Truth — if we keep his commandments — is what is operating in the chapter when Jubilees says Joseph remembered Yahuah (God). Remembrance and commandment-keeping are not separable. The wife’s calumny (verse 10) is the chapter’s underline of how often the world inverts the testimony of the upright. The accuser of Joseph is the woman whose advance he refused. The accusation is the inverse of the truth. Joseph goes to prison on the strength of the slander. And Yahuah (God) gave Joseph favour in the sight of the chief of the prison guards and compassion before him, for he saw that Yahuah (God) was with him, and that Yahuah (God) made all that he did to prosper. Verse 12. The chapter does not dwell on the unfairness. It tracks the favor. Joseph is in the wrong place; Yahuah (God) is with him in the wrong place; the right thing happens in the wrong place because the favor of heaven is not geography-bound. The reader who is suffering inside one of the houses, under accusation that is not true, who has been told they are rebellious for honoring the Sabbath or Pesach or the dietary instructions, who has been told their family has divided over the awakening because they were contentious — that reader is being shown a paradigm here. The favor follows the upright into the wrong place. The wrong place becomes the right place because Yahuah (God) is there. Joseph interprets the dreams of the chief butler and the chief baker (verses 14–18). The butler is restored; the baker is hanged; the butler forgets Joseph. The chapter ends on the forgetting. But the chief butler forgot Joseph in the prison, although he had informed him what would befall him, and did not remember to inform Pharaoh how Joseph had told him for he forgot. The forgetting is the chapter’s structural note. The chosen-seed body is forgotten by the one it served well. Two years pass before remembering happens. The reader who has been in the prison of obscurity, doing the right thing for those who do not reciprocate, is being told what Jubilees keeps telling: the long arc is Yahuah’s (God’s). The forgetting is not the verdict. The verdict comes later.

chapters.title: Pharaoh’s Dreams and Joseph’s Rise

verses.text: And in those days Pharaoh dreamed two dreams in one night concerning a famine which was to be in all the land, and he awoke from his sleep and called all the interpreters of dreams that were in Egypt, and magicians, and told them his two dreams, and they were not able to declare (them).
And then the chief butler remembered Joseph and spake of him to the king, and he brought him forth from the prison, and he told his two dreams before him.

And he said before Pharaoh that his two dreams were one, and he said to him: “Seven years will come (in which there will be) plenty over all the land of Egypt, and after that seven years of famine, such a famine as has not been in all the land.

And now let Pharaoh appoint overseers in all the land of Egypt, and let them store up food in every city throughout the days of the years of plenty, and there will be food for the seven years of famine, and the land will not perish through the famine, for it will be very severe.”

And Yahuah (God) gave Joseph favour and mercy in the eyes of Pharaoh, and Pharaoh said to his servants: “We shall not find such a wise and discreet man as this man, for the spirit of Yahuah (God) is with him.”

And he appointed him the second in all his kingdom and gave him authority over all Egypt, and caused him to ride in the second chariot of Pharaoh. And he clothed him with byssus garments, and he put a gold chain upon his neck, and (a herald) proclaimed before him “’Êl ’Êl wa’ Abîrĕr,” and he placed a ring on his hand and made him ruler over all his house, and magnified him, and said to him: “Only on the throne shall I be greater than you.”

And Joseph ruled over all the land of Egypt, and all the princes of Pharaoh, and all his servants, and all who did the king’s business loved him, for he walked in uprightness, for he was without pride and arrogance, and he had no respect of persons, and did not accept gifts, but he judged in uprightness all the people of the land.

And the land of Egypt was at peace before Pharaoh because of Joseph, for Yahuah (God) was with him, and gave him favour and mercy for all his generations before all those who knew him and those who heard concerning him, and Pharaoh’s kingdom was well ordered, and there was no Satan 1 and no evil person (therein).

And the king called Joseph’s name Sĕphânṭîphâns, 2 and gave Joseph to wife the daughter of Potiphar, the daughter of the priest of Heliopolis, the chief cook. 3 11. And on the day that Joseph stood before Pharaoh he was thirty years old when he stood before Pharaoh. And in that year Isaac died. And it came to pass as Joseph had said in the interpretation of his two dreams, according as he had said it, there were seven years of plenty over all the land of Egypt, and the land of Egypt produced abundantly, one measure (producing) eighteen hundred measures.
And Joseph gathered food into every city until they were full of corn until they could no longer count and measure it for its multitude.

chapters.commentary: Pharaoh dreamed two dreams in one night concerning a famine which was to be in all the land. Two dreams. One night. One famine. Verse 1 plants the chapter’s frame: heaven was already ordering the famine before any human institution had a name for it. Joseph is brought up from the prison at the end of two years (the forgetting in chapter 39 ends here), and the chapter’s spine is in his interpretation. Seven years will come (in which there will be) plenty over all the land of Egypt, and after that seven years of famine, such a famine as has not been in all the land. And now let Pharaoh appoint overseers in all the land of Egypt, and let them store up food in every city throughout the days of the years of plenty, and there will be food for the seven years of famine, and the land will not perish through the famine, for it will be very severe. Verses 3–4. Joseph does not stop at interpretation; he gives policy. Stewardship under heaven’s foreknowledge is the chapter’s pattern. The reader is being shown what wisdom under revelation looks like when it does not panic — it counsels, it ordains overseers, it stores in the fat years against the lean years, it takes the dream as the engineering specification it is. And Yahuah (God) gave Joseph favour and mercy in the eyes of Pharaoh, and Pharaoh said to his servants: “We shall not find such a wise and discreet man as this man, for the spirit of Yahuah (God) is with him.” The line lives in Egyptian mouths. Pharaoh names the spirit of Yahuah (God). Pharaoh, the king of the foremost imperial system on the earth in his day, recognizes the favor on the Hebrew slave he has just hauled out of prison. The chapter is showing what testimony is when it operates from the inside out. Joseph did not preach to Pharaoh. Joseph served. Pharaoh saw. Pharaoh said the line aloud. The pulpit’s habit of asking the awakening believer to witness by haranguing strangers in public places is dismantled by the pattern here. The witness is the life. The recognition follows when the favor is genuine. He walked in uprightness, for he was without pride and arrogance, and he had no respect of persons, and did not accept gifts, but he judged in uprightness all the people of the land. Verse 8. The chapter is drawing a line of vocational character. The covenant body in exile, doing its work without pride and without partiality and without bribery, is what opens doors no harangue could open. Verses 6–10 show the elevation: second chariot, gold chain, the herald’s proclamation, the ring on the hand, ruler over all Egypt, only Pharaoh above him on the throne, the renaming to Sĕphânṭîphâns, the marriage to Asenath the daughter of the priest of Heliopolis. Pause on the marriage. Joseph, the pure son who refused the Egyptian woman in chapter 39, marries an Egyptian woman in chapter 40 — the daughter of the priest of Heliopolis, the high priest of On, the cult of the sun. The reader who has been told in any of the houses that intermarriage is the absolute line will need to reconcile this with Jubilees’ own framing. Two things to say. First, Asenath is given to him by the king’s command; she is not chosen by Joseph in the way Yahudah (Judah) chose his Canaanite wife in chapter 34 against the patriarchal pattern. Second, later tradition (and the underlying Yahudi (Jewish) reading Jubilees inherits) holds that Asenath was either of Hebrew descent or converted fully — the daughter through whom Manasseh and Ephraim were born is depicted as joined to the covenant body, not as remaining outside it. The book is not setting up a second pattern that contradicts chapter 30; it is showing the providential arrangement Yahuah (God) made for the preserving of the line through Egypt’s apparatus. Manasseh and Ephraim will be among the twelve tribes. Ephraim will, in fact, become the poetic name for the whole northern kingdom in the prophets — the scattered seed of Yashar’el (Israel) whose gathering Hosea, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel name with that very name. The line that matters carries. Verse 12 is one Jubilees inserts that Genesis does not pause on. And in that year Isaac died. The chronology is corrected. Isaac, who in the earlier commentary blessed Esau and Jacob jointly in chapter 36, dies in the year of Joseph’s elevation. The patriarchal generation has now finished its handoff. The scene shifts from Hebron to Egypt permanently. The covenant body is preparing — and does not know it is preparing — to be carried into the iron furnace. The chapter closes with Joseph filling the storehouses through seven years of plenty. Joseph gathered food into every city until they were full of corn until they could no longer count and measure it for its multitude. The man who could not be counted as a person — sold into slavery, accused, imprisoned, forgotten — has now produced grain that cannot be counted. The reversal is precise. The chapter is showing the reader what Yahuah (God) does with a forgotten man inside an imperial machine. He counts what cannot be counted, and the system that thought it was using him discovers it is being used.

chapters.title: Yahudah (Judah) and Tamar

verses.text: And in the forty-fifth jubilee, in the second week, (and) in the second year, Yahudah (Judah) took for his first-born Er, a wife from the daughters of Aram, named Tamar.

But he hated, and did not lie with her, because his mother was of the daughters of Canaan, and he wished to take him a wife of the kinsfolk of his mother, but Yahudah (Judah), his father, would not permit him.
And this Er, the first-born of Yahudah (Judah), was wicked, and Yahuah (God) slew him.
And Yahudah (Judah) said to Onan, his brother: “Go in to your brother’s wife and perform the duty of a husband’s brother to her, and raise up seed to your brother.”

And Onan knew that the seed would not be his, (but) his brother’s only, and he went into the house of his brother’s wife, and spilt the seed on the ground, and he was wicked in the eyes of Yahuah (God), and He slew him.

And Yahudah (Judah) said to Tamar, his daughter-in-law: “Remain in your father’s house as a widow till Shelah my son be grown up, and I shall give you to him to wife.” And he grew up; but Bêdsû’êl, the wife of Yahudah (Judah), did not permit her son Shelah to marry. And Bêdsû’êl, the wife of Yahudah (Judah), died in the fifth year of this week.
And in the sixth year Yahudah (Judah) went up to shear his sheep at Timnah. And they told Tamar: “Behold your father-in-law goes up to Timnah to shear his sheep.”
And she put off her widow’s clothes, and put on a veil, and adorned herself, and sat in the gate adjoining the way to Timnah.
And as Yahudah (Judah) was going along he found her, and thought her to be an harlot, and he said to her: “Let me come in to you”; and she said to him: “Come in,” and he went in.

And she said to him: “Give me my hire”; and he said to her: “I have nothing in my hand save my ring that is on my finger, and my necklace, and my staff which is in my hand.” And she said to him: “Give them to me until you do send me my hire”; and he said to her: “I will send to you a kid of the goats”; and he gave them to her, (and he went in to her,) and she conceived by him.
And Yahudah (Judah) went to his sheep, and she went to her father’s house.

And Yahudah (Judah) sent a kid of the goats by the hand of his shepherd, an Adullamite, and he found her not; and he asked the people of the place, saying: “Where is the harlot who was here?” And they said to him: “There is no harlot here with us.”

And he returned and informed him, and said to him that he had not found her; “I asked the people of the place, and they said to me: ‘There is no harlot here.’” And he said: “Let her keep (them) lest we become a cause of derision.”

And when she had completed three months, it was manifest that she was with child, and they told Yahudah (Judah), saying: “Behold Tamar, your daughter-in-law, is with child by whoredom.” And Yahudah (Judah) went to the house of her father, and said to her father and her brothers: “Bring her forth, and let them burn her, for she has wrought uncleanness in Yashar’el (Israel).”
And it came to pass when they brought her forth to bum her that she sent to her father-in-law the ring and the necklace, and the staff, saying: “Discern whose are these, for by him am I with child.”
And Yahudah (Judah) acknowledged, and said: “Tamar is more righteous than I am. And therefore let them burn her not.”
And for that reason she was not given to Shelah, and he did not again approach her.
And after that she bare two sons, Perez and Zerah, in the seventh year of this second week. And thereupon the seven years of fruitfulness were accomplished, of which Joseph spake to Pharaoh.

And Yahudah (Judah) acknowledged that the deed which he had done was evil, for he had lain with his daughter-in-law, and he esteemed it hateful in his eyes, and he acknowledged that he had transgressed and gone astray; for he had uncovered the skirt of his son, and he began to lament and to supplicate before Yahuah (God) because of his transgression.
And we told him in a dream that it was forgiven him because he supplicated earnestly, and lamented, and did not again commit it.

And he received forgiveness because he turned from his sin and from his ignorance, for he transgressed greatly before our Elohim (God); and every one that acts thus, every one who lies with his mother-in-law, let them burn him with fire that he may bum therein, for there is uncleanness and pollution upon them; with fire let them bum them.

And do you command the children of Yashar’el (Israel) that there be no uncleanness amongst them, for every one who lies with his daughter-in-law or with his mother-in-law has wrought uncleanness; with fire let them bum the man who has lain with her, and likewise the woman, and He will turn away wrath and punishment from Yashar’el (Israel). And to Yahudah (Judah) we said that his two sons had not lain with her, and for this reason his seed was established for a second generation, and would not be rooted out.
For in singleness of eye he had gone and sought for punishment, namely, according to the judgment of Abraham, which he had commanded his sons, Yahudah (Judah) had sought to burn her with fire.

chapters.commentary: The chapter is hard. Genesis 38 is hard. Jubilees does not soften it. What Jubilees adds is the heavenly verdict, and the heavenly verdict is the chapter’s whole load. Verse 1 names Yahudah (Judah)’s daughter-in-law: Tamar, daughter of an Aramaean. Yahudah’s (Judah’s) firstborn Er hates her — because his mother was of the daughters of Canaan, and he wished to take him a wife of the kinsfolk of his mother — and Yahuah (God) slays him for his wickedness (verse 3). Onan is given to Tamar, refuses to raise seed to his brother, and is also slain by Yahuah (God) (verse 5). Yahudah (Judah) withholds Shelah from Tamar. Bêdsû’êl, Yahudah’s (Judah’s) Canaanite wife, dies in the fifth year. Tamar, denied the seed she has the covenant right to have raised up to her dead husbands, takes matters into her hands. Verses 8–18 narrate the encounter at Timnah. Tamar veils, sits at the gate, and Yahudah (Judah) goes in to her thinking her to be an harlot. She conceives. She keeps his pledge — the ring, the necklace, the staff. Three months later, when her pregnancy is visible, Yahudah (Judah) calls for her to be burned for whoredom. She produces the pledge. Yahudah (Judah) acknowledges, and said: “Tamar is more righteous than I am. And therefore let them burn her not.” The chapter’s first pressure point is the line that Yahudah (Judah) is forced to say in his own mouth about a daughter-in-law who deceived him. Tamar is more righteous than I am. The chapter is not minimizing the deception. It is naming the relative righteousness inside it. Tamar sought, by the means available to a woman whose father-in-law had denied her the seed she had the right to bear, the levirate seed the covenant required. Yahudah (Judah) had withheld it. She acted to secure the line. The chapter is teaching the reader that the maintaining of the chosen-seed body has, more than once, depended on the courage of women who had to act outside the men’s compromised arrangements: Sarah working with Abraham over Hagar, Rebecca steering the blessing to Jacob, Tamar at Timnah, Ruth at Boaz’s threshing floor. The pattern is the chapter’s quiet doctrine. The Father uses the women the men have failed. The second pressure point is Jubilees’ verdict on Yahudah (Judah). Yahudah (Judah) acknowledged that the deed which he had done was evil, for he had lain with his daughter-in-law, and he esteemed it hateful in his eyes, and he acknowledged that he had transgressed and gone astray; for he had uncovered the skirt of his son, and he began to lament and to supplicate before Yahuah (God) because of his transgression. And we told him in a dream that it was forgiven him because he supplicated earnestly, and lamented, and did not again commit it. And he received forgiveness because he turned from his sin and from his ignorance, for he transgressed greatly before our Elohim (God). Verses 23–25. This is not the Genesis form. Genesis 38 leaves the chapter at the birth of Perez and Zerah. Jubilees inserts the angelic dream, the lamenting, the forgiveness, and the explicit notice that the ground of the forgiveness was Yahudah’s (Judah’s) ignorance — he had not known that the woman at the gate was his daughter-in-law — and his immediate turn upon finding out. Read this with the lens the inherited reading of Paul presses, and the verses contradict the lens. The Christianized reading of Romans 4 collapses forgiveness into bare mental assent, with repentance optional and the obedient turn absent. Jubilees says forgiveness was granted to Yahudah (Judah) because he supplicated earnestly, and lamented, and did not again commit it. The 1234 of Truth — he that says I know him and keeps not his commandments is a liar — is operating in the chapter. The relationship between repentance and forgiveness is not collapsed into a sola-fide formula. It is held inside the covenant body’s actual practice: confess, lament, turn, and the Father, who runs to the prodigal, forgives. The chapter is dismantling the Christianized misreading of justification before the misreading exists. Yahudah (Judah) is not justified by failing to keep the covenant; he is forgiven because he turned from the failure. The distinction matters. Justification is by faith and the Messiah’s (Christ’s) atonement. The pattern of the covenant life is repentance and turning. The Reformation collapsed the two questions and produced the antinomian gospel. Jubilees keeps them separate. The third pressure point is verse 27. And to Yahudah (Judah) we said that his two sons had not lain with her, and for this reason his seed was established for a second generation, and would not be rooted out. Pause on what Jubilees is saying. Tamar conceived from Yahudah (Judah). The line of the kings — Perez through David through the Messiah (Christ) — is preserved through this encounter. The reader who has been told that the messianic line is genealogically immaculate has been told a small piece of a larger thing. The covenant body’s bloodline runs through Tamar of Aram, Rahab of Jericho, Ruth of Moab, and Bathsheba the wife of Uriah — the four women Matthew names in the genealogy of the Messiah (Christ). The Father did not preserve a sterile line. He preserved a real line, and the real line is full of moments where the covenant body almost lost itself and the women acted to keep it. The fourth pressure point is the tares-among-wheat architecture the yoshi-voice framework holds. Er the firstborn of Yahudah (Judah) was a son of Belial — wicked, and Yahuah (God) slew him. Onan was a son of Belial — wicked in the eyes of Yahuah (God), and He slew him. Yahudah’s (Judah’s) own firstborn line was a tare. The chosen-seed body does not run on bloodline alone. The fathers of the covenant produced sons of Belial, and those sons were taken out so the line could carry. Hophni and Phinehas in 1 Samuel 2 will be the same pattern in the Levitical line. The reader who is being told by any of the houses that the awakening believer’s family has to a one been preserved is being misled. Even Yahudah (Judah) lost his first two sons to their own wickedness. The line carries through the third — Shelah, preserved — and the surrogate line raised up through Tamar — Perez and Zerah. The covenant body is sifted at every generation. The sifting is what the Father does to keep the line clean enough for the gathering at the end. A note on intermarriage and the chapter’s framing. Jubilees has been hard on Canaanite intermarriage all the way through (chapter 30, chapter 25, chapter 22). The chapter holds that line — Yahudah’s (Judah’s) marriage to a Canaanite woman is the ground for the firstborn hatred of his Aramaean wife (Er despises Tamar because his mother is a Canaanite and Tamar is not). At the same time, the ground of the preservation is that the line carries through the woman who was not of the daughters of Canaan. The framework is consistent. The chapter is not racial; it is covenantal. Aram is inside the patriarchal kinship network — Rebecca was of Aram, Leah and Rachel were of Aram, the wives that the patriarchs sought were from the kinship body. Tamar of Aram fits the pattern. Bêdsû’êl the Canaanite did not. The Christian habit of reading the Old Testament purity laws as ethnic exclusion is dismantled by the chapter’s actual choreography. The laws are about covenant integrity, not ethnic chauvinism. The stranger and the sojourner of Torah will be welcomed, fed, protected, loved; the Canaanite covenant-betrothal will be refused. The distinctions are real and they are maintained.

chapters.title: Joseph and His Brothers

verses.text: And in the first year of the third week of the forty-fifth jubilee the famine began to come into the land, and the rain refused to be given to the earth, for none whatever fell.
And the earth grew barren, but in the land of Egypt there was food, for Joseph had gathered the seed of the land in the seven years of plenty and had preserved it.
And the Egyptians came to Joseph that he might give them food, and he opened the storehouses where was the grain of the first year, and he sold it to the people of the land for gold.

(Now the famine was very sore in the land of Canaan), and Jacob heard that there was food in Egypt, and he sent his ten sons that they should procure food for him in Egypt; but Benjamin he did not send, and (the ten sons of Jacob) arrived (in Egypt) among those that went (there.)

And Joseph recognized them, but they did not recognize him, and he spake to them and questioned them, and he said to them: “Are you not spies, and have you not come to explore the approaches of the land?” And he put them in ward.
And after that he set them free again, and detained Simeon alone and sent off his nine brothers. And he filled their sacks with corn, and he put their gold in their sacks, and they did not know.
And he commanded them to bring their younger brother, for they had told him their father was living and their younger brother.

And they went up from the land of Egypt and they came to the land of Canaan; and they told their father all that had befallen them, and how the lord of the country had spoken roughly to them, and had seized Simeon till they should bring Benjamin.
And Jacob said: “Me have you bereaved of my children! Joseph is not and Simeon also is not, and you will take Benjamin away. On me has your wickedness come.”

And he said: “My son will not go down with you lest perchance he fall sick; for their mother gave birth to two sons, and one has perished, and this one also you will take from me. If perchance he took a fever on the road, you would bring down my old age with sorrow to death.” For he saw that their money had been returned to every man in his sack, and for this reason he feared to send him.

And the famine increased and became sore in the land of Canaan, and in all lands save in the land of Egypt, for many of the children of the Egyptians had stored up their seed for food from the time when they saw Joseph gathering seed together and putting it in storehouses and preserving it for the years of famine.
And the people of Egypt fed themselves thereon during the first year of their famine.
But when Yashar’el (Israel) saw that the famine was very sore in the land, and there was no deliverance, he said to his sons: “Go again, and procure food for us that we die not.”

And they said: “We shall not go; unless our youngest brother go with us, we shall not go.” And Yashar’el (Israel) saw that if he did not send him with them, they should all perish by reason of the famine.
And Reuben said: “Give him into my hand, and if I do not bring him back to you, slay my two sons instead of his soul.” And he said to him He will not go with you."
And Yahudah (Judah) came near and said: “Send him with me, and if I do not bring him back to you, let me bear the blame before you all the days of my life.”

And he sent him with them in the second year of this week on the first day of the month, and they came to the land of Egypt with all those who went, and (they had) presents in their hands, stacte and almonds and terebinth nuts and pure honey.

And they went and stood before Joseph, and he saw Benjamin his brother, and he knew him, and said to them: “Is this your youngest brother?” And they said to him: “It is he.” And he said: “The Yahuah (God) be gracious to you, my son!” And he sent him into his house and he brought forth Simeon to them and he made a feast for them, and they presented to him the gift which they had brought in their hands.
And they ate before him and he gave them all a portion, but the portion of Benjamin was seven times larger than that of any of theirs.
And they ate and drank and arose and remained with their asses.

And Joseph devised a plan whereby he might learn their thoughts as to whether thoughts of peace prevailed amongst them, and he said to the steward who was over his house: “Fill all their sacks with food, and return their money to them into their vessels, and my cup, the silver cup out of which I drink, put it in the sack of the youngest, and send them away.”

chapters.commentary: The famine arrives in the first year of the third week of the forty-fifth jubilee. Verse 1. Jubilees keeps dating things. The calendar is the book’s running spine. The famine that Pharaoh dreamed in chapter 40 is now landing. Jacob’s household sends ten sons to Egypt for food — but Benjamin he did not send. Verse 4. The structure is a mirror of chapter 34: ten brothers without their twelfth. Last time they returned without Joseph; this time Jacob refuses to let Benjamin travel because the loss of Joseph already tore him in half. The chapter is staging the test deliberately. Joseph recognizes them. They do not recognize him. The asymmetry is load-bearing. The man who was sold has the eyes of recognition; the brothers who sold him have only the eyes of need. The chapter is making a point that runs all the way through the awakening pattern: those who have been put outside the covenant frame for telling the truth about what was lost — Sabbath-keepers in Christian families, sacred-name hearers in Christian and Yahudi (Jewish) and Hebrew-roots families — recognize their kin even when their kin do not yet recognize them. The recognition is not symmetrical until repentance happens. Joseph knows it. Joseph waits. The reader who is grieving the slow recognition in their own family is being shown what to do: hold the recognition without forcing it, set the test that lets the truth come out, and wait for the moment when the brothers’ goodness shows. Joseph models the patience. Joseph accuses them of being spies. He puts them in ward. He releases them. He keeps Simeon. He sends nine back. He fills their sacks and returns their gold without their knowing. He commands them to bring the youngest. Verses 5–8. The test is being designed. The point of the test is not punishment — Joseph could have walked into the room and embraced them at any moment. The point of the test is to find out whether the brothers who sold the favored son will protect the second favored son when he is in the same kind of jeopardy. The chapter is not letting the reader miss this. The whole testing arc that runs from chapter 42 through chapter 43 is one sustained question: have the men changed? Reuben offers his two sons as collateral for Benjamin. Slay my two sons instead of his soul. Verse 18. Jacob refuses. He will not go with you. Verse 18. The famine deepens. Yahudah (Judah) comes near. Send him with me, and if I do not bring him back to you, let me bear the blame before you all the days of my life. Verse 19. Jacob relents. The point of the chapter is who comes near and what they offer. Reuben offers his sons; the offer is morally hideous and Jacob sees through it. Yahudah (Judah) offers his own person and his own blame for life. The chapter is again putting Yahudah (Judah) at the front of the body. The man whose own house was almost rooted out by the deaths of Er and Onan is the man who comes near and offers himself. The repentance that Yahudah (Judah) entered at the end of chapter 41 — he turned from his sin and from his ignorance — has produced a man who can stand surety for his brother. The covenant body does not pretend the past is unconsequential; the covenant body lets the past forge the present. In Egypt, the brothers stand before Joseph. And they presented to him the gift which they had brought in their hands… And he said: “Is this your youngest brother?” And they said to him: “It is he.” And he said: “The Yahuah (God) be gracious to you, my son!” Verses 20–21. Joseph blesses Benjamin in his brothers’ hearing. The brothers do not yet know who is blessing. The chapter is producing the irony with a soft hand; it does not need to underline. Joseph then has the meal prepared. Benjamin’s portion is seven times larger than that of any of theirs (verse 23). Jubilees does not flag the seven; it lets the number speak. The number of completion, the number of the sabbath, the number of the heavenly tables — the favored brother gets seven portions because he is the next in the chosen-seed sequence the chapter is tracking. The test continues into the night. The cup is planted. The morning comes.

chapters.title: Joseph and His Brothers

verses.text: And he did as Joseph had told him, and filled all their sacks for them with food and put their money in their sacks, and put the cup in Benjamin’s sack.

And early in the morning they departed, and it came to pass that, when they had gone from thence, Joseph said to the steward of his house: “Pursue them, run and seize them, saying, ‘For good you have requited me with evil; you have stolen from me the silver cup out of which my lord drinks.’ And bring back to me their youngest brother, and fetch (him) quickly before I go forth to my seat of judgment.”
And he ran after them and said to them according to these words.

And they said to him: “Elohim (God) forbid that your servants should do this thing, and steal from the house of your lord any utensil, and the money also which we found in our sacks the first time, we your servants brought back from the land of Canaan.

How then should we steal any utensil? Behold here are we and our sacks; search, and wherever you find the cup in the sack of any man amongst us, let him be slain, and we and our asses will serve your lord.”

And he said to them: “Not so, the man with whom I find, him only shall I take as a servant, and you will return in peace to your house.” And as he was searching in their vessels, beginning with the eldest and ending with the youngest, it was found in Benjamin’s sack.
And they rent their garments, and laded their asses, and returned to the city and came to the house of Joseph, and they all bowed themselves on their faces to the ground before him.

And Joseph said to them: “You have done evil.” And they said: “What shall we say and how shall we defend ourselves? Our lord has discovered the transgression of his servants; behold we are the servants of our lord, and our asses also.”

And Joseph said to them: “I too fear Yahuah (God); as for you, go you to your homes and let your brother be my servant, for you have done evil.. Know you not that a man delights in his cup as I with this cup? And yet you have stolen it from me.”

And Yahudah (Judah) said: "O my lord, let your servant, I pray you, speak a word in my lord’s ear; two brothers did your servant’s mother bear to our father; one went away and was lost, and has not been found, and he alone is left of his mother, and your servant our father loves him, and his life also is bound up with the life of this (lad). And it will come to pass, when we go to your servant our father, and the lad is not with us, that he will die, and we shall bring down our father with sorrow to death.

Now rather let me, your servant, abide instead of the boy as a bondsman to my lord, and let the lad go with his brethren, for I became surety for him at the hand of your servant our father, and if I do not bring him back, your servant will bear the blame to our father for ever."
And Joseph saw that they were all accordant in goodness one with another, and he could not refrain himself, and he told them that he was Joseph.
And he conversed with them in the Hebrew tongue and fell on their neck and wept. But they knew him not and they began to weep.

And he said to them: "Weep not over me, but hasten and bring my father to me; and you see that it is my mouth that speaks and the eyes of my brother Benjamin see. For behold this is the second year of the famine, and there are still five years without harvest or fruit of trees or ploughing.

Come down quickly you and your households, so that you perish not through the famine, and do not be grieved for your possessions, for Yahuah (God) sent me before you to set things in order that many people might live.
And tell my father that I am still alive, and you, behold, you see that Yahuah (God) has made me as a father to Pharaoh, and ruler over his house and over all the land of Egypt.
And tell my father of all my glory, and all the riches and glory that Yahuah (God) has given Me."

And by the command of the mouth of Pharaoh he gave them chariots and provisions for the way, and he gave them all many-coloured raiment and silver. And to their father he sent raiment and silver and ten asses which carried com, and he sent them away.
And they went up and told their father that Joseph was alive, and was measuring out corn to all the nations of the earth, and that he was ruler over all the land of Egypt.

And their father did not believe it, for he was beside himself in his mind; but when he saw the wagons which Joseph had sent, the life of his spirit revived, and he said: “It is enough for me if Joseph lives; I will go down and see him before I die.”

chapters.commentary: The pursuit. The discovery. The brothers’ return to the city in their torn garments. The chapter compresses what Genesis takes longer to show. Joseph said to them: “I too fear Yahuah (God); as for you, go you to your homes and let your brother be my servant, for you have done evil. Know you not that a man delights in his cup as I with this cup? And yet you have stolen it from me.” Verse 10. The line is set up to elicit the speech that will end the test, and Yahudah (Judah) gives it. Verses 11–13 are Yahudah’s (Judah’s) speech, and the speech is the chapter’s load. Two brothers did your servant’s mother bear to our father; one went away and was lost, and has not been found, and he alone is left of his mother, and your servant our father loves him, and his life also is bound up with the life of this (lad). And it will come to pass, when we go to your servant our father, and the lad is not with us, that he will die, and we shall bring down our father with sorrow to death. Now rather let me, your servant, abide instead of the boy as a bondsman to my lord, and let the lad go with his brethren, for I became surety for him at the hand of your servant our father, and if I do not bring him back, your servant will bear the blame to our father for ever. Yahudah (Judah) offers his life for Benjamin’s. This is the inversion of Yahudah’s (Judah’s) own role in chapter 34’s loss of Joseph, where he was the one who proposed the sale into Egypt to save the brothers from killing him. The same man who sold his brother into Egypt is now offering himself as a bondsman in Egypt to save another brother from the same fate. The repentance has come full circle. The covenant body’s standing has been redeemed in the person of its leading son. This is the moment Jubilees has been building. Joseph saw that they were all accordant in goodness one with another, and he could not refrain himself, and he told them that he was Joseph. And he conversed with them in the Hebrew tongue and fell on their neck and wept. But they knew him not and they began to weep. Verses 14–15. The chapter flags two details. First, the brothers were accordant in goodness one with another. The test was designed to find this out. They had it. The covenant body had been re-knit. Second, Joseph speaks in the Hebrew tongue. The Egyptian lord drops the Egyptian language and the brothers hear their mother tongue from a face they thought was foreign. The pattern is the awakening pattern. The moment of recognition in the covenant body comes when the language of the fathers is heard from the mouth of the one the body did not yet recognize. Sacred names. The festivals named in their seasons. The Sabbath kept on the day Yahuah (God) hallowed. These are the Hebrew tongue of the awakening. When they are heard in the mouth of someone the family had thought was lost or foreign, the recognition follows. Verses 16–20 are Joseph’s speech to his brothers, and it is one of the most theologically loaded passages in Genesis or Jubilees. Yahuah (God) sent me before you to set things in order that many people might live. And tell my father that I am still alive, and you, behold, you see that Yahuah (God) has made me as a father to Pharaoh, and ruler over his house and over all the land of Egypt. And tell my father of all my glory, and all the riches and glory that Yahuah (God) has given Me. Pause on the formula. Yahuah (God) sent me. The selling into Egypt was not a tragedy that Yahuah (God) made the best of. The selling was a sending. The brothers’ sin was used by Yahuah (God) — not approved, not endorsed — to produce the preserving of many lives. The doctrine is precise: Yahuah (God) does not collaborate in sin, but the sin of Yahuah’s (God’s) covenant body has never been able to overrule the long arc of his sending. The pattern is true at chapter 43 about the selling of Joseph; the pattern is true at the cross about the betrayal of Yahusha (Jesus); the pattern is true about the scattering of Yashar’el (Israel) — Yahuah (God) used the divorce of Hosea 1 to send the seed into the nations so they could preserve the knowledge of the covenant body across the centuries until the gathering. Yahuah (God) sent me before you is the keystone phrase the prophets and the apostolic writings will quote in different forms. Joseph in chapter 43 names the architecture of the entire scattering and gathering arc. A theological note for the reader who has been told that the loss of Joseph and the loss of the ten northern tribes were unrelated. They are not unrelated. Joseph is the type. The Father takes the favored son out of the body at seventeen, sends him into the foreign land, hides him in the foreign land, raises him there, makes him a ruler of provision, and brings him back when the body is so hungry it can no longer pretend it is not hungry. The northern kingdom — Ephraim, Yosef, the house of the north — is the body the prophets give the same shape to. The scattered seed is being preserved in the foreign lands. The Father will bring them back when the body is so hungry it cannot pretend any longer. Hosea, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and Zechariah all draw on this Joseph pattern when they prophesy the gathering. The Christian reading collapses the scattered tribes into a metaphor for the church, which means the Joseph pattern in chapter 43 has nothing to do with anything that ever literally happens. The Yahudi (Jewish) reading collapses them into Yahudah (Judah) alone, which means the favored son is functionally not coming home. The Hebrew roots reading makes Joseph a metaphor for any Torah-keeper, which means the line the prophets drew between Ephraim and the nations is erased. All three readings are versions of the binary lie. Jubilees in chapter 43 is naming the second category — the scattered seed — by its prototype. The reader is to hold that. Pharaoh sends the brothers home with chariots, provisions, raiment, and silver. Jacob, told that Joseph is alive, did not believe it, for he was beside himself in his mind; but when he saw the wagons which Joseph had sent, the life of his spirit revived, and he said: “It is enough for me if Joseph lives; I will go down and see him before I die.” Verse 24. The patriarch’s spirit is revived. The covenant body’s father lives long enough to see the lost favored son restored. The chapter is showing the reader that the long twenty-two-year grief of Yom Kippur — the grief the earlier commentary on chapter 34 named — has its end. Yom Kippur is not the last word. Joseph is alive. The family will be reunited. The chapter is showing that restoration follows confession. Yahudah (Judah) confessed. The brothers were accordant in goodness one with another. The favored son revealed himself. The father’s spirit revived. The pattern is the gathering pattern. It will play again at the end of the age, and the end of the age will look very much like chapter 43.

chapters.title: Jacob’s Journey to Egypt

verses.text: And Yashar’el (Israel) took his journey from Haran from his house on the new moon of the third month, and he went on the way of the Well of the Oath, and he offered a sacrifice to the Elohim (God) of his father Isaac on the seventh of this month.
And Jacob remembered the dream that he had seen at Bethel, and he feared to go down into Egypt.

And while he was thinking of sending word to Joseph to come to him, and that he would not go down, he remained there seven days, if perchance he should see a vision as to whether he should remain or go down.

And he celebrated the harvest festival of the first-fruits with old grain, for in all the land of Canaan there was not a handful of seed (in the land), for the famine was over all the beasts and cattle and birds, and also over man.

And on the sixteenth Yahuah (God) appeared to him, and said to him, “Jacob, Jacob”; and he said, “Here am I.” And He said to him: “I am the Elohim (God) of your fathers, the Elohim (God) of Abraham and Isaac; fear not to go down into Egypt, for I will there make of you a great nation.

I shall go down with you, and I shall bring you up (again), and in this land will you be buried, and Joseph will put his hands upon your eyes. Fear not; go down into Egypt.” And his sons rose up, and his sons’ sons, and they placed their father and their possessions upon wagons.
And Yashar’el (Israel) rose up from the Well of the Oath on the sixteenth of this third month, and he went to the land of Egypt.

And Yashar’el (Israel) sent Yahudah (Judah) before him to his son Joseph to examine the Land of Goshen, for Joseph had told his brothers that they should come and dwell there that they might be near him.
And this was the goodliest (land) in the land of Egypt, and near to him, for all (of them) and also for the cattle.

And these are the names of the sons of Jacob who went into Egypt with Jacob their father. Reuben, the first-born of Yashar’el (Israel); and these are the names of his sons: Enoch, and Pallu, and Hezron and Carmi–five.
Simeon and his sons; and these are the names of his sons: Jemuel, and Jamin, and Ohad, and Jachin, and Zohar, and Shaul, the son of the Zephathite woman–seven.
Levi and his sons; and these are the names of his sons: Gershon, and Kohath, and Merari–four.
Yahudah (Judah) and his sons; and these are the names of his sons: Shela, and Perez, and Zerah–four.
Issachar and his sons; and these are the names of his sons: Tola, and Phûa, and Jâsûb, and Shimron–five. Zebulon and his sons; and these are the names of his sons: Sered, and Elon, and Jahleel–four.

And these are the sons of Jacob, and their sons, whom Leah bore to Jacob in Mesopotamia, six, and their one sister, Dinah: and all the souls of the sons of Leah, and their sons, who went with Jacob their father into Egypt, were twenty-nine, and Jacob their father being with them, they were thirty.
And the sons of Zilpah, Leah’s handmaid, the wife of Jacob, whom she bore to Jacob, Gad and Asher.
And these are the names of their sons who went with him into Egypt: the sons of Gad: Ziphion, and Haggi, and Shuni, and Ezbon, (and Eri) and Areli, and Arodi–eight.
And the sons of Asher: Imnah, and Ishvah, (and Ishvi), and Beriah, and Serah, their one sister–six. All the souls were fourteen, and all those of Leah were forty-four.
And the sons of Rachel, the wife of Jacob: Joseph and Benjamin.
And there were born to Joseph in Egypt before his father came into Egypt, those whom Asenath, daughter of Potiphar priest of Heliopolis bare to him, Manasseh, and Ephraim–three.
And the sons of Benjamin: Bela and Becher, and Ashbel, Gera, and Naaman, and Ehi, and Rosh, and Muppim, and Huppim, and Ard–eleven.
And all the souls of Rachel were fourteen. And the sons of Bilhah, the handmaid of Rachel, the wife of Jacob, whom she bare to Jacob, were Dan and Naphtali.
And these are the names of their sons who went with them into Egypt. And the sons of Dan were Hushim, and Sâmôn, and Asûdî, and ’Îjâka, and Salômôn–six.
And they died the year in which they entered into Egypt, and there was left to Dan Hushim alone.
And these are the names of the sons of Naphtali: Jahziel, and Guni, and Jezer, and Shallum, and ‘Îv.
And ‘Îv, who was born after the years of famine, died in Egypt. And all the souls of Rachel were twenty-six.
And all the souls of Jacob which went into Egypt were seventy souls. These are his children and his children’s children, in all seventy; but five died in Egypt before Joseph, and had no children.

And in the land of Canaan two sons of Yahudah (Judah) died, Er and Onan, and they had no children, and the children of Yashar’el (Israel) buried those who perished, and they were reckoned among the seventy nations.

chapters.commentary: And Yashar’el (Israel) took his journey from Haran from his house on the new moon of the third month, and he went on the way of the Well of the Oath, and he offered a sacrifice to the Elohim (God) of his father Isaac on the seventh of this month. Verse 1. The chapter opens with Jacob keeping the festival the first chapter of Yom-Kippur week was already keeping in the patriarchs’ rhythm: the Feast of Weeks at the Well of the Oath in the third month — the same festival Jubilees has chapter 6 instituted on Noah’s altar after the Flood and chapter 22 held with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob together. The chapter is showing the patriarch refusing to let the famine and the journey unsettle the calendar. He stops at the Well of the Oath. He waits. He keeps the appointed feast. He sacrifices. The covenant body’s father will not move into Egypt without keeping the festival first. Verse 4 names what the keeping cost: he celebrated the harvest festival of the first-fruits with old grain, for in all the land of Canaan there was not a handful of seed (in the land), for the famine was over all the beasts and cattle and birds, and also over man. Old grain. There was no first-fruits to offer because the year had produced no first-fruits. Jacob kept the festival anyway, with last year’s grain. The chapter is teaching the reader that the appointed feasts are not for the years when keeping them is easy. The feast is older than the harvest; the feast belongs to Yahuah (God) before it belongs to the earth’s particular yield. The Sabbath is not for the people of leisure; the festival is not for the people of plenty. The patriarch keeps with what he has when the year has given him nothing. The covenant body in any age — including the awakening remnant in the lean times of the present age — is to keep the festivals with old grain when the new is not there. Yahuah (God) appears to him. Jacob, Jacob. Verse 5. The double name is the Sinai pattern — Moses, Moses — and the Genesis pattern — Abraham, Abraham at the binding of Isaac — and the gospels’ pattern — Saul, Saul. The doubling marks revelation that is direct and personal. I am the Elohim (God) of your fathers, the Elohim (God) of Abraham and Isaac; fear not to go down into Egypt, for I will there make of you a great nation. I shall go down with you, and I shall bring you up (again), and in this land will you be buried, and Joseph will put his hands upon your eyes. Fear not; go down into Egypt. Verses 5–6. The covenant is unbroken across the descent. I shall go down with you. The chapter is making the doctrinal point that the chosen-seed body is not abandoned in exile. The descending is part of the pattern. The exile of Yashar’el (Israel) into the nations — the long second exile that the prophets will later name — is anticipated here in the first exile into Egypt. The Father goes down with the body. The Father brings the body back up. Joseph will put his hands upon your eyes — the favored son who was sent ahead will close the eyes of the patriarch who has come down to him. The architecture of the gathering at the end of the age is already visible. The seventy souls (verses 11–34) are the patriarchal census of the descent. Jubilees lists them tribe by tribe, with Levi’s three sons named, Yahudah’s (Judah’s) three sons named (with Er and Onan already dead and not counted), and so on. The closing line of the list (verse 34) is one Genesis does not give: and in the land of Canaan two sons of Yahudah (Judah) died, Er and Onan, and they had no children, and the children of Yashar’el (Israel) buried those who perished, and they were reckoned among the seventy nations. The seventy souls of Jacob’s descent answer to the seventy nations of chapter 10’s table — Noah’s grandsons, the seventy from whom all the peoples of the earth descend. The number is structural. Yashar’el (Israel) is one nation among the seventy in Yahuah’s (God’s) ordering, and Yashar’el (Israel) goes down to Egypt with seventy souls so that the parallel is locked in. The chapter is saying the covenant body holds, in itself, the count of the nations. The body that will be sent into the nations and then gathered out of them is patterned, from the start, on the seventy of the nations themselves. This is not heathen-becoming-Yashar’el (Israel) by faith. This is Yashar’el (Israel) carrying, in its own seventy souls, the answer to the seventy of the nations.

chapters.title: Jacob in Egypt

verses.text: And Yashar’el (Israel) went into the country of Egypt, 2172 A M. into the land of Goshen, on the new moon of the fourth month, in the second year of the third week of the forty-fifth jubilee.
And Joseph went to meet his father Jacob, to the land of Goshen, and he fell on his father’s neck and wept.

And Yashar’el (Israel) said to Joseph: “Now let me die since I have seen you, and now may Yahuah Elohim (the LORD God) of Yashar’el (Israel) be blessed, the Elohim (God) of Abraham and the Elohim (God) of Isaac who has not withheld His mercy and His grace from His servant Jacob.

It is enough for me that I have seen your face whilst I am yet alive; yea, true is the vision which I saw at Bethel. Blessed be Yahuah my Elohim (the LORD my God) for ever and ever, and blessed be His name.”

And Joseph and his brothers ate bread before their father and drank wine, and Jacob rejoiced with exceeding great joy because he saw Joseph eating with his brothers and drinking before him, and he blessed the Creator of all things who had preserved him, and had preserved for him his twelve sons.

And Joseph had given to his father and to his brothers as a gift the right of dwelling in the land of Goshen and in Rameses and all the region round about, which he ruled over before Pharaoh. And Yashar’el (Israel) and his sons dwelt in the land of Goshen, the best part of the land of Egypt; and Yashar’el (Israel) was one hundred and thirty years old when he came into Egypt, And Joseph nourished his father and his brethren and also their possessions with bread as much as sufficed them for the seven years of the famine.

And the land of Egypt suffered by reason of the famine, and Joseph acquired all the land of Egypt for Pharaoh in return for food, and he got possession of the people and their cattle and everything for Pharaoh.

And the years of the famine were accomplished, and Joseph gave to the people in the land seed and food that they might sow (the land) in the eighth year, for the river had overflowed all the land of Egypt.

For in the seven years of the famine it had not overflowed and had irrigated only a few places on the banks of the river, but now it overflowed and the Egyptians sowed the land, and it bore much corn that year.

And this was the first year of the fourth week of the forty-fifth jubilee. And Joseph took of the corn of the harvest the fifth part for the king and left four parts for them for food and for seed, and Joseph made it an ordinance for the land of Egypt until this day.

And Yashar’el (Israel) lived in the land of Egypt seventeen years, and all the days which he lived were three jubilees, one hundred and forty-seven years, and he died in the fourth year of the fifth week of the forty-fifth jubilee. And Yashar’el (Israel) blessed his sons before he died and told them everything 1 that would befall them in the land of Egypt; and he made known to them what would come upon them in the last days, and blessed them and gave to Joseph two portions 2 in the land.

And he slept with his fathers, and he was buried in the double cave in the land of Canaan, near Abraham his father in the grave which he dug for himself in the double cave in the land of Hebron. 3 16. And he gave all his books and the books of his fathers to Levi his son that he might preserve them and renew them for his children until this day. 4

chapters.commentary: Jacob enters Goshen. Joseph meets his father. He fell on his father’s neck and wept. Verse 2. Jacob’s first words are the chapter’s center. Now let me die since I have seen you, and now may Yahuah Elohim (the LORD God) of Yashar’el (Israel) be blessed, the Elohim (God) of Abraham and the Elohim (God) of Isaac who has not withheld His mercy and His grace from His servant Jacob. It is enough for me that I have seen your face whilst I am yet alive; yea, true is the vision which I saw at Bethel. Blessed be Yahuah my Elohim (the LORD my God) for ever and ever, and blessed be His name. Verses 3–4. The patriarch named Yashar’el (Israel) blesses Yahuah (God) using the name. The Bethel vision he had as a younger man — the ladder, the promises, the angels ascending and descending — is named true. The covenant body’s testimony at the late-life moment is to confirm the youth-vision. The chapter is showing the reader that the long arc is faithful. What was promised at Bethel held through Laban’s house, through Esau’s coalition, through the loss of Joseph at seventeen, through the famine, through the descent into Egypt. The patriarch sees the favored son’s face and pronounces that he has seen enough. Verses 6–10 narrate the practical settlement: Goshen, Rameses, the best part of the land, food enough for the seven years, the gradual acquisition of all Egypt for Pharaoh in return for grain. The chapter notes that Joseph acquired all the land of Egypt for Pharaoh in return for food, and he got possession of the people and their cattle and everything for Pharaoh. Verse 8. The reader who has been told that the Joseph-policy was a generous public-distribution program is being shown the full consequence: the famine produced a complete transfer of property from the people to the king. Joseph the covenant-body steward administered an arrangement that, at the end of seven years, had reduced free Egyptian peasants to Pharaoh’s serfs. The chapter is not wringing its hands. It is recording it. The reader is being shown that the same crisis that preserved the covenant body’s life concentrated political power in the imperial center. This is the architecture that, two generations later, will produce the new king who knew not Joseph and the iron furnace of chapter 46. Concentrated power inherited by a hostile administrator becomes the bondage of those whose lives the original administrator saved. The pattern is structural; it has not stopped operating in any age. Verse 14 is the patriarch’s last act. And Yashar’el (Israel) blessed his sons before he died and told them everything that would befall them in the land of Egypt; and he made known to them what would come upon them in the last days, and blessed them and gave to Joseph two portions in the land. The patriarch sees the last days. Jubilees does not unfold the content here — Genesis 49 does — but the book notes that the patriarch’s deathbed prophecy reaches all the way to the end of the age. Last days is the same prophetic phrase Isaiah 2:2 uses, the same phrase Jeremiah 23:20 uses, the same phrase Daniel 10:14 uses. The patriarch on his deathbed sees the gathering. The chapter is making sure the reader does not miss it. The favorite-son Joseph receives the double portion that will become Manasseh and Ephraim — the architecture by which the northern kingdom is named Ephraim in the prophets and is the body whose gathering Hosea 1, Jeremiah 31, and Ezekiel 37 announce. Verse 16 is the chapter’s last note, and it is one Jubilees inserts that Genesis does not. And he gave all his books and the books of his fathers to Levi his son that he might preserve them and renew them for his children until this day. The patriarchal library — all the books, not one book — is given to Levi for preservation and renewal across the generations. The Torah is not new at Sinai. The patriarchs had books. Adam wrote, Enoch wrote, Noah received, Abraham left writings (chapter 39 already named them), Jacob is depicted as the trustee of the whole patriarchal library, and Levi is given the keeping of it. The covenant body’s literature was always in priestly hands before Sinai, and Sinai is the public ratification of what had already been kept in the household chain. The Christian habit of dating revelation from Sinai forward — and then abolishing what Sinai gave because it was supposedly a temporary arrangement — is dismantled by Jubilees’ own framing. The books were before Sinai. The books were Adam’s. The Torah is the book of the household before it is the book of the nation. It cannot be abolished without abolishing the patriarchal inheritance itself.

chapters.title: The Death of Joseph and the Oppression

verses.text: And it came to pass that after Jacob died the children of Yashar’el (Israel) multiplied in the land of Egypt, and they became a great nation, and they were of one accord in heart, so that brother loved brother and every man helped his brother, and they increased abundantly and multiplied exceedingly, ten weeks of years, all the days of the life of Joseph.

And there was no Satan nor any evil all the days of the life of Joseph which he lived after his father Jacob, for all the Egyptians honoured the children of Yashar’el (Israel) all the days of the life of Joseph.

And Joseph died being a hundred and ten years old; seventeen years he lived in the land of Canaan, and ten years he was a servant, and three years in prison, and eighty years he was under the king, ruling all the land of Egypt.
And he died and all his brethren and all that generation.
And he commanded the children of Yashar’el (Israel) before he died that they should carry his bones with them when they went forth from the land of Egypt.

And he made them swear regarding his bones, for he knew that the Egyptians would not again bring forth and bury him in the land of Canaan, for Mâkamârôn, king of Canaan, while dwelling in the land of Assyria, fought in the valley with the king of Egypt and slew him there, and pursued after the Egyptians to the gates of ’Êrmôn. But he was not able to enter, for another, a new king, had become king of Egypt, and he was stronger than he, and he returned to the land of Canaan, and the gates of Egypt were closed, and none went out and none came into Egypt.
And Joseph died in the forty-sixth jubilee, in the sixth week, in the second year, and they buried him in the land of Egypt, and his brethren died after him.

And the king of Egypt went forth to war with the king of Canaan in the forty-seventh jubilee, in the second week in the second year, and the children of Yashar’el (Israel) brought forth all the bones of the children of Jacob save the bones of Joseph, and they buried them in the field in the double cave in the mountain.

And the most (of them) returned to Egypt, but a few of them remained in the mountains of Hebron, and Amram your father remained with them 1. 11. And the king of Canaan was victorious over the king of Egypt, and he closed the gates of Egypt. And he devised an evil device against the children of Yashar’el (Israel) of afflicting them; and he said to the people of Egypt:

“Behold the people of the children of Yashar’el (Israel) have increased and multiplied more than we. Come and let us deal wisely with them before they become too many, and let us afflict them with slavery before war come upon us and before they too fight against us; else they will join themselves to our enemies and get them up out of our land, for their hearts and faces are towards the land of Canaan.”

And he set over them taskmasters to afflict them with slavery; and they built strong 2 cities for Pharaoh, Pithom and Raamses, and they built all the walls and all the fortifications which had fallen in the cities of Egypt.
And they made them serve with rigour, and the more they dealt evilly with them, the more they increased and multiplied.
And the people of Egypt abominated the children of Yashar’el (Israel).

chapters.commentary: The chapter opens with the body’s flourishing. After Jacob died the children of Yashar’el (Israel) multiplied in the land of Egypt, and they became a great nation, and they were of one accord in heart, so that brother loved brother and every man helped his brother, and they increased abundantly and multiplied exceedingly, ten weeks of years, all the days of the life of Joseph. Verse 1. Pause. The covenant body in Egypt, under the favored son’s protection, lived in concord. Brother loved brother, every man helped his brother. The phrase is the chapter’s structural counterweight to what is coming. Verse 2: there was no Satan nor any evil all the days of the life of Joseph which he lived after his father Jacob. The two verses together name what makes a covenant community in exile actually function: the absence of the accuser, the love between brothers, the practical helping. This is what the awakening community is reaching for. Jubilees just named what it looks like when it is happening: brother loving brother, the family helping the family, no accuser walking through the camp. When the awakening remnant lives in this way, the chapter is the witness that it has been done before, and that for the ten weeks of years Joseph lived after Jacob’s death, the covenant body in the foreign land was in concord and was protected. Joseph dies at one hundred and ten. Verse 3 narrates the math: seventeen years he lived in the land of Canaan, and ten years he was a servant, and three years in prison, and eighty years he was under the king, ruling all the land of Egypt. Eighty years of authority. The favored son who was hidden for seventeen ruled the imperial system for eighty. Verse 5: he commanded the children of Yashar’el (Israel) before he died that they should carry his bones with them when they went forth from the land of Egypt. Joseph knows the exodus is coming. He does not know when. He gives instructions for what to do when it comes. The covenant body in exile is supposed to keep the bones of its fathers and to carry them out when the going-out comes. The instruction is preserved for forty-three jubilees. Moses himself will carry the bones of Joseph in Exodus 13:19. The chapter is showing the reader the architecture of intergenerational obedience: the patriarch gives an instruction, the covenant body holds it for centuries, the moment of keeping arrives, the instruction is executed without alteration. Verses 6–7 add a detail Genesis does not. Mâkamârôn, king of Canaan, while dwelling in the land of Assyria, fought in the valley with the king of Egypt and slew him there, and pursued after the Egyptians to the gates of ’Êrmôn. But he was not able to enter, for another, a new king, had become king of Egypt, and he was stronger than he, and he returned to the land of Canaan, and the gates of Egypt were closed. The political shift: a war between Canaan and Egypt at the borders, a new strong king of Egypt, the gates of Egypt now closed. The new king is the new king who knew not Joseph of Exodus 1:8. Jubilees gives the geopolitical context Genesis does not — the covenant body’s shift from welcome to oppression is set against a closed-borders moment in Egyptian-Canaanite relations. The reader who is being told that the Yashar’el (Israel) bondage was a sudden inexplicable cruelty is being shown that Yashar’el (Israel) bondage emerged from a geopolitical realignment in which the new administrator saw the covenant body as a strategic risk. The pattern is structural and recurs: covenant bodies in exile are tolerated under one regime and turned against under the next, and the turning is rarely about the covenant body’s behavior. It is about the new regime’s calculus. Verse 9 records the children of Yashar’el (Israel) bringing forth the bones of the children of Jacob — except Joseph’s — and they buried them in the field in the double cave in the mountain. Jubilees holds the geography. The patriarchs are buried at Hebron. The chapter records that the covenant body in Egypt sent funeral parties to Hebron, in the forty-seventh jubilee, to keep the patriarchal graves in their proper place. The covenant body in exile keeps the geography of the inheritance even when the body itself is not yet living in it. Amram your father remained with them. Verse 10. Moses’ father is one of the ones who stayed in the mountains of Hebron. The chapter is plotting the circuit of the deliverer’s family. The Levite line that will produce Moses is moving between Egypt and Hebron in the long generation before the deliverer is born. Verses 11–16 narrate the oppression. The new king of Egypt, having defeated the king of Canaan, closes the gates and turns inward. Behold the people of the children of Yashar’el (Israel) have increased and multiplied more than we. Come and let us deal wisely with them before they become too many, and let us afflict them with slavery before war come upon us and before they too fight against us; else they will join themselves to our enemies and get them up out of our land, for their hearts and faces are towards the land of Canaan. Verse 13. The new regime fears defection. Jubilees flags it: their hearts and faces are towards the land of Canaan. The covenant body even after generations in Egypt has not lost its directional attachment to the inheritance. The hearts are towards Canaan. The faces are towards Canaan.
